Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effect of climate variability on bee phenology and abundance
Non-Technical Abstract: My five-year research plan is split across five projects. (Projects 1 and 2) Assessing how climate variability affects bee phenology and abundance and the mechanisms involved. We will add to a 10-year dataset that is addressing how climate and flowering patterns directly and indirectly affect the phenology and abundance of bees, and how bee life history traits may buffer them (or make them more susceptible) to changes in climate. This dataset is publicly available online and is well-resolved to the species level, making it an exemplary resource for not only my lab and the RMBL community but also the scientific community at large. (Project 3) Exploring the secondary chemistry of floral rewards and how particular pollen species affect bee disease. There is growing recognition that secondary compounds are not only expressed in foliar tissue, but also floral tissue and nectar and pollen rewards. We are building off a tritrophic effects framework to assess how nectar and pollen diets have indirect effects on bees by mediating host-parasite interactions. (Project 4) Investigating invasive plant biology. We will continue a long-term management project on Linaria vulgaris assessing how various management strategies affect L. vulgaris abundance and spread. (Project 5) Tick distributions in Gunnison County. Ticks are important vectors of disease transmission in humans, domesticated animals, and wildlife. We will continue monitoring tick distributions north of Almont and across an elevation gradient from Almont to Mexican Cut.

Evolutionary Ecology of Floral Color
Non-Technical Abstract: Flower color is central to plant-pollinator interactions, but several outstanding questions remain. How do floral colors vary geographically, i.e. across elevations or between habitats? What are the roles of abiotic agents (e.g. climate) and biotic agents (e.g. pollinators) in shaping floral colors within communities and across gradients? Has climate change shifted the timing or composition of floral colors presented to pollinators? The proposed research will attempt to answer these and other questions by expanding a database of floral spectra from flowering species in the RMBL area (currently at 212 species). This database can be used to estimate both 'raw' and pollinator-relevant measures of color for each plant species, which in turn can be connected to other RMBL datasets and ongoing experiments (e.g. phenology datasets, snowmelt manipulation experiments, and vegetation surveys) to answer the specific questions.

The importance of pollen theft to plant reproductive success.
Non-Technical Abstract: The importance of pollen theft to reproductive success in Polemonium foliosissimum. Over 75% of the flowering plants in temperate regions are pollinated by insects, and the evolution of floral traits has most often been attributed to attracting pollinators. Plants reward their mutualist pollinators primarily with nectar and pollen. Yet, not all insects that utilize nectar and pollen for food are pollinators. Here, I wish to examine how pollen thieves ? small flies in the family Muscidae ? affect reproductive success in the sub-alpine plant, Polemonium foliosissimum (commonly called ?sticky polemonium?). When watching these flies, one can see that they often completely strip the anthers of pollen and they don?t pollinate the plant. In addition to robbing the plant of pollen, they may render plants functionally female (i.e., removing much of their male gametes) and alter sex-ratios for a sticky polemonium which has an unusual mating system whereby some plants are typical hermaphrodites and others don?t produce pollen. Thus, these pollen thieves may have important consequences in enhancing pollen limitation for both females and hermaphrodites, altering sex ratios and, ultimately, affecting the ecology and evolution these plants as well as others.
Research Area: Community ecology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory
Non-Technical Abstract: Water resources from the Colorado River have been dwindling over the past 100 years. We want to develop robust models to predict how water resources will change in the next few decades but need to know how all of the physical processes, from the bedrock through the surface and into the atmosphere, interact in the mountainous watersheds to produce streamflow. The Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) campaign is a targeted effort to measure all of the known physical processes in the atmosphere that determine the water output of these watersheds simultaneously. SAIL will work in conjunction with the Watershed Function SFA which measures all of the known surface and sub-surface physical processes, and together, these efforts will develop a set of benchmarks for predictive models for water across the American West.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate science; Meteorology; Modeling; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Physiological drivers of ecological processes along elevational gradients
Determinants of upper-elevation range limits in cavity-nesting bees
Non-Technical Abstract: In recent decades, rapid warming has altered the environmental conditions experienced by many organisms. One of the most commonly documented biological responses to warming is range shifts, in which populations shift their distributions primarily towards higher latitudes and altitudes to track areas of climatically suitable habitat. Range shifts in bees may be of particular interest. Many aspects of bee life-histories, including their development, survival, and reproduction, are directly linked to temperature; yet bees are also indirectly affected by the availability of other factors such as floral resource abundance and nest-site availability, which may themselves be affected by temperature. I am proposing two field studies that investigate the potential for upslope range shifts in cavity-nesting bees by exploring the variables that determine their upper range limits. In the first study, I ask whether the potential for range shifts in cavity-nesting bees is limited by the lack of nesting cavities at high elevations where trees and dead wood (nesting substrates) may be scarce. In the second study, I ask whether the potential for range shifts in cavity-nesting bees is limited by the short duration of periods of favorable temperatures for offspring development at high-elevations. My proposed fieldwork will combine both observational and experimental techniques to address these questions.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Insect biology; Phenology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Herbivorous Effects on Carbon Cycling
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the carbon cycle is of increasing importance as climate change continues to progress. Current and future warming will complicate this understanding as the carbon cycle continues to adapt to altered conditions. The ultimate fate of soil carbon, where the majority of carbon is stored in terrestrial ecosystems, is of a particular concern. This research will continue the global effort of describing how the carbon cycle may change under altered herbivory levels. Herbivory is an important but often overlooked component of the carbon cycle. The presence or absence of herbivores can alter carbon fluxes between the atmosphere and soil. Herbivores can determine if soils will become a net source or sink for CO2 through interactions with plants and soil microbes and thereby affect our efforts at modeling future climate conditions. This study will investigate the effects of herbivores along an elevational gradient on soil respiration and possible mechanisms by which this may occur. Research undertaken at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory will contribute to a growing network of data collected from mountainous research areas around the world including New Zealand, Tasmania, and Argentina.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Landscape biology; Microbiology; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Forecasting population dynamics in changing environments
Non-Technical Abstract: Effectively responding to rapid global change will require precise, accurate predictions of how ecological systems will respond. However, our current methods for modeling the performance of individuals, populations, and species are optimized to explain observed data rather than to predict future change. We will develop an ecological forecasting platform to predict the near-term population trajectories, using the long-lived plant Valeriana edulis . We will use this platform to (i) determine the forcastability & forecast limits for key metrics of individual and population performance, (ii) hone the forecast skill of models by learning from forecast errors, and (iii) measure the ability of sparse local data to predict landscape-scale patterns in plant performance.
Research Area: Climate change; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Marmot Social Structure
Non-Technical Abstract: Fitness consequences of social group architecture in yellow-bellied marmots. Repeated interactions between individuals form social groups. These groups are complex systems, dynamic in their nature and pattern of interaction. A large body work has explored the consequences of dyadic interactions, and how variation in social interactions alter the makeup and structure of social groups. However, less work has explored the feedback between a social group and the individuals who comprise it. Therefore, I will explore the relationship between social architecture ? the structure and makeup of all social interactions in a social group ? and fitness. I will quantify social architecture using social network analysis and a suite of measures little used in behavioral ecology. These measures describe the connectivity, general sociability, size, reciprocity, centrality, and social homophily of a group. By using a long-studied population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer) this work will provide unique insights into the adaptive value of the social group for individuals and contribute to our understanding of the evolution and maintenance of sociality.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils
Non-Technical Abstract: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils: Development of an integrated soil functional mapping framework. Soils serve critical roles in most terrestrial ecosystems. In particular, the accumulation of soil organic matter is an important function supporting ecosystem productivity and serving as a feedback to climate change. With the more frequent occurrence of extensive and persistent drought conditions in the Western US, there is an urgent need to improve our ability to map soil organic matter and forecast how it may respond. To address this need, we are developing and testing an integrated framework for measurement, mapping, and modeling of soil functions at a regional scale in the East River and surrounding watersheds. This work will result in development of detailed maps of soil properties, a community accessible archive of soil samples, and an integrated framework for modeling changes in soil functions (not limited to soil organic matter storage) across the region.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stream flow phenology and biogeochemistry
Non-Technical Abstract: Effect of advancing stream peak flow hydrology on stream biogeochemistry and primary productivity Climate change is causing streams to reach their peak flows earlier due to advancing snowmelt timing and declining snowpack volume. My ongoing research aims to understand how this advancing flow phenology impacts stream nutrient cycling, primary producers, and grazing invertebrates. By studying seasonal patterns of nutrient uptake and algal accrual in streams that vary in timing of peak flow, I can use a space-for-time substitution to investigate how climate-driven advances in peak flow will alter this foundational ecosystem process and stream food webs.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Variability of aerosol, CCN, and INP in mountainous terrain
Non-Technical Abstract: Particles in the air, called aerosols, are needed for clouds to form and produce both rain and snow. The number of these particles and their ability to form liquid droplets or ice crystals can have large impacts on when and where clouds form and how much precipitation the clouds produce. Therefore, understanding aerosol concentrations and variability is crucial in understanding and modeling their role in Earth?s hydrologic cycle. This is especially true in mountains which are a vital source of water for a large percentage of the globe and which are especially sensitive to changes in precipitation. Complex terrain can also lead to more variable aerosol concentrations, making it harder to understand how these particles will interact with clouds and affect precipitation and how this might change in the future. In this project we will set up a network of aerosol measurements around the RMBL Gothic location to measure the vertical and horizontal variability of aerosol concentrations for more than 1 year to better understand aerosol properties and their variability in this important region.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate change; Climate science; Hydrology; Meteorology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term study of wildflowers
Non-Technical Abstract: Long-term study of flowering abundance and phenology, plant demography, and other intriguing questions about montane species. Abstract This research focuses on understanding variation in timing and abundance of flowering in sub-alpine wildflower communities in the vicinity of RMBL, and the variation in phenology and abundance of the associated bee community. One aim of this work is to elucidate environmental variables that generate this phenological variation. Another goal is to determine the consequences of this variation for plant demography and for animals that interact with the wildflowers. There seem to be effects of climate change on flowering phenology and floral abundance at the species and community level. Side-projects include long-term work on plant demography, root phenology, hummingbird demography, insect abundance and phenology sampled with a Malaise trap, effects of a plant rust on its host, frost effects on flowers, a seed collection, and experimental reduction of deer abundance in the townsite.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Lupine scent
Non-Technical Abstract: Title: Elevation-based variation in Lupinus argenteus floral scent Non-technical abstract: Like color and shape, floral scent helps plants communicate with animals. But attraction via scent is not limited to pollinators, scent can also attract herbivores and, potentially, the natural enemies of these herbivores. Likewise, even while attracting some species, scent can repel others. Thus, floral scent plays many important roles in the ecology and reproductive biology of the plants which produce it. There is enormous variation in floral scent both between and within plant species, and this holds implications for variation in the interactions between individual plants and their environments. However, variation in scent within and among plant species remains poorly understood. Some populations of silvery lupine (Lupinus argenteus) have conspicuously strong scent, while others seem completely scentless. This variation appears to depend on elevation, with populations high in the alpine zone emitting strong scent, and lower montane and sub-alpine populations emitting little if any scent, and populations at intermediate elevations exhibiting a mixture of these traits. In 2017 and 2018 we analyzed lupine scent from one sub-alpine, one alpine, and one intermediate population near RMBL. We found that these populations showed strong differences in scent characteristics, and that, in the intermediate population, some individuals produce more alpine- or subalpine-like scent characteristics. We hope to conduct further studies to try to understand which factors are important for generation this variation, what the significance of this variation is for the plants and the animals that they interact with, and whether and how climate change may affect these plant traits and their impact on their communities.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Insects on Ligusticum
Non-Technical Abstract: Insect abundance and phenology on Ligusticum porteri Plants are targeted by a variety of insect herbivores. These herbivores vary in abundance from place to place and over time. The purpose of this project is to monitor the abundance of insects and other arthropods on the host plant Ligusticum porteri (Porter's lovage). Over the last decade, our weekly counts of insects on focal plants near RMBL have revealed important patterns of insect abundance. Specifically, aphid colonization of host plants depends on snowmelt date. Very few flowering stalks are colonized in early snowmelt years, as a function of host plant drought stress and altered interactions with aphid natural enemies. By continuing to monitor insect abundance at these populations, we will have a unique multi-year dataset of insect abundance. Such datasets can give insights into changing patterns of insect abundance.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Early Snowmelt, Changing Phenology and Drought Exposure for Subalpine Plants
Non-Technical Abstract: Early Snowmelt, Changing Phenology and Increased Drought Exposure: Consequences for Plant Survival and Reproduction of Four Subalpine Plant Species Abstract: Snowmelt is a vital source of spring soil moisture in high elevation plant ecosystems. Climate change is causing a shift to earlier snowmelt timing which can cause changes in flowering phenology and a higher risk of drought for high elevation plant species. Drought stress represents a significant barrier to plant reproduction and can reduce plant floral characteristics and survival. The proposed project will study impacts of climate change-induced early snowmelt on a subalpine plant community at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab in Gothic, Colorado in the summer field season of 2021. I will conduct an early snowmelt manipulation and monitor the physiology, floral characteristics, pollination, and demography of four perennial plant species from May until August. The species are from three genera and represent a gradient of phenological flower timing. I hypothesize that there will be differential effects depending on the timing of flowering of the study species. Earlier flowering species will be less effected by drought stress while later flowering species may have increased exposure to drought stress. The proposed project will produce a multi-species data frame that can be used both in further study of climate impacts and to inform management of high elevation species in the future.
Research Area: Climate change; Phenology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Fungal Priority Effects
Non-Technical Abstract: The Importance of Neighbor-Driven Priority Effects for Structuring Communities of Plant Root-Associated Fungi Priority effects, in which the order of arrival of species shapes the composition of a local species assemblage, can be a prominent mechanism for structuring communities. However, empirical tests have thus far been restricted to simple, species-poor communities. Understanding how priority effects scale with species richness is important for understanding their relevance in the diverse, complex communities that commonly occur in nature. Symbioses provide a tractable system for exploring the dependence of priority effects on species richness. In particular fungal endophytes are ideal since roots of an individual plant can harbor hundreds of species of fungi. In this study, we address the question: What is the relative importance of species richness in modifying the strength of priority effects for fungal community assembly?
Research Area: Community ecology; Microbiomes

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: SPLASH
Non-Technical Abstract: The Study of Precipitation, Lower Atmosphere and Surface for Hydrometeorology (SPLASH) is a study proposed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to study environmental parameters connected to weather and water over mountainous terrain. As part of this effort, we will make measurements of atmospheric properties like temperature, winds, humidity, precipitation, clouds and turbulence as well as surface properties, like snow cover, soil moisture, snow reflectivity and more. Together, these observations are meant to inform the development and evaluation of modeling tools used by the National Weather Service and other entities to provide predictions over mountainous areas. The SPLASH campaign is envisioned to take place between fall 2021 and summer 2022.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate change; Climate science; Hydrology; Long-term research; Meteorology; Modeling; Snow Science; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Modeling the seasonal abundance and population dynamics of solitary bees
Non-Technical Abstract: To predict the number of individuals of a species that are active on a landscape, it is important to understand how species? abundances change throughout a season ? we call this the phenological abundance curve. The shape of solitary bees? phenological curves are unknown, which often limits the scope of our studies to the community level. This makes it challenging to determine how factors such as climate change are affecting bee emergence phenology. This gap in knowledge is due to limits in how frequently we can sample bee destructively without affecting the very populations that we want to study. To address this gap, I will gather fine-scale time-series data on the abundance of three native, solitary bee species that are found around the RMBL. By marking bees of these species that can be identified in the field with a non-toxic paint, I will be able to overcome the challenge of measuring their populations without affecting them. I will then use these data to develop a mechanistic model to describe how emergence and mortality rates interact to shape bees? seasonal abundances. Further, I will measure how bees? foraging decisions and habitat preferences vary across space in order to more accurately estimate bee abundance. This work will allow us to examine the population dynamics and phenological responses to climate change of bee species beyond the three that are the focus of this study.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Modeling; Phenology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: QUANTITATIVE NESTEDNESS; SNOWMELT ACCELERATION AND POLLINATION NETWORKS
Non-Technical Abstract: QUANTITATIVE NETWORK STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; SNOWMELT ACCELERATION AND POLLINATION NETWORK STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION This renewal research application covers two distinct but related projects, both of them focused on pollination networks, their responses to perturbation, and the relationship between structure and function. The first project was approved by the RMBL research committee in my 2016 application, and the second project was approved as an extension in 2017. Both of these projects are collaborative efforts between PI Brosi and his graduate students Xingwen Loy and Connor Morozumi. The first project, ?Quantitative Network Structure and Function? is currently funded by NSF and has two primary objectives: A) accurately measuring of quantitative network structure (i.e. intensity of interactions) with a focus on testing predictions about quantitative structure from theoretical work we are leading; and B) comparing network structure and function (seed production across multiple plant species) in drought (2018) vs. non-drought years (2016, 2017, and 2019 hopefully!). The second project, ?Snowmelt Acceleration and Pollination Network Structure and Function?, is focused on temporally shuffling interaction partners in pollination networks via medium-scale (10 x 14 m) snowmelt acceleration experiments that are controlled and spatially replicated. The temporal re-shuffling occurs via changes in plant flowering phenology in manipulated patches, whereas we expect the pollinator community to remain relatively unchanged given that the scale of movement of individual pollinators is typically much larger than the spatial scale of our plots.
Research Area: Community ecology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Flax Rust Project: The effects of climate change on plant pathogens
Non-Technical Abstract: The Flax Rust Project: Effects of climate change on the evolution and epidemiology of plant pathogens The potential for climate change to exacerbate the burden of human infectious diseases has been increasingly recognized, but less attention has been given to the effects of climate change on infectious diseases of plants. Plant pathogens are critical components of natural ecosystems, but also pose a serious threat to agricultural production and food security. Since the summer of 2018, the Flax Rust Project has used a wildflower native to the Rocky Mountains (Linum lewisii) and its fungal pathogen (Melampsora lini) to study how climate change might affect the ways in which infectious diseases of plants spread and evolve. The natural gradient of temperature and humidity that occurs down the slope of the mountains on which this study system occurs provides a good approximation for climate change. Previous work in the system has focused on the effects of climate change on the dynamics of the flax rust disease at within-host scales, and how such effects might modulate the population-level spread of disease. In this project plan, I detail plans for future work aimed at 1) building a long-term epidemiological data set to link climate change to disease dynamics, 2) identifying factors facilitating or limiting the spread of flax rust at the landscape scale, 3) investigating how plant immunological factors might modulate pathogen epidemiology, and 4) predicting how climate change might drive the evolution of plant pathogen aggressiveness and specificity.
Research Area: Climate change; Disease ecology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Heritability in Female Yellow-bellied Marmot Dispersal
Non-Technical Abstract: Heritability in Female Yellow-bellied Marmot Dispersal Dispersal is the permanent movement of individuals from their natal home range to a location for reproduction. Dispersal is a key component in maintaining genetic variation and is viewed as an adaptive decision; however, the decision rules influencing dispersal may no longer be optimal in rapidly changing environments. Climate change creates mismatches between species? life history traits, decision rules, and the environment, and this gap may be enhanced in species whose habitats are especially sensitive to rapid changing climate. At least two processes can permit adaptive responses in a changing environment: phenotypic plasticity and/or possessing sufficient additive genetic variation to permit the evolution of a new optimal response. While a lot is known about the environmental drivers of dispersal, relatively less is known about the heritability of dispersal. Therefore, I propose to use the quantitative genetic ?animal model? to estimate the heritability of female natal dispersal in a population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer). I will use archival data and collect new data to answer this question. Starting mid-April and through early September 2021, I will substantially expand the dispersal database by studying the fate of 59 females born in 2020. Previous studies of yellow-bellied marmot dispersal investigated known social, environmental and body condition factors that may explain variation. By decomposing sources of variation with the animal model, I will estimate the relative effect size of these variables and directly estimate the additive genetic variation for dispersal tendency.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Genetics; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How the Floral Nutrient Landscape Influences Plant-Pollinator Interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: The Interconnecting Threads in the Web of Life: How the Floral Nutrient Landscape Influences Plant-Pollinator Interactions Abstract: Wild bumble bees are critical pollinators in both natural and agricultural ecosystems, particularly in temperate and alpine environments. They rely exclusively on food provided by plants in the form of pollen and nectar. The populations of many wild bee species, including wild bumble bees, are declining. Global pollinator declines are attributed in part to nutritional stress caused by reduced floral food diversity and abundance. Yet, we know little about most wild bumble bee species' dietary requirements and preferences despite their ecological importance. To date, a complete nutrient landscape for wild bumble bees (the nutritional composition of pollen and nectar of flowering plants in a community) has never been quantified under natural conditions. Additionally, we do not yet know how nutrients in pollen and nectar influence bumble bees' dietary choices and how nutrients influence plant-pollinator interactions. To address these knowledge gaps, my research builds on an ongoing long-term study of bumble bee foraging interactions at the RMBL by conducting (i) multiple years of bee-flower interaction observations; (ii) protein, lipid, and carbohydrate analysis of pollen and the quantification of sugar content in nectar collected from bumble bee-visited plants; and (iii) using these nutrient data to explore webs of interactions among plants and pollinators. By incorporating nutrition into the study of pollination, my research will contribute to our understanding of the basic biology of local plants and bumble bees, how the availability of nutrients for bumble bees changes over time, and how nutrients in pollen and nectar influence plant-pollinator interactions.
Research Area: Insect biology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Behavioral Ecology of Burying Beetles
Non-Technical Abstract: Behavior and Ecology of Burying Beetles and their Small Mammal resource. Studies of the impacts of human recreation on wildlife. I have a long-term research project on the behaviors and population dynamics of the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator and their required reproductive resource of small mammal carcasses. These studies increase our understanding of reproductive behaviors, including parental care and communication and the factors that influence population dynamics, species interactions, and ecosystem function. The long-term data is being shared with other RMBL scientists to understand the role of environmental variables on species and population dynamics. A new research study proposes to determine the effects of human recreation on wildlife activity on the trails near RMBL. The results of these projects are used in management decisions and for science education resources for K-12 and college-level students. I use a variety of research techniques including behavioral observations, population censuses, molecular genetic techniques, GIS models, and isotopic and chemical analyses to study trophic interactions and nutrient cycling.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: River food web phenology
Non-Technical Abstract: Food web phenology in a changing climate: a trophic dynamics and bioenergetics approach Warming temperatures associated with global climate change are altering the phenology, or timing, of species life history events worldwide. Differential responses among interacting species have the potential to alter the structure and function of biological communities and ecosystems. Understanding how emerging phenological asynchrony among species scales from population responses to higher level ecological dynamics is a priority question in global change research. This project seeks to understand how changing patterns of summer river temperatures, from warming air temperatures and reduced mountain snowpack, alter the phenology of riverine food webs. Riverine organisms are presently understudied from a phenological change perspective but may be particularly susceptible to warming temperatures due to their life history characteristics. We will measure the timing of peak biomass, productivity and energy demand (of trout) across multiple trophic levels (algae, aquatic invertebrates, trout) over multiple years in the East River at Gothic, CO, as well as several other nearby rivers in a space-for-time approach, to assess the effects of warming water temperatures on patterns of phenological synchrony in riverine food webs. The basic premise of this study is that warming will not affect the phenology of algal populations (light controlled), the main source of stream primary production, but will advance aquatic insect emergence (season biomass loss from the stream) and peak insect productivity, resulting in a mismatch between trout energetic demand and their main prey source.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Food web biology; Phenology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Modeling the Breakdown of a Polyphenic Population
Non-Technical Abstract: Modeling the Breakdown of a Polyphenic Population Through Field Sampling and Individual-based Modeling The goal of this research is to investigate the stability of the polyphenism in the population of Arizona tiger salamander (Ambystoma mavortium nebulosum) at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve (MCNP) and the Kettle Ponds near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). Specifically, I will quantify the strength of phenotype-environment mismatch necessary to produce phenotypes without developmental plasticity (i.e., a generalist, fixed phenotype) that have a selective advantage over polyphenic individuals. I will approach this goal with two specific methodologies, one short-term and one long-term. My short-term goal is to conduct field sampling during summer 2021 to assess the effect of fairy shrimp (Branchinecta coloradensis) density on metamorph salamander fitness. The results of the first project will directly inform my second, long-term goal of using quantitative modeling to forecast future population dynamics under various climate change scenarios.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Species Interactions; Theory; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Controls on Denitrification and Nitrous Oxide Release from Shale Bedrock
Non-Technical Abstract: The chemical transformations and transport that control nitrogen remains uncharacterized in shale bedrock. Shales may act as a potential hotspot for denitrification due to an abundance of electron donors such as organic matter and sulfide minerals; however, there is uncertainty in the denitrification process in shales. A mechanistic understanding of shale denitrification, which produces gaseous N2 and N2O, is vital to (1) characterizing the global nitrogen budget; and (2) predicting greenhouse gas fluxes from bedrock and their response to environmental change To address this critical knowledge gap, we propose to study the conditions that control and promote N2 and N2O production within the Mancos shale in the East River watershed, CO through combined field monitoring of subsurface environments and laboratory incubation experiments. In this study, we will specifically seek to characterize the magnitude of denitrification rates from the Mancos shale in response to chemical amendments across the watershed and how it varies in response to changes in moisture conditions, oxygen concentrations, and mineralogical availability of electron donors. Our results will quantify denitrification rates and greenhouse gas fluxes from shale bedrock environments. In addition, to providing fundamental insights into a relatively uninterrogated process and its potential effects on shales.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The effects of global climate change on subalpine mutualisms
Non-Technical Abstract: Bottom-up effects of mutualism breakdown among subalpine legumes and N-fixing bacteria on the specialist solitary bee Osmia iridis Climate change affects species and their interactions, resulting in novel communities and modified ecosystem processes. Climatic change can disrupt interspecific interactions, including those between mutualists. Mutualistic interactions profoundly influence the structure and stability of ecological communities and can link species to a common fate. However, research on climate change-driven effects has largely focused on pairwise mutualisms, neglecting the higher-order interactions that can arise when species interact with multiple mutualists. In this project, I aim to explore the effects of climate change on tripartite interactions involving belowground mutualists (N-fixing bacteria), legume plants, and their specialist pollinators. Warming temperatures, advanced snowmelt, and drought are likely to cause a breakdown in the mutualism between N-fixing bacteria and legumes, leading to changes in the strength of the mutualism between plants and their pollinators. Climate-induced shifts in legume flowering phenology and decreases in legume floral functional trait quality caused by this breakdown are potentially increasing foraging time and energy demands for bees and altering their floral preferences. Such costs could translate to reduced fitness and novel selection pressures for both bees and flowering plants in the short-term.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Microbiology; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Abiotic and biotic controls on chemical weathering rates and solute generation
Non-Technical Abstract: Abiotic and biotic controls on chemical weathering rates and solute generation Precipitation is subject to a variety of bio-physical transformations before leaving watersheds as streamflow. One key transformation is chemical weathering, which is driven by interactions among rock, water, and biota. Globally, mountain watersheds are hotspots for solute generation, but our process-level understanding regarding the mechanisms and drivers of chemical weathering in steep, high elevation landscapes is incomplete. By employing a multi-scale approach, the project aims to address the following questions in the Rocky Mountains at the East River community watershed: 1) Does landscape-scale heterogeneity in vegetation, climate, and geology impart unique, spatially-variable signatures on soil production and chemical weathering rates? 2) What roles do the legacies of Pleistocene glaciation and Holocene geomorphic processes play in determining modern-day solute concentrations in surface waters? 3) Are physical erosion and chemical weathering rates linked at the watershed scale, and can these rates be predicted from watershed characteristics? At the soil profile scale, soil production and chemical weathering rates will be quantified with cosmogenic nuclides, specifically in situ-produced and meteoric 10Be, and geochemical mass balance at sites that span biotic, climatic, and geologic gradients in order to isolate the key drivers of chemical weathering. At the landform scale, solute concentrations in surface waters will be used to assess whether surficial deposits generated by different geomorphic processes impart unique weathering signatures. At the watershed-scale, 10Be will be used to measure erosion rates. A series of reactive transport models will be constructed to place the field-based findings into a framework for making predictions regarding the roles that vegetation, climate, and geomorphology play in solute generation.
Research Area: Climate science; Geology; Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Using a turf transplant experiment to study plant functional traits
Non-Technical Abstract: Long Title of Project: Assessing plant functional traits and community response to climate change in the Rocky Mountains using a turf transplant experiment Non-technical Abstract: The goal of this study is to learn how plant water relation traits will respond to a warming environment and to continue studying changes in community composition. The turf transplant experiment was established in 2017 by Lorah Seltzer in order to recreate the conditions of a warming, drying climate by transplanting small pieces of turfs from low to high elevations, and vice-versa. We will continue to measure a variety of plant and community characteristics, as well as plant water relations traits, to assess changes to plant functioning and composition to a drying and warming environment.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Microbial facilitation of floral exploitation
Non-Technical Abstract: Microbial facilitation of floral exploitation in a subalpine pollination mutualism This summer, I will explore the ecological interactions between plants, flower-visiting insects, and the microbes that inhabit flowers. Recently, nectar-inhabiting microbes, including yeasts and bacteria, have been identified as potentially significant mediators of plant-insect interactions. However, the chemical cues produced by nectar microbes and the effects they have on insect foraging behaviors and plant reproduction remain unclear. In subalpine meadows at the Rocky Mountain Biological Research Station (RMBL, Elk Mountains, Colorado) I will examine interactions between a threatened wildflower (Corydalis caseana ssp. Brandegeei; Brandegee?s fumewort), nectar microbial communities, and bumblebee floral visitors.
Research Area: Community ecology; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Microbiology; Plant biology; Pollination; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating the nuanced consequences of pollinator declines for plants
Non-Technical Abstract: Investigating the nuanced consequences of pollinator declines for plants: Studying the effects of pollinator declines to floral longevity and seed production Climate change is driving pollinator declines. 87% of flowering plants depend on animal pollinators and need to invest energy in flowers to reproduce. Plants are found to produce more seeds when receiving more pollen, and plant size tends to affect flower and seed production. However, it remains unknown how plants will respond to decreased pollination services. Plants may manage resources either to avoid over investment in flowers that may go unpollinated or to produce more flowers to possibly compensate for decreased pollination. changes in pollination services, flower production, seed production, and plant size will be linked using generalized linear mixed effects models and generalized linear models. This project will inform how changes in pollination affect resource allocation to reproductive effort and why (e.g., via changes to floral production or longevity). Linking flower production and longevity with reproductive output will inform how changing pollination services affect plant reproduction and whether adjustments in reproductive effort can compensate for reduced pollination services. Taken together, this experiment will have the potential to inform future conservation efforts for plant populations as we continue to experience pollinator declines.
Research Area: Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Vegetation's influence on mountain watershed function
Non-Technical Abstract: Vegetation's influence on mountain watershed function: Mountain systems provide refuge to species, and people, which has led an abundance of plant species in and unique to mountain regions. They are also essential for the well-being of people in and beyond the mountains via the water stored as snow, especially regions such as the U.S Southwest where rainfall and glacial meltwater inputs are low or less reliable. Our research is a component of the U.S. DOE's community watershed research and aims to understand how the essential role of plants in species-rich mountain region influence the function of a mountain watershed. To that end, we are using models from hillslopes to watersheds to identify what characteristics of vegetation influence water supply and biogeochemical cycling. Through co-design, this information will inform field collection of data to improve the parameterization of the models, which in turn can further refine our approaches for sampling the diversity of life zones and topographies across the mountain watersheds in the Crested Butte area. The aim of all this work is to improve prediction seasonally and annually of water availability in the rivers through which snowmelt and groundwater-derived from snow provide water to communities across the west.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Examining warming induced shifts in tundra soil microbial function
Non-Technical Abstract: Atmospheric warming is disproportionate across the Earth's surface and tundra ecosystems are experiencing a faster rate of temperature increase than other parts of the globe. These environments store a significant amount of carbon that, under climatic change, has the potential to be released into the atmosphere, positively feeding back to global temperature rise. Soil microbes regulate ecosystem processes that determine the soil carbon response and therefore, understanding how warming and warming-related changes affect the soil microbial community can improve predictions of ecosystem functions and services under climatic change. This project will analyze microbial processes in control and experimental plots at RMBL by taking advantage of preexisting experiment infrastructure established by the WARM project. The independent and combined treatments of warming and changing plant composition in WARM will allow us to examine the direct and indirect effects of warming on soil microbial function.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Microbiology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Life history tradeoffs of high elevation breeding sparrows
Non-Technical Abstract: This study is a long-term investigation into the life histories (e.g., reproduction, behavioral ecology, age, sex) of mountain white-crowned sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha; MWCS) and Lincoln?s sparrows (Melospiza lincolnii; LISP). Lincoln?s sparrows are being included to supplement reproductive data given their highly similar nesting ecology to the MWCS. This study aims to elucidate the extent and the nature of life-history tradeoffs associated with endoparasite loads, elevation-based weather and climate patterns, habitat quality, and landscape context. Reproductive metrics of interest include nest success, clutch size, and number of young fledged. We are also interested in gaining insight of the breeding behaviors of MWCS, including nestling provisioning rates and incubation on-off bouts. This will be tested observationally using field sites at different elevations and of varying habitat structure. Methodologies include bird capture, measuring and banding as well as nest searching and monitoring and video camera recording during the nestling stage.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Disease ecology; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: FUNGAL HOST SPECIFICITY AND FITNESS IN THE CORALLORHIZA MACULATA COMPLEX
Non-Technical Abstract: PHYLOGEOGRAPHY, FUNGAL HOST SPECIFICITY, AND FITNESS IN THE CORALLORHIZA MACULATA SPECIES COMPLEX Orchids are one of the most diverse plant families with over 25,000 species spread across the world. Out of the total, approximately 200 species have reduced capacity or longer photosynthesize and instead steal nutrients from fungi, like the coralroot orchids ( Corallorhiza maculata complex). This parasitic relationship may limit how many plants we can see in each forest. Due to their rarity, these orchids may be lost due to climate change, deforestation, and herbicide use. To conserve these rare species for future generations, DNA sequencing allows for the identification of what fungi these orchids are using, how these orchids vary across the United States, and how different fungi may improve plant fitness.
Research Area: Genetics; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Understanding Watershed Processes in Complex Terrain: Snodgrass Hydrology
Non-Technical Abstract: Much of the world's water supply comes from complex, inaccessible mountainous regions both hard to measure and monitor. The impacts of heterogeneous environmental conditions and the partitioning of water in these locations are poorly understand and an important factor in determining the effects of climate change on these systems. The project's aim is to collect a combination of stream flows, hand-collected measurements and tower-based weather data over several years on an example hillslope in the East River watershed. The data will be fed into a computer model to determine key parameters and the importance of modeling different landscape characteristics. The results should influence what data is needed to be collected to get an accurate portrayal of water fluxes and stores in these regions.
Research Area: Hydrology; Long-term research; Modeling; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Aquatic invertebrate adaptations in subalpine ephemeral ponds
Non-Technical Abstract: Climate change is warming higher elevation areas more quickly than lower elevation areas, causing species to move up as the habitat becomes more hospitable. Some species known mostly from northern North America (i.e. Canada) extend their home ranges southward into higher elevation areas (i.e. the Rocky Mountains or Sierra Nevada Range) where the climate is similar to areas further north. As these high elevation areas warm, they may become unsuitable for the species who used them as the edge of their ranges, causing those species to become locally extinct. Helophorus electus and Helophorus parasplendidus sperryi are two species of aquatic beetle found at the Mexican Cut Preserve, a subalpine habitat with numerous ponds. Aside from a couple records from the early 1900s housed in insect collections, there are very few records of these species in the U.S. (they are mostly known from Canada). These taxa could be those that become locally extinct with climate change. Previously, aquatic insect research at Mexican Cut has mainly focused on caddisfly populations, overlooking the beetle taxa. My research goal is to better understand what habitats Helophorus use, their role in the ephemeral pond community, and how climate change might affect species distribution (e.g. create more habitat as ponds become more ephemeral, benefiting the beetles; cause more competition as they share the remaining habitat with other species, a drawback for the beetles).
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Community ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Drivers of pollinator niche variation
Non-Technical Abstract: In this project, I propose to examine how interactions between plants and their insect pollinators vary among individuals and populations of pollinators. I will examine the variety of flowers visited by individual pollinators that belong to multiple species and see if temperature affects these patterns of floral visitation. I will use the pollen on these insects' bodies as a record of these individuals' floral visitation events. I will also examine how genetic similarity and body size measurements affect these patterns of floral visitation and pollen collection in a group of important pollinators -- bumble bees. Finally, I will predict how these patterns of plant-pollinator interaction influence the likelihood of species loss in communities experiencing disturbance events like increased temperatures.
Research Area: Climate change; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Floral volitile ecology of Lupinus argenteus
Non-Technical Abstract: Like color and shape, floral scent helps plants communicate with animals. But attraction via scent is not limited to pollinators, scent can also attract herbivores and, potentially, the natural enemies of these herbivores. Likewise, even while attracting some species, scent can repel others. Thus, floral scent plays many important roles in the ecology and reproductive biology of the plants which produce it. There is enormous variation in floral scent both between and within plant species, and this holds implications for variation in the interactions between individual plants and their environments. However, variation in scent within and among plant species remains poorly understood. Some populations of silvery lupine (Lupinus argenteus) have conspicuously strong scent, while others seem completely scentless. This variation appears to depend on elevation, with populations high in the alpine zone emitting strong scent, and lower montane and sub-alpine populations emitting little if any scent, and populations at intermediate elevations exhibiting a mixture of these traits. In 2017 and 2018 we analyzed lupine scent from one sub-alpine, one alpine, and one intermediate population near RMBL. We found that these populations showed strong differences in scent characteristics, and that, in the intermediate population, some individuals produce more alpine- or subalpine-like scent characteristics. We hope to conduct further studies to try to understand which factors are important for generation this variation, what the significance of this variation is for the plants and the animals that they interact with, and whether and how climate change may affect these plant traits and their impact on their communities.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Topographic controls on transpiration in the East River watershed
Non-Technical Abstract: Transpiration is the upwards flow of water from soil to atmosphere by vegetation. This flux of water is a critical component of the photosynthetic process and an important control on the energy balance of leaves. The spatial and temporal patterns in transpiration have a dominant control of the hydrological balance of watersheds because the use of this water by plants effects how much water delivered by snow or rain remains available downstream for streamflow or groundwater recharge. While transpiration has been an obvious source of interest to ecologists and hydrologists for decades, continuous and distributed measurements of transpiration in alpine systems remain limited. The lack of observed information on transpiration has made it difficult to develop models to predict how and why transpiration varies between species, across hillslopes or in response to climate drivers such as drought. We will use a technique called sap flow to make continuous measurements of transpiration for lodgepole pine, Engelmann spruce, subalpine fir and quaking aspen across topographic gradients in the East River watershed. We will use this data to test how differences in factors such as slope, relief, lithology and upslope drainage influences the water demands between species. We will also test how these abiotic factors interact with biotic factors such as the effective rooting depth and conductivity of xylem tissues to modulate transpiration. We will complement the measurements of transpiration with periodic measurements of the stable isotope ratios of xylem and soil water to help understand the sources of water (such as snow melt vs. summer rain) as well as the soil depth trees are drawing water from. The detailed measurements of transpiration from sap flow will be complemented by a more experimental approach based on continuous measurements of the diameter of trees ? i.e. dendrometry. Changes in the daily cycle of tree circumference is related to storage of water in trees and can therefore be related to total water use. This technique has the advantage of using lower cost and more robust sensors but is less reliable. The work collectively will shed light on how trees compete for available water, particularly at the interface between aspen and conifer stands. This data will be collected synergistically with measurements of canopy temperature from drone flights which can provide spatial information on water use that complements the tree-level temporally continuous data from sap flow. In addition, this data will be used for model validation of a recently developed land surface model. The information gathered on transpiration will also be broadly applicable to understanding the resilience of typical fir, pine, spruce and aspen ecosystems in the western US to climate change.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Hydrology; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Boechera stricta microbiome evolution II
Non-Technical Abstract: The microbes living on and inside plant organs (the microbiome) can greatly impact the health and growth of the host plant. However, despite recent research into the processes and mechanisms behind these relationships, there is still much to learn about how they evolved. This proposal outlines a plan to study the evolution of plant-microbiome interactions using the wild perennial mustard Boechera stricta as a model system. The project will (1) collect longitudinal data on the microbiome composition of plants from wild B. stricta populations along an elevational transect in Gothic Valley over multiple years, (2) isolate bacteria and fungi from roots of the same plants to create a collection of native strains for use in future experiments, and (3) collect soil samples from nearby existing common garden experiments for use as inocula in future experiments. This work will provide preliminary data and resources for future studies and help build a research program focused on the evolution of B. stricta and its microbes in the context of climate change and water stress.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Microbiomes; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Individual variation in predictability, its evolutionary consequences.
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the processes underlying biodiversity is a real challenge, especially with the major biological crisis we are facing. To comprehend how and why living beings diversify, studying phenotypic variation among individuals is essential. Two levels of variation are mainly used to assess differences between individuals: variation in mean and in plasticity. Another component of variation has received limited attention: predictability. Such variation provides information on how predictable an individual is in expressing a trait. It was long considered to be homogeneous across individuals of a species and without biological interest. Nevertheless, variation has been measured and its evolutionary implication has been shown, mainly in livestock. Therefore, it is crucial to extend predictability studies to free-living animal and integrate this component into evolutionary research. Through the long-term data set on yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer) and advanced analytic tools, I plan to assess the implication of predictability in evolutionary processes. I believe that being predictable or not may be part of adaptive strategies and under natural selection. Hence, it should be considered to get a more complete knowledge of evolutionary mechanisms. In a context where human pressure on wildlife is constantly increasing, it would help biologists to predict more accurately population size variations and adaptive dynamics of species.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Bumble bee thermal tolerance, climate variation, and population trends
Non-Technical Abstract: Where species live and when they are active is determined by their ability to cope with environmental conditions, including temperature. Individual animals may differ in their ability to cope with extreme hot and cold temperatures, and some of these differences may be because of their body size and life stage. With rising global temperatures with climate change, understanding how and why animals vary in their ability to cope with extreme temperatures may help us predict which species are most vulnerable. For bumble bees, rising global temperatures are believed to contributed to population declines. However, we do not currently know how individual variation in bumble bee?s ability to cope with extreme temperatures relates to population declines. This is especially concerning because bumble bees are important pollinators of both crops and wild plants. My research proposes to help fill this knowledge gap and help better predict the futures of bumble bee species under climate change.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Microbial Genomics Analysis of the Mt. Emmons Acidic, Metal-Impacted Fen
Non-Technical Abstract: The Mt. Emmons Fen is a unique acidic, naturally metal-impacted wetland system in the Crested Butte area. Sensitive to environmental changes, the Fen provides opportunity to examine how microorganisms, such as the bacteria, can be used as early sentinels of disturbance. Vulnerable to mining impacts, climate change, and hydrological aging, bacterial species and genomic diversities can provide timely information about ecosystem parameters and predict shifts in ecosystem functioning, e.g., carbon sequestration/degradation, elemental cycling, tolerance to metal toxicity. This work continues to build our understanding of the background microbial ecology of the Mt. Emmons Fen in an effort to protect this rare ecosystem.
Research Area: Microbiology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Global change and the functional ecology of grasses
Non-Technical Abstract: Grasses are one of the most ecologically and economically important plant families. As climate changes, the composition of grassland communities can change and the ecological strategies employed by the resident species can shift. Understanding these responses is critical for predicting the responses of grasslands to climate change. These responses will then feed back to climate change, influence agricultural productivity and change ecosystem processes such as fire dynamics. This study is part of a larger project examining how grass species change their ecological strategies as conditions change. We do this through the lens of functional traits - measurable traits of individuals that affect their fitness in a particular environment. Our work at RMBL fits into a larger picture we are developing of grass trait patterns across the western US and globally.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Socially-driven fitness consequences of environmental variation
Non-Technical Abstract: In recent years, anthropogenically-driven climate change has significantly altered environmental conditions. These changes have caused changes in the traits of many organisms, including social behavior; this is important because social behavior impacts an individual?s ability to survive and reproduce. While other work has studied how environmental variation impacts social aspects like mating and group organization, a neglected area is how environmental variation impacts the strength and quantity of an individual?s relationships. This can be studied by analyzing an individual?s position in their social network and the social structure of their group. Therefore, I will use social network analysis to explore the relationships between environmental variation, social structure, and individual fitness. By using a long-studied populations of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer) at RMBL, this work will provide insights into social selection pressure as climate change continues and will contribute to our ability to understand and predict the impacts of climate change on social species.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Long-term research; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Scoping for Development of a Biogeochemical Study in East River
Non-Technical Abstract: The study is an initial exploration and scoping effort that will lead to development of a research proposal. It is envisioned that a future study will focus on quantifying and predicting how the changing magnitude and timing of snowmelt effects the rates and timing of chemical reactions driving the carbon cycle and downstream delivery of organic matter and nutrients. Through this work, new understanding will be gained about the role of mountain headwaters in the river continuum. Undergraduate and graduate students will be trained through in aspects of hydrology, biogeochemistry, ecosystem ecology, numerical modeling, and water resource management.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Atmospheric Science; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Geology; Hydrology; Landscape biology; Microbiology; Modeling; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effects of microclimate heterogeneity on plant-pollinator interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: Among factors hypothesized to play a role in maintaining insect pollinator diversity, small-scale environmental heterogeneity may be particularly important, but has been relatively little-studied. To fill this gap, we propose to compare plant, pollinator, and plant-pollinator interaction composition among transects that represent high and low levels of microclimate diversity, making use of five microclimate study sites established by Dr. Ian Breckheimer in the Upper Gunnison Watershed. Sampling will occur weekly during the growing seasons of 2023 and 2024. Data will be used to model how pollinator and plant-pollinator interaction diversity/composition metrics vary as a function of floral resource and microclimate diversity/composition metrics.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How does bee body size impact pollination efficacy in subalpine meadows?
Non-Technical Abstract: Future warming conditions in the Colorado Rocky mountains has the potential to impact the density and composition of wildflowers, with indirect effects on the bees that pollinate them and rely on them for food. As part of a larger project testing for possible effects of warm and cold conditions on body size of solitary bees collected from RMBL over several years, in the field I will test how body size variation within bee species affects their ability to pollinate wildflowers. To do this, I will bag flowers of the target plant species pre-opening, capture females of the target bee species with a net and chill to immobilise so I can measure it's body width under the microscope and confirm species identity. I will then allow the bee to warm up once placed in a field cage with the bagged flower and 2-3 other flowers of the same species. I will allow the bee to visit 3 flowers before removing the bag from the target flower. Once the bee has visited it, I will take the stigma to count deposited pollen grains. I will compare pollen counts to body size of each test bee.
Research Area: Insect biology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The relationship between temporal & functional traits in plant communities
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants vary in their flowering time, ranging from early flowering species that mark the start of spring, to colourful blooms at the height of summer. But with recent climate change, we are seeing advances in the timing of these life history events or phenologies, particularly in temperate and alpine plant communities. The timing of phenological events within a growing season determine the environment a plant experiences, their access to pollinators, as well as the intensity of competition for resources. Despite its ecological importance, few studies have addressed the relationships between phenology and species growth strategies, but there has been considerable work associating other leaf and floral traits to such characteristics and environmental conditions. Without knowing the relationship of phenology in species overall trait profiles, it is difficult to predict the effects of phenological shifts on individual plants and their communities. In this study, we will test whether differences in the timing of phenological events of flowering plants follow similar trends in growth strategies as seen for other commonly measured leaf and floral traits. We predict that species with traits we associate with faster growth rates will favour earlier flowering, while species that exhibit slower growth strategies, but more tolerance for competition, will flower later in the growing season. This work will further our understanding of the role of phenology within broader trait syndromes and allow us to better predict the possible effects of continued phenological shifts on plant community dynamics.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Assessing corticosterone and Bd infection in Ambystoma mavortium nebulosum
Non-Technical Abstract: Amphibian biodiversity has greatly diminished in recent years due to disease. Panzootic pathogenic fungi Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) causes the deadly disease chytridiomycosis (chytrid), a primary driver of catastrophic global amphibian declines and extinctions. The pathogenesis of chytrid is still unclear, as certain species and individuals within a species are differentially affected. Susceptibility and mortality of Bd are influenced by prolonged chronic stress. Prolonged glucocorticoid activity deleteriously affects many of the same physiological processes as Bd infections, and corticosterone is the primary glucocorticoid released by amphibians in response to stress. Thus, the objective of our study is to assess the relationship of corticosterone variation and Bd spore load in Arizona tiger salamanders (ATS; Ambystoma mavortium nebulosum). We used a non-invasive skin swabbing method to collect baseline corticosterone from paedomorph (aquatic morph; N = 13), metamorph (terrestrial morph; N = 31), and larval (immature; N = 6) ATS in June and July 2022. Baseline samples were collected within three minutes of capture. Bd samples were then collected via skin swabbing, and biometrics for individual animals measured. Additional samples will be collected in summer of 2023, and will allow us to consider corticosterone and Bd spore load variation by morph, sex, location, and body condition. Our study will provide a greater understanding of the pathogenesis of Bd and the interacting effects of glucocorticoid production and polyphenic life history on disease resistance. My results will develop the use of corticosterone as a predictor of Bd susceptibility and severity of infection.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Disease ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Ecohydrologic Controls of Sub-Alpine Forest Soil Respiration
Non-Technical Abstract: NON-TECHNICAL ABSTRACT: Mountainous ecosystems are currently experiencing a lot of change in their water inputs. With the dominant water source, snowpack, decreasing and melting earlier. This change in the primary water source not only influences the aboveground functioning of the ecosystem, but also the belowground part as well. The belowground ecosystem is comprised of microbes that breakdown organic matter and plant roots that are growing to access crucial nutrients and water. Both the microbes and roots respire CO2 when they are conducting these functions in the belowground ecosystem. Our research aims to understand how changes in moisture inputs, such as changes in snow depth and monsoon rains influences these belowground ecosystem up an elevation gradient in the East River Watershed, near Crested Butte Colorado. We will quantify the CO2 produced by both the microbes and the roots up the elevational gradient and see how each respond to environmental changes within and between years. To do this, we will combine continuous soil CO2 measurements, spatially distributed soil surface CO2 measurements and radiocarbon methods which will enable us to separate the plant and microbial sources of the CO2. These methods will allow us to identify how these two sources of CO2 vary in space and time. These measurements will be paired with both biological measurements of forest green up, tree growth, microbial activity, and environmental measurements of air and soil temperature, soil moisture, and snowpack melt. These sampling sites will be taken in the two dominant forest types, Spruce/Fir, and Aspen in the East River Watershed. Our work is motivated by our overarching hypothesis that separately quantifying how belowground microbe and roots are influenced by the changing water inputs, is necessary for understanding the belowground forested ecosystems resilience to a changing environment.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Long-term research; Microbiology; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Integrating resource allocation, vision, and fitness in Speyeria mormonia
Non-Technical Abstract: Using the Mormon fritillary ( Speyeria mormonia) butterfly as a study system, I will study the adult morphology and reproductive behavior of adults in the field, while also examining how these traits are affected by larval dietary stress in the laboratory. At the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL), I will complete behavior observations, assess visual capabilities of males, determine the fecundity of females, and measure both male and female adult morphology (I.e., wing size, wing color, and body size). Moreover, I will be examining the density of S. mormonia larval host plants ( Viola spp.) each year. These data will be collected every year to determine whether there is an observable change throughout time and whether this change can be explained by other variables. These data collected at RMBL will also be compared to laboratory data at the University of South Carolina in which I will conduct an experiment examining whether larval dietary stress impacts adult behavior and morphology to determine whether these measurements vary from field measurements. These experiments can allow us to assess the potential impacts of resource deficiencies on adult reproduction and survival. Additionally, comparing data across-years will provide a better understanding of how this system changes across time and whether there are realized, observable effects of larval resource deficiency on adult fitness.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Insect biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term effects of nitrogen deposition and bears in ecological networks
Non-Technical Abstract: Human activities have doubled the amount of biologically-available nitrogen on Earth, much of which is emitted to the atmosphere and falls to the ground far from its source. This blanket of fertilizer, called ?atmospheric nitrogen deposition, has well-studied ecological effects near sources of nitrogen emissions, but much less is understood about the elevated, yet low-level, deposition that occurs more broadly. In particular, it is unclear how low-level nitrogen fertilization indirectly affects relationships among plants, herbivores and predators, especially across the long timespans over which nitrogen deposition occurs. I propose to study how long-term, low-level nitrogen deposition impacts a community composed of plants, arthropods and black bears. My previous research showed that bears can indirectly benefit plants by eating ants and suppressing positive relationships between ants and herbivorous insects, but that the effects of bears weakened under short-term nitrogen enrichment. Here, I will extend this ongoing experiment to a total of 18 years to evaluate how long-term exposure to low-level nitrogen enrichment affects these relationships. I will also study spatial and temporal variation in bear consumption of ants. This work will aid our understanding of the repercussions of nitrogen pollution and inform the management of both nitrogen deposition and bears.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Atmospheric Science; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Wildflower Reproduction Phenology and Seed Traits under Early Snowmelt
Non-Technical Abstract: As snow melts earlier in the spring due to climate change, it has the potential to cause shifts in flowering time, especially for spring wildflowers. However, research on this topic often focuses solely on flowering time, with little regard for subsequent seed production and maturation timing. Cohesive research on the entire reproductive stage (flowering and seed production) is crucial for truly understanding the effects of early snowmelt on wildflower reproduction. Therefore, for three seasons, I will monitor the flower-to-seed interval for six subalpine spring wildflower species at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory from both early snowmelt and control plots. I will then collect a subset of these seeds and analyze their viability, germination, and traits in the Chicago Botanic Garden laboratory and greenhouses. This will then allow me to relate snowmelt date to both wildflower reproduction phenology and seed output characteristics. The results of this study will provide novel insight into early snowmelt impacts on spring wildflowers, as well as provide a framework for restorationists who struggle to determine the appropriate seed collection timing and quantity under climate change.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term monitoring of bee-plant interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: Our primary research project is an ongoing long-term (8-year) monitoring of wild pollinator populations, floral resources, plant-pollinator interactions, and local climate. Since 2015, we have extensively monitored the abundance and activity of wild bumble bees and floral resource availability at six permanent study sites within the East River Valley at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL).
