Our long-term research aims to address a series of outstanding questions focused on our fundamental understanding of the population and community ecology of plant-pollinator interactions and mutualism. With ongoing monitoring, our project will generate a more mechanistic and predictive understanding of the demographic responses of wild pollinators in the context of pollinator declines and climate change, as well as how and why species interact in nature.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Evolution and epidemiology in plant?pathogen systems under climate change
Non-Technical Abstract: Environmental context plays a large role in the transmission and evolution of infectious diseases. As a result, climate change will cause large perturbations to host?pathogen systems. Although the potential impacts of climate change on disease dynamics have received considerable attention, less is known about the capacity for hosts and pathogens to adapt to changing environments. Established in 2018, the Flax Rust Project leverages the powerful system of Lewis flax ( Linum lewisii ), a supalpine wildflower abundant on the slopes near RMBL, and flax rust ( Melampsora lini ), its fungal pathogen. Populations occur across a steep elevational gradient, allowing the measurement of a wide variety of weather conditions that contribute to the spread of disease. Through long-term observation of disease transmission in study populations, we investigate how hosts balance adaptation to both their abiotic environment and their pathogens. This question is of critical importance for forecasting plant?pathogen epidemics in a warming world.
Research Area: Climate change; Disease ecology; Genetics; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Evolutionary Ecology of Floral Color
Non-Technical Abstract: Flower color is central to plant-pollinator interactions, but several outstanding questions remain. How do floral colors vary geographically, i.e. across elevations or between habitats? What are the roles of abiotic agents (e.g. climate) and biotic agents (e.g. pollinators) in shaping floral colors within communities and across gradients? Has climate change shifted the timing or composition of floral colors presented to pollinators? The proposed research will attempt to answer these and other questions by expanding a database of floral spectra from flowering species in the RMBL area. This database can be used to estimate both 'raw' and pollinator-relevant measures of color for each plant species, which in turn can be connected to other RMBL datasets and ongoing experiments (e.g. phenology datasets, vegetation surveys) to answer the specific questions.
Research Area: Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating Heterospecific Pollen Growth in an Alpine Plant Community
Non-Technical Abstract: Mountain ecosystems harbor high plant diversity relative to lower altitude ecosystems, and, due to short growing seasons at high altitudes, many alpine plants tend to flower at the same time. During the normal flowering plant reproductive cycle, pollen (which carry sperm) must be deposited on female reproductive tissue from the same species. Pollen grains will grow a structure called a pollen tube, which grows into the flower and releases the sperm, fertilizing an egg and leading to the development of a seed. When many plants flower concurrently, like at the tops of mountains, there is the potential for pollen from a different plant species to be deposited on the female tissue of a flower. Scientists know a great deal about the flowering plant reproductive cycle when pollen from the same species is deposited on a flower, and much less about the consequences of foreign pollen deposition. It has been shown that foreign pollen deposition results in decreased seed production, but do not know why. I hypothesize that foreign pollen tube growth could decrease seed production by blocking same-species pollen tubes, creating a ?traffic jam? in the flower. In 2022, I experimentally exchanged pollen between species recorded when I saw pollen tubes growing. I found that pollen tubes grew in 93.6% of cases. This suggests that pollen tube growth following foreign pollen deposition may be occurring widely in the alpine meadows of the Rocky Mountains, and could be an important biological interaction among plant species. My research in 2023 will build on these results and investigate if pollen tubes grow to different lengths in foreign flowers and if the genes involved in the pollen tube growth and recognition process differ in same-species crosses vs. different species crosses. These data will help us to understand the importance of this interaction in shaping the evolution of flower traits and alpine plant community dynamics.
Research Area: Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Impact of Climate Change on Ecosystem Structure and Function
Non-Technical Abstract: I will be doing research in the WaRM (Warming and Removal in Mountains) project and the DOE-funded snowmelt manipulation to study the effects of climate change on ecosystem function. Last summer in the WaRM plots, I found that warmer temperatures reduced plant biomass regardless of when in the season the biomass was measured, likely due to a reduction in soil moisture. This inspired the research I'll be doing the next few summers, looking to see how changes in snowmelt date influence carbon dynamics via changes in the plant community, microbial community, and abiotic conditions. I will also take the project a step further and see how reductions in biomass might influence grazing in public grazing lands in Colorado.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Microbiology; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Receiver roles in hummingbird courtship
Non-Technical Abstract: Animal signals are often complex and dynamic; signalers can combine color, pattern, sound, and motion to communicate information for a variety of purposes. Receivers also have an important impact on signal design and evolution. Their perceptual capabilities, psychology, and behavior influence the way signalers transmit information. Despite their recognized importance, receiver dynamics remain relatively understudied compared to signaler and environmental dynamics. This is particularly true in courtship displays where male signalers are often communicating information to female receivers. In broad-tailed hummingbird (Selasphorus platycercus) courtship displays, male signaling traits?color, sounds, and behavior?and their interaction with the signaling environment are fairly well described, but female dynamics have yet to receive the same consideration. The goal of this project is to account for the influence of female behavior on broad-tailed courtship displays in the Colorado Rockies. This project integrates traditional behavioral observation techniques with new quantitative behavioral techniques?including 3D pose estimation and computer animation?to understand how female behavior influences both male display traits and her own perception of courtship displays. This project will also aid in developing new technologies combining 3D modeling, animation, and color metrics to study complex and dynamic animal coloration.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Determinants of upper-elevation range limits in cavity-nesting bees
Non-Technical Abstract: In recent decades, rapid warming has altered the environmental conditions experienced by many organisms. One ofthe most commonly documented biological responses to warming is range shifts, in which populations shift theirdistributions primarily towards higher latitudes and altitudes to track areas of climatically suitable habitat. Rangeshifts in bees may be of particular interest. Many aspects of bee life-histories, including their development, survival,and reproduction, are directly linked to temperature; yet bees are also indirectly affected by the availability of otherfactors such as floral resource abundance and nest-site availability, which may themselves be affected bytemperature. I am proposing two field studies that investigate the potential for upslope range shifts in cavity-nestingbees by exploring the variables that determine their upper range limits. In the first study, I ask whether the potentialfor range shifts in cavity-nesting bees is limited by the lack of nesting cavities at high elevations where trees anddead wood (nesting substrates) may be scarce. In the second study, I ask whether the potential for range shifts incavity-nesting bees is limited by the short duration of periods of favorable temperatures for offspring development athigh-elevations. My proposed fieldwork will combine both observational and experimental techniques to addressthese questions.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Insect biology; Phenology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Spatial Ecology of Environmental Change in the Upper Gunnison Watershed
Non-Technical Abstract: In response to accelerating climate change and other anthropogenic impacts, mountain ecosystems are rapidly shifting in both structure and function, leaving the systems themselves and the services they provide at significant risk of disruption. Despite the importance of these systems, many of the mechanisms contributing to their vulnerability or resilience are still poorly understood. Some of the largest uncertainties have to do with the roles that fine-scale spatial patterns in environmental and ecological processes play in larger-scale system behavior, and the degree to which these patterns attenuate and/or reinforce responses to regional and global environmental change. My research investigates four aspects of this outstanding problem, bringing perspectives from landscape ecology, physiological ecology, and remote sensing to bear on them in close collaboration with a diverse network of collaborators. Primary Research Projects: 1. Landscape Phenology - Reconstructing spatial patterns of flowering and floral resources for pollinators. 2. Vegetation Community Composition and Change - Understanding vulnerability of Gunnison Basin plant communities to climate change. 3. Microclimate Mapping - Tracking fine-scale patterns and historical trends in snow and near-surface microclimates. 4. Forest Dynamics and Evapotranspiration - Unpacking forest structure, climate, and landscape controls on evapotranspiration. In addition to this primary research, as RMBL staff I continue to build data resources for the broader research community as part of the RMBL Spatial Data Platform and operate a fee-for-service program allowing researchers access to RMBL?s Uncrewed Aircraft Systems and sensors.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Landscape biology; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: N. hostilis effects on timing, amount and distance of subsidy exports
Non-Technical Abstract: Emergent aquatic insects can be a large source of nutrients that are transported from aquatic to terrestrial environments. Many terrestrial organisms such as birds, spiders, and invertebrates rely on these pulsed allochthonous resources. However, nutrient movement is not confined only to aquatic-to-terrestrial processes. Aquatic ecosystems rely on terrestrial inputs of nutrients through dropped leaves, nutrient run off, and terrestrial insects falling into the water. These inputs can be very important in high alpine ponds which generally have low primary production. The timing and strength of these resource pulses are subject to change due to the effects of climate change. Range shifts of aquatic insects with varied phenology may interrupt or enhance the transportation of nutrients across ecosystem boundaries. This research will investigate how the population boom of a range shifting caddisfly impacts nutrient and biomass exports from high elevation wetlands. The phenology and emergence timing of this caddisfly may add temporal variability to the availability of allochthonous resources for terrestrial ecosystems. While this research will further scientific advancement, this will also enhance public outreach through tours of the field station and research sites, and develop future scientists by working with and mentoring undergraduate students.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How interactions with mutualists & predators shape plant coexistence
Non-Technical Abstract: Plant community structure is controlled by interactions between individuals that are mediated by shared resources, mutualists, and enemies. It is difficult to study each of these three classes of interactions in parallel due to their great complexity. We propose to isolate the relative effects of each class of interactions by a study of perennial plant coexistence. Perennial plants have life cycles in which competition via resources, pollinators, and seed predators are separated temporally. We will therefore manipulate floral communities to parameterize a model which separates the effects of different forms of interaction on the viability of plant coexistence and pathways of community assembly.
Research Area: Community ecology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Physiological drivers of plant community and ecosystem processes
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The effects of advanced plant phenology on herbivory and plant demography.
Non-Technical Abstract: The annual timing of life cycle events, known as phenology, can have strong effects on survival, growth, and reproduction, and can also affect species interactions. Phenology is often regulated by seasonal climatic cues, and therefore climate change is advancing phenology to earlier dates in many species across the world. However, plant phenology is advancing at a faster rate than the organisms that eat plants (herbivores), which invites the possibility of temporal misalignment between plants and herbivores that typically interact. Herbivory strongly impacts plant survival, growth, and reproduction, and therefore plant populations. Changes to plant populations can have ecosystem-wide consequences, so it is critical to investigate how altered timing of plant-herbivore interactions affects plants. However, almost no research considering this link focuses on consequences for plants, instead focusing on the herbivores. My research therefore investigates how advanced plant phenology changes herbivory and subsequently plant growth and reproduction. To do this, I will experimentally induce early plant phenology by causing the snow to melt early, since early snowmelt will be a major consequence of climate change. I will observe herbivory and plant growth and reproduction to decipher how plant performance is affected by altered plant-herbivore phenology.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Nitrogen Gas Emissions from Shale Critical Zone Environments
Non-Technical Abstract: The weathering of nitrogen from shale bedrock has been recognized as an important component of the global nitrogen cycle. However the fate of this nitrogen remains largely uncharacterized. Mass balance considerations of global shale denudation rates and nitrogen concentrations suggest that shale weathering accounts for up to 25% of global unmanaged nitrogen inputs to the terrestrial environment. Crucially, due to an abundance of electron donors such as organic matter and sulfide minerals, shale bedrock environments may act as denitrification hotspots. The release of gaseous N2 (inert) and N2O (strong greenhouse gas), to the atmosphere. We will work towards quantifying the role of shale environments as a global source of N2O is therefore vital to (1) predicting the response and potential amplifying feedbacks of shale denitrification to a warming climate; (2) understanding natural drivers of climate variations in the past.To address this critical knowledge gap, we propose to study the conditions that promote N2 and N2O production and atmospheric efflux within the Mancos shale critical zone in the East River watershed. Ultimately we will characterize the environmental variables that promote the release of N2O relative to N2. To accomplish this, we will use a combination of field observations and laboratory incubations to determine the roles of moisture saturation, oxygen availability, and microbial function in driving observed N2O yields.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Geology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Context-dependent effects of nectar microbes on pollination mutualisms
Non-Technical Abstract: Interactions among plants, pollinators, and nectar robbers have long served as an important model system for exploring ecological shifts between states of cooperation and conflict. Yet, despite their extensive study, the mechanisms that underlie shifts between these states, and constancy within, remain surprisingly unclear. Nectar microbes represent understudied but potentially significant interactors that may shape the foraging conditions under which floral visitors may decide to cooperate or cheat. This project will (1) employ the use of culture-dependent and culture-independent approaches to characterize the nectar microbiome of five montane wildflowers after legitimate vs. nectar robber floral visits; (2) assess how nectar microbes influence floral odor, nectar chemistry, and visitor behaviors; and (3) measure feedbacks of the microbes and floral visitor community on components of plant reproduction. By studying nectar microbes, their impact on floral phenotype, and whether they reinforce or facilitate the breakdown of pollination, we will gain a broader understanding of the factors that shape plant reproduction and pollination mutualisms.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Microbiology; Plant biology; Pollination; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: General Observations of Plant-Lichen and Plant-Herbivore Interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: We wish to conduct a series of surveys/observations in the US Forest Service?s Gunnison District and at RMBL examining plant and insect populations along with plant-lichen interactions. Our general research interests focus on insect host-pathogen interactions, plant-herbivore interactions, and plant demography. The areas of current interest include: 1) plant-lichen interactions between a common aster and a common lichen [the main focus of our current research]; 2) long-term dynamics of grasshopper populations in the area; 3) population dynamics of the aspen tortrix along with its associated diseases and parasites; 4) anti-herbivore defenses in heartleaf bittercress and the implications of these defenses for herbivore fitness; and 5) ant-aphid mutualisms and how they may affect plant-pollinator interactions particularly on fireweed. The current plan is focused on observational studies and no manipulative experiments are being planned at this time. In the near future, we are considering potential experiments that may include manipulations in the plant-lichen system.
Research Area: Community ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The effects of tri-trophic interactions on insect population dynamics
Non-Technical Abstract: I will investigate the relative effects of various biotic interactions (e.g., predation, intraguild predation, parasitism) on the introduced population of Gillette?s Checkerspot (Euphydryas gillettii) at Gothic, Colorado. Knowledge of the relative magnitude of biotic drivers, oftentimes regulated by abiotic factors, is necessary to understand how populations persist.
Research Area: Insect biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Drought response as escape from apparent maladaptation
Non-Technical Abstract: The native butterfly Pieris macdunnoughii lays eggs on a non-native, invasive mustard, Thlaspi arvense. The larvae won't eat the plant. This reflects maladaptation on the part of the butterfly to the plant. This maladaptation has persisted for over 150 generations in the Gothic area, in the face of strong selection pressures. We will explore the role of drought in altering plant chemistry, hence larval ability to eat the plant, as a mechanisms that may have allowed the apparent maladaptation to persist in the population.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Natural variation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and larval development
Non-Technical Abstract: I am interested in how the environment affects organism development through natural genetic variation of metabolic processes. I am proposing a study using Colias butterflies to look at how microclimate difference influence the natural genetic variation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, a glycolytic enzyme, and larval development. Using a field set-up involving four locations with varying microclimates, I will be able to determine if warming affects the survival and development of whichever genotypes are found to be present in the study population. I will also be conducting plant surveys throughout areas with populations of Colias butterflies to monitor nitrogen levels of suitable host plants over the span of three years. These findings will lead to the development of larval feeding studies aimed at connecting host plant quality and larval metabolic efficiency.
Research Area: Genetics; Insect biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: LateSt-Iso: Ecohydrology via high-frequency stable isotope measurements
Non-Technical Abstract: There is a need to better understand how mountain vegetation uses water to better predict both forest health and downstream water availability in a more drought-prone future. We use state-of-the-art high frequency stable isotope measurements to identify how rain and snowmelt infiltrate into and move through the soil, as well as how this water is taken up and used by plants, in the East River, Colorado. In June 2022, we installed an in-situ measurement system based on vapor probes to observe 2H, 18O, and 17O ratios of water in the soil, plants, and air. Specifically, we measured these isotope ratios at sub-daily frequency along three soil profiles down to 90 cm depth and in six trees (3 aspen and 3 Engelman spruce) using a cavity ring down spectrometer in the field. This sub-daily isotope data is unprecedented for the studied ecosystem and the very first application of the in-situ system in North America. In addition to this novel isotope technique, we instrumented the site with matric potential sensors along two soil profiles to observe subsurface water availability and the three investigated trees were equipped with sap flow sensors to measure transpiration flux. Meteorological data were gathered at nearby weather stations and by the SAIL campaign, a DOE ARM site close to our instrumented forest.
Research Area: Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating the floral VOC profile of Polemonium brandegeei
Research Area: Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Temporal Effects of Beavers on Biogeochemical Processes
Non-Technical Abstract: The western United States (U.S.) is experiencing severe drought conditions exacerbated by climate change. As annual precipitation and runoff generation decline, American beaver (Castor canadensis) populations are increasing, in part due to reintroduction efforts aimed at restoring water resources. With time beaver institute a pattern of dam building and abandonment that drastically influence the river corridor through alterations to the geomorphology the biogeochemistry. Specifically, previous work has shown that beaver dams have variable impacts on the production of methylmercury (MeHg), a neurotoxin that can bioaccumulate and biomagnify with successive trophic levels. Methylation is driven by myriad geomorphological characteristics and biogeochemical processes. The first step for understanding mercury (Hg) dynamics in a beaver-dominated river corridor is to discern the unique geomorphological characteristics beaver create and how they influence biogeochemical parameters. Once locations on the landscape are identified that will potentially have high rates of methylation, a greater breadth of samples will be taken in future years and quantified for total mercury (THg), MeHg, sulfate (SO42-) reduction rates (SRR), methylation and demethylation rates among other biogeochemical measurements. Together, the data will reveal the dominant mechanisms within differently aged beaver ponds that drive the production and export of MeHg providing information to stakeholders about the implications beaver have for water quality. Effectively communicating science to the community that uses the resource under investigation is crucial. Final steps will include making CZ case studies that can be used by the geoscience community for undergraduate teaching and to present to the community that the research was conducted in.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Seasonal Cycles Unravel Mysteries of Missing Mountain Water
Non-Technical Abstract: Snow provides over 60% of water supplies in the Western United States, and in general, spring snow measurements provide a good prediction of summer streamflow. However, in some years, these streamflow predictions are not accurate, and water managers struggle to efficiently allocate water resources. In many studies, warming temperatures correspond to less observed streamflow per unit precipitation input. However, key elements, including basin heterogeneity, gauge undercatch, groundwater flow, and water storage, are often not represented in models or predictions, and physical hydrologic models diverge widely in their hydrologic sensitivity to warming. We will combine distributed observations and modeling to test the following hypotheses. 1) Fall rainstorms recharge soil moisture and groundwater, increasing subsurface connectivity and the efficiency of winter snowpack to generate streamflow. 2) More uniformly-distributed snow cover leads to greater subsurface water connectivity and more efficient water delivery to the stream. More variable snow cover, either through a greater elevational gradient or increased patchiness, leads to less effective recharge and greater evaporative losses. Only modeling that represents subsurface water transfer from snow-covered to snow-free grid cells will represent these effects. 3) Warming temperatures and increased rain relative to snow over recent decades have changed snow distributions in ways that decrease runoff efficiency, increasing the frequency of snow free areas at lower elevations fed by snow at higher elevations, which increases basin total evapotranspiration. Our questions require both long timeseries and detailed, distributed observations. We propose to first investigate our hypotheses over the well-instrumented East River (Colorado) and Tuolumne River (California) basins. These long-term observations are augmented with detailed distributed surface flux observations obtained during the 2021-23 multi-agency atmospheric campaigns of SAIL, SPLASH, and SOS in the East River basin. We will use models to establish essential process representations and to directly test hypotheses. We will then test for the essential minimum observations and process representations to expand to larger scales. Our study will directly inform modelers and water managers of the key processes that must be represented to accurately predict runoff originating from seasonal snow in mountain watersheds, leading to improved understanding, prediction, and planning at seasonal and longer timescales.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Hydrology; Meteorology; Microbiomes; Modeling; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Interactive effects of biotic and abiotic conditions on local adaptation
Non-Technical Abstract: Climate change is imposing novel selection, disrupting local adaptation, shifting geographic distributions, and altering species composition and diversity of ecological communities. Accordingly, climate change acts directly on species through new abiotic conditions, as well as indirectly through altered biotic interactions. Here, we seek to test mechanistic hypotheses about evolution in complex environments where correlated suites of traits evolve in response to abiotic and biotic agents of selection. Specifically, we propose to examine the mechanistic basis of local adaptation to current abiotic and biotic conditions in the emerging ecological model plant, Boechera stricta (Brassicaceae), in the Colorado Rocky Mountains. We focus on plant-herbivore interactions, as they provide exceptional opportunities for dissecting the direct and indirect effects of climate change. We will then predict plant evolutionary responses to projected future abiotic and biotic environments. To evaluate how abiotic conditions and the biotic community have interacted to shape local adaptation and exert selection on functional traits (Aim 1), we will first conduct a multifactorial manipulation of herbivory, snow dynamics, and water availability in three field gardens at different elevations. We will then characterize herbivore communities across elevational gradients to project future distributions and abundances (Aim 2). Finally, based on these projections, we will investigate how adaptive landscapes will shift under climate change by exposing B. stricta transplants to current and future abiotic conditions and herbivore levels in high and low elevation gardens (Aim 3 and 4). We hypothesize that climate change favors novel suites of traits, such as the rapid development of high elevation families combined with the drought tolerance and herbivore resistance of low elevation families. Further, to test the hypothesis that genetic trade-offs restrict adaptation, we will contrast natural accessions with existing genetic constraints vs. recombinant inbred lines that allow an unconstrained response to selection. Finally, we will examine the genetic basis of local adaptation by mapping quantitative trait loci and test whether the fitness of local alleles declines under climate change. Despite extensive work characterizing local adaptation, we still know little about the processes through which species adapt to the simultaneous, likely interactive, effects of multiple abiotic and biotic agents of selection. Dissecting the contributions of climatic and biotic factors to local adaptation and selection will enable us to forecast how climate change could alter adaptive evolution and influence the risk of extinction. The proposed studies will reveal the extent to which climate change could favor novel suites of traits, whether genetic constraints could restrict adaptation, and whether climate change could increase the vulnerability of local populations to decline. Collectively, our field experiments will identify the functional traits and genetic basis of local adaptation to complex environments and evaluate the evolutionary and ecological consequences of projected future, novel environments.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Phenology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Are hemiparasitic plants the "Robinhood" of sub-alpine communities?
Non-Technical Abstract: Root hemiparasitic plants are found in almost every ecosystem and can profoundly affect surrounding plants in the community. These organisms use unique belowground structures to attach to host plants and extract nutrients and water but maintain the ability to photosynthesize independently. Yet, they remain significantly understudied outside of agricultural environments and thus are often omitted from our understanding of plant population, community, and ecosystem ecology. This is surprising as they have been shown to increase plant community diversity through the direct effect of parasitism on aboveground plant competition, increase litter decomposition, and alter microbial community composition through the belowground effects of increased litter lability and mycorrhizal suppression. My work aims to provide a complete perspective of plant parasitism by investigating the above and belowground impacts of hemiparasitic plants on community structure, nutrient cycling, and biodiversity. In the Rocky Mountains, a root hemiparasitic plant, Castilleja septentrionalis, is highly abundant across habitat types and elevations, with the potential to play a fundamental role in ecosystem dynamics. To better understand these unique and charismatic organisms, I will conduct a multi-year field experiment, collect demographic data, characterize microbial communities, and quantify carbon and nitrogen cycling. Ultimately, my results will shift the negative perspective of parasitism within plant communities towards a better understanding of their benefits to natural ecosystems.
Research Area: Community ecology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Thresholds and tipping points in ecosystem responses to global warming
Non-Technical Abstract: Climate change is currently modifying the myriad linkages between soils, plants, animals and the atmosphere. Being able to predict these changes in advance allows us to conserve key components of natural environments and, more practically, preserve the vital services that nature provides to humans, such as clean air. Of particular concern are tipping points, where a certain linkage appears to be stable but then suddenly and dramatically shifts to another state, or collapses entirely. One way of thinking about nature is to think about the ?flow? of various chemical elements, like carbon and nitrogen, through different organisms over time. For example, a plant breathes in carbon dioxide and uses it to make a new leaf, which gets eaten by a worm, where the carbon is used for energy and is eventually breathed back out into the atmosphere. For our project, we are assessing whether mountain ecosystems are likely to reach future tipping points in these flows of carbon and nitrogen. One method of predicting the future is to use natural gradients in temperature, such as the slope of a mountain. As you walk down from the top of a mountain to the bottom, you are effectively walking through a simulation of global warming. For our project, we are walking along mountain gradients around the world, measuring how much plants are breathing and how much carbon and nitrogen is stored in leaves, wood, soils and tiny animals in the soil. In this way, we hope to predict whether the linkages between different aspects of nature will change gradually or abruptly as climate change progresses. Identifying abrupt changes will provide an important timeframe for land managers to conserve mountain environments and prevent losses of ecosystems services.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Light-Absorbing Components of Organic Carbon in Aerosol and Snow
Non-Technical Abstract: Composition and Photochemical Transformations of Light-Absorbing Components of Organic Carbon in Aerosol and Snowpack Samples Collected at RMBL The scope of this project is to collect samples of light-absorbing organic carbon materials present in atmospheric aerosol and snowpack in support of the DOE funded and organized Surface-Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL)1 field campaign co-located at the RMBL site. Collected samples will be returned to laboratories of the co-investigators for in-depth chemical analysis. The analysis efforts will be focused on characterization of the chemical composition and optical properties of complex organic matter in aerosols and snowpack to establish a relationship between the composition of atmospheric particles and their impact on the snow albedo and snow photochemistry. A complimentary combination of molecular-level characterization and chemical imaging approaches will be used to elucidate atmospheric ageing processes governing evolution of chemical composition and optical properties of organic carbon in the area of study ? a very challenging knowledge gap needed to improve predictive understanding of aerosol effects on climate.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Sublimation of Snow (SOS)
Non-Technical Abstract: Snow is a vital part of water resources, but sublimation may remove 10% to 90% of snowfall from the system. Due to a critical lack of reliable direct measurements of snow sublimation, we do not fully understand the physics that govern current rates of sublimation, let alone how those amounts might change with the climate. We propose to deploy NSF's Integrated Surface Flux System (ISFS) for winter 2022-2023 in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Energy?s Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) at the Kettle Ponds site in the East River Watershed, Colorado. SAIL will measure vertical and horizontally distributed wind fields from radiosondes, a radar wind profiler, a doppler lidar, and distributed meteorological stations. We plan to deploy the ISFS system to provide surface flux observations at multiple levels to better understand how basin-scale wind fields interact with surface turbulence and fluxes. These measurements, combined with energy and mass balance observations and terrestrial lidar scans of the evolving snowfield, will provide benchmarks of the most reliable approaches to measuring snow sublimation in different conditions and improve understanding of sensible and latent heat fluxes in complex terrain.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate science; Hydrology; Meteorology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Epigenetic variation & accelerated aging in the seasonal habitat of marmots
Non-Technical Abstract: Aging is a universal consequence of life, yet this cost is experienced differently between species and potentially between different populations. Long-term studies in wild mammals have shown that lifespan expectancy is tied to many proximate environmental factors, such as social dominance and resource limitation. However, how these factors influence biological, or epigenetic aging, is not well understood. Yellow-bellied marmots ( Marmota flaviventer ) are obligate hibernators that annually experience conditions known to increase longevity (e.g., major caloric restriction and reduced metabolic rate during torpor). The alpine habitats of these animals are highly sensitive to anticipated phenological shifts affecting plants and animals under climate change. Adult marmots show evidence of decreasing epigenetic aging by modulating DNA methylation during the winter months. Thus, this long-studied marmot population, which survives within seasonal periodicity, can provide insight to a species-specific response to climatic change via an epigenetic mechanism. I will conduct a longitudinal study of DNA methylation variation across years and between marmot populations at high elevation sites in the Rocky Mountains. This data on seasonal lifetime variation in epigenetic modification will inform how species may survive fluctuating and physiologically challenging environments.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Decoupling plant and mycorrhizal fungal phenology in the Anthropocene
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants do not live in isolation. Instead, they associate with multitudes of organisms, including mycorrhizal fungi belowground. These fungi acquire most plant nutrients and water in exchange for sugar. However, interactions between plants and mycorrhizal fungi may be disrupted as the climate changes. This project examines the potential for relationships between plants and mycorrhizal fungi to be disrupted as snowmelt timing shifts with global warming. We will examine the growth and composition of plants and fungi as well as soil nutrient concentrations in slopes and aspects with different snowmelt dates and in a three year long snowmelt manipulation. All data will be fed into an ecosystem model to scale our findings to the global scale.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Microbiomes; Modeling; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Parasitic plants as drivers of ecosystem processes
Non-Technical Abstract: In recent years, there has been increased interest in how hemiparasitic plants impact plant community diversity, richness, and productivity. While this work has highlighted the impact that hemiparasitic plants have on aboveground plant community structure, little is known about the role these plants play belowground. Given the prevalence of parasitic plants in natural ecosystems and the diversity of parasitic habits, it is of utmost importance that we study the impact that these ecosystem engineers have on their environment from a holistic perspective. In this study, I aim to investigate the effects of Castilleja sulphurea on neighboring plant populations and community dynamics, nutrient cycling, and soil microbial communities by assessing their direct and litter-mediated effects. My work will provide a comparison of the two pathways, ultimately contributing to a greater understanding of how parasitic plants impact surrounding plant communities and ecosystem nutrient cycling.
Research Area: Community ecology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Conflicting Selection on Flower Size in Iris missouriensis
Non-Technical Abstract: Animal pollinators play a significant role in the reproduction of flowering plants. These pollinators can act as strong agents of selection on various floral traits such as flower size. While pollinators are known to impose selection, other factors such as drought and thermal stress can impose selection on the same floral traits. Flower size acts as a visual cue to attract pollinators as it is generally associated with greater floral rewards. Consequently, in arid environments, a larger floral display can result in greater transpiration through the floral organs. I am investigating this balance of conflicting selection using the Rocky Mountain Iris (Iris missouriensis) that occurs across the natural aridity gradient of the Colorado Rocky Mountains. I hypothesize that flower size will decrease with increasing aridity such that larger flowers will occur at higher elevations where drought mediated selection is relaxed and smaller flowers at lower elevations where aridity is the greatest and imposes selection for smaller flowers. I have documented this natural cline in flower size that is consistent with my hypothesis. I will confirm pollinator preference for larger flowers using 3D printed I. missouriensis flowers and experimentally evaluate conflicting pollinator- and drought-mediated selection using a common garden experiment with water and pollen supplementation treatments. Evaluating the balance of selection between abiotic and biotic factors will illuminate factors influencing plant-pollinator interactions, supporting conservation of flowering species by providing a more robust understanding of their evolutionary response to climate change.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stream flow phenology and biogeochemistry
Non-Technical Abstract: Effect of advancing stream peak flow hydrology on stream biogeochemistry and primary productivity Climate change is causing streams to reach their peak flows earlier due to advancing snowmelt timing and declining snowpack volume. My ongoing research aims to understand how this advancing flow phenology impacts stream nutrient cycling, primary producers, and grazing invertebrates. By studying seasonal patterns of nutrient uptake and algal accrual in streams that vary in timing of peak flow, I can use a space-for-time substitution to investigate how climate-driven advances in peak flow will alter this foundational ecosystem process and stream food webs.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Hydrology; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Age at primiparity in yellow-bellied marmots
Non-Technical Abstract: When to start reproducing is a key question for any species since it can impact survival, total reproduction over a lifetime (number of offspring), longevity, but also population dynamics and generation time. Reproduction is a process that requires a lot of energy and resources. Breeding early has been shown to decrease survival and/or future fecundity. However, postponing reproduction means lost in opportunities to reproduce and increases the chances of dying without producing any offspring. Then, a trade-off in age at first reproduction arises, with large variation observed even within population of certain species. In addition, behavioural interactions can also affect age at first reproduction. For instance, reproduction can be delayed in subordinates. I plan to investigate the causes and consequences of age at first reproduction in yellow-bellied marmots. This hibernator can start to reproduce before reaching adult size, which is around 4 years of age. It also reproduces only once per year, shows wide variation in age at first reproduction (ranging from 2 to 7 years), and exhibits lot of variation in its social organisation. Indeed, females can be solitary or be part of a group of two to several dozens of individuals. I will use behavioural, reproductive, life-history and pedigree data obtained from a long-term study of individually marked marmots for over 60 years. Maximizing the richness of the data, I will also determine the impact of age of first reproduction of the mother on her offspring?s survival and reproduction. This work will therefore provide new insights on the biological factors regarding an important life-history parameter.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Context-Dependent Life History Responses to Climate Change
Non-Technical Abstract: Larval salamanders either metamorphose into terrestrial adults (metamorphs) or forego metamorphosis to become gilled, aquatic adults (paedomorphs). Paedomorphs are primarily subject to environmental changes in the aquatic habitat whereas metamorphs are subject to environmental variation affecting both the aquatic and terrestrial environments. Metamorphs and paedomorphs are thus likely to be asymmetrically impacted by climate change. My objectives are to understand how past and future climate variation and climate change impact amphibians using a combination of modeling and field studies. I propose to: A) Compare temperature and water stress impacts of ongoing climate trends under different environmental contexts (in the aquatic and terrestrial environments along an elevational gradient) using data logger-implanted paedomorphs and metamorph salamanders as mobile temperature sensors, salamander biophysical models in different environments. B) Study the thermal physiology of wild aquatic and terrestrial salamanders at different elevations to better understand sources of exposure and resilience to the changing thermal environment they are subjected to under climate change. C) Determine the effects of abiotic correlates, e.g., temperature and precipitation, on breeding activity in a wide-ranging frog species.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effect of nitrogen and soil microbes on floral volatile emissions
Non-Technical Abstract: Floral scent is an important trait of flowering plants because of its role in attracting pollinators. Recent advancements in the field have found floral scent to respond plastically to changes in the environment, such as temperature and water availability. Because of this, climate change has the potential to alter floral scent emission in some species. This could impact plant-pollinator interactions and consequently plant reproduction. One way plants are able to adjust more quickly to environmental changes is by forming symbiotic relationships with soil microorganisms. Soil microbes help plants acquire water and nutrients, like nitrogen, that are essential for growth and reproduction. Soil microbes can also influence floral traits, including floral scent. Since one of the main compounds found in floral scent profiles is nitrogen, changes in soil nitrogen and soil microbes may influence floral scent. Still, little is known about how soil microbes and nitrogen availability in the soil, alone or in concert, affect floral scent. I propose a two part experiment investigating the role of nitrogen availability and soil microbes on floral scent. In the first experiment, I will test the effects of soil nitrogen availability in two species of Ipomopsis (scarlet gilia and slendertube skyrocket). Since soil microbes play an important role in allocating nitrogen in plants, for the second experiment I plan on examining the effect of soil microbes and soil nitrogen availability on floral scent in scarlet gilia ( I. aggregata ). To better understand the role of climate change in these interactions, I will investigate differences in floral scent of plants grown in soil from areas exposed to early snowmelt compared to areas with normal snowmelt.
Research Area: Climate change; Plant biology; Pollination; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Assessing drivers of vegetation functional change
Non-Technical Abstract: We use physiological, experimental, theoretical, and observational methods to try to understand what regulates diversity (phylogenetic and functional) and dynamics of subalpine communities and ecosystems at different scales. In particular, we are interested in understanding how diversity influences ecosystem functioning. We are interested in the relative importance of abiotic (namely, climate) and biotic (species interactions, community assembly, and competition) factors in controlling plant community and ecosystem response to climate change. At the largest scales, we study the flux of carbon dioxide from subalpine meadows along an elevational gradient and its relationship to temperature, water availability, plant functional traits and species identity. We also use remote sensing techniques as well as macro ecological approaches to study large scale processes. At the smallest scale, we are studying the mechanisms of community assembly of subalpine meadows.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Quantifying controls of dynamic storage on critical zone processes
Non-Technical Abstract: The critical zone is a thin layer at the Earth?s surface where rock, soil, water, air, and living organisms interact. The critical zone supports life on Earth. In the western United States, the critical zone is sensitive to changes in the environment, such as fires or droughts. This project studies how processes in the critical zone respond to changes in the environment. Data are collected from the Coal Creek catchment. The project links the fields of water science, forest ecology, rock chemistry and soil chemistry. The project connects the way water moves and is stored in the ground to how trees grow and to how soil and rocks change. Studying these interactions is important to understanding how Earth will respond to future changes in climate. Researchers from six universities work together. Students are trained in several areas of Earth science.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Studying clouds and precipitation with a cloud radar and a snowflake camera
Non-Technical Abstract: We plan to enhance the instrumentation suite of the ongoing Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) of the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program at RMBL by a 94 GHz scanning cloud radar and a novel video in situ snowfall camera for the period Sep 2022 ? June 2023. Our goal is to study riming (the adherence of water droplets when ice particles fall through a supercooled liquid layer in a cloud) and secondary ice production (SIP) processes that enhance the number of ice particles during snowfall formation in complex terrain.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Does Climate Change Promote Cannibalism?
Non-Technical Abstract: Polyphenism (environmentally-cued polymorphisms) occur when multiple discrete morphologies are produced in different individuals of the same species in varying environments. Arizona tiger salamanders (Ambystoma mavortium nebulosum) exhibit a cannibalistic polyphenism in which cannibal morphs possess vomerine teeth and larger, U-shaped heads than toothless typical morphs. Cannibalism can strongly impact tiger salamander populations and their surrounding communities due to their keystone role in subalpine freshwater ponds. Several studies have found that the cannibal morphology is positively correlated with salamander density, as well as size variation in salamander populations. However, no previous studies have examined the impact of temperature on tiger salamander cannibalism. This is significant, as the Rocky Mountains where Arizona tiger salamanders live have warmed by 1°C on average, and models predict that the region could warm an average of about 1.5-3°C by 2050. Along with increased temperatures, reduced snowpack accumulation has also resulted in drier conditions for temporary subalpine ponds. In my study, I aim to determine how the proportion of cannibal morphs in natural populations has changed over time and whether increased temperatures and pond drying rates influence the production of the cannibal morphology. I will gather data for my first objective through field sampling; I will seine ponds around the Gunnison basin in order to collect data on cannibal frequency to compare to previous studies to determine whether cannibal frequency has changed over time. To complete my second objective, I will conduct weatherport experiment at the RMBL in which I will have two temperature treatments (ambient and 3°C warmer) and three density treatments in order to determine whether increased temperatures and density levels directly influence the development of the cannibal morphology in tiger salamanders. Understanding how rapidly changing climate conditions impact polyphenisms in this system may increase our understanding of the relationship between climate and polyphenisms in other systems, ultimately helping us mitigate the effects of climate change on environmentally-sensitive species.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: General Observations of Plant-Lichen & Plant-Herbivore Interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: We wish to conduct a series of surveys/observations in the US Forest Service?s Gunnison District and at RMBL examining plant and insect populations along with plant-lichen interactions. Our general research interests focus on insect host-pathogen interactions, plant-herbivore interactions, and plant demography. The areas of current interest include: 1) plant-lichen interactions between a common aster and a common lichen [the main focus of our current research]; 2) long-term dynamics of grasshopper populations in the area; 3) ant-aphid mutualisms and how they may affect plant-pollinator interactions particularly on fireweed; 4) population dynamics of the aspen tortrix along with its associated diseases and parasites; and, 5) anti-herbivore defenses in heartleaf bittercress and the implications of these defenses for herbivore fitness. However, as one can tell from the above, the current plan is focused on observational studies and no manipulative experiments are being planned at this time.
Research Area: Modeling; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Soulé Butterfly Re-survey
Non-Technical Abstract: This project exploits a butterfly monitoring data set collected by Michael Soulé and his Earthwatch teams from 1982-1991. He collected data on the number of butterflies of specified species seen every 3 days along the Copper Creek trail from RMBL to the first crossing. We propose a re-survey, to examine changes in phenology, abundance and species diversity in the intervening 30-40 years. Additionally, we propose to set up a long-term monitoring program involving RMBL docents to continue this data collection.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Effects of Tri-Trophic Interactions on Plant-Insect Population Dynamics
Non-Technical Abstract: I am interested in studying the relative effects of various biotic interactions (e.g., predation; parasitism; competition) and changing climate on the population dynamics of plant-insect relationships. Specifically, I am using the introduced population of Gillette?s checkerspot (Euphydryas gillettii) at Gothic, Colorado to carry out research projects focusing on the effects of predators and parasitoids on pollinator health. Knowledge of the impacts of both biotic and abiotic drivers of population growth is necessary to understand how populations persist in spite of global change.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Authoring disciplinary identities in a community of science practice
Non-Technical Abstract: The purpose of this research is to understand how people learn to do scientific research while participating in research groups and communities of research groups. A community of practice is a "group of people who share a concern or a passion for something they do and learn how to do it better as they interact regularly". A community of science practice (COSP) is a group of people associated with a science discipline(s) who understand and share specialized language, norms, and practices for participation and knowledge generation in the discipline(s). Identity formation as part of a COSP involves learning to legitimately participate in the specialized practices and discourses of the discipline. Such learning is conceptualized as a trajectory of apprenticeship where novices first learn through legitimate forms of peripheral participation, taking on more responsibility and ownership over time as they move towards full participation in the community. COSP research has described full participation as generating new knowledge through research. Structured research experiences are important forms of apprenticeship in a COSP. Although research experiences can have powerful effects on peoples' persistence in science education and research, more research is needed to understand the learning trajectories across different forms of legitimate participation in a COSP, from peripheral to full. This research focuses specifically on how people negotiate and author their science identities through legitimate forms of participation in a COSP.
Research Area: Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stream Corridor Hydrologic Controls on Carbon Dioxide Fluxes
Non-Technical Abstract: Rivers and streams are increasingly recognized as important sources of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere; however, the full magnitude of emissions and the processes that control them remain highly uncertain. This project will combine innovative field characterizations of stream hydrology and carbon processing with advanced computer models to improve our ability to predict and scale stream CO2 fluxes. Results of this research will advance our understanding of an important component of the global carbon cycle and the ability to monitor changes into the future, and generated computer models will be made publicly available. This research will also comprise the training of a PhD student and undergraduate researcher, and it will serve as the focus of a 1-day educational module for a diverse group of high school students through the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory?s summer Field Biology course.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Hydrology; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Fitness consequences of multiple early-life stressors
Non-Technical Abstract: Early-life experiences can have a disproportionate impact on an individual?s fitness. However, much of this research has focused on the effects of single stressors (e.g., food scarcity) under a controlled lab environment. In a world where natural populations must simultaneously contend with multiple anthropogenic threats?such as climate change, urbanization, and pollution?we must understand the cumulative impact of multiple early life stressors on the long-term fitness, ecology, and behavior of wild populations. Having established the utility of a novel cumulative early adversity (CEA) index in predicting survival and longevity in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer), I now ask how CEA affects the reproductive decisions and of female yellow-bellied marmots and the fitness of their offspring. Life-history theory predicts that organisms with shorter lifespans should invest more in early reproduction. Therefore, I predict that females that experience higher CEA will be more likely to produce more offspring earlier in life and at a lower body mass. Furthermore, parental experiences can have intergenerational effects. I predict mothers that experience higher CEA will have offspring with shorter lifespans. My research will highlight the cumulative impact of early adversity on the reproductive decisions and lifetime fitness of a wild population. It will increase our understanding of how early adversity influences not only life-history evolution but also population demography and abundance, which is critical for conservation.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Evaluating Differences in Pollination Efficiency
Non-Technical Abstract: Pollinators are essential for reproduction in 87% of flowering plants. Therefore, the pollinator species will determine the quantity and quality of seeds that a plant produces, with quality indicated by the genetic diversity of progeny. More genetically diverse populations contain a variety of genes that increases tolerance to environmental change and importantly climate change. Despite the importance of measuring the quality component of pollination efficiency, few studies consider this component. To address this deficit, my research will take place at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL), where I will study Delphinium nuttallianum, a perennial endemic to montane meadows. D. nuttallianum is pollinated by one hummingbird species and several bumble bee and bee species, each of which differs in several key morphological and behavioral traits, which has implications for the pollen quantity and quality delivered. By examining differences in pollination services between these species, my study seeks to demonstrate the importance of considering both the quantity and quality measurements of pollination efficiency when determining the relative importance of pollinator species to plant reproduction. Accurately determining the relative importance of pollinators to plant reproduction is essential for the implementation of effective conservation strategies that focus on the long-term maintenance of plant populations and genetic diversity.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Context dependent responses to climate change in Arizona Tiger Salamanders
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the drivers behind the variable response of organisms to climate change has been a focus of ecological research over the last decade. Ectothermic species are among those especially sensitive to changes in the environment and have been known to display variable responses to the changing temperatures. One source of variation comes from the polyphenism displayed by ectotherms, like salamanders, to respond to diverse conditions in their environment. I will determine the effect of polyphenism on ectothermic animal responses to climate change using high elevation Arizona Tiger salamanders located at Mexican Cut Nature Preserve (MCNP). I will conduct critical thermal limit experiments with metamorphic, paedomorphic, and larvae salamanders. I will collect salamanders from ponds within MNCP to determine differences between displayed morphs as well as age classes. I expect metamorphic salamanders to display the widest thermal tolerance range amongst the adult and larval salamanders. I will also conduct a combined lab and field acclimation experiments to determine the natural ability for these organisms to respond to changes in their environment. I will collect salamanders from within MCNP at different portions of the active season (early, mid-season, and late) and conduct critical thermal experiments to calculate changes in critical limits across each degree change in temperature. My study will examine the relationship between environmental cues, temperature, and morphology and contribute to a growing field to understand amphibian responses to climate change in order to develop plans to respond and conserve populations globally. This project will also expand upon the existing research occurring at Mexican Cut through Dr. Howard Whiteman and his colleagues.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Aquatic Biology; Community ecology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Impacts of Early Snowmelt on Subalpine Plant Reproduction and Survival
Non-Technical Abstract: Snowmelt is a vital source of spring soil moisture in high elevation plant ecosystems. Climate change is causing a shift to earlier snowmelt timing which can cause changes in flowering phenology and a higher risk of drought for high elevation plant species. Drought stress represents a significant barrier to plant reproduction and can reduce plant floral characteristics and survival. The proposed project will study the impacts of climate change-induced early snowmelt on a subalpine four plant species at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab in Gothic, Colorado in the summer field season of 2022. I will conduct an early snowmelt manipulation and monitor the physiology, floral characteristics, pollination, and demography of four perennial plant species from May until August. The species are from three genera and represent a gradient of phenological flower timing. I hypothesize that there will be differential effects depending on the timing of flowering of the study species. Earlier flowering species will be less effected by drought stress while later flowering species may have increased exposure to drought stress. The proposed project will produce a multi-species data frame that can be used both in further study of climate impacts on sensitive subalpine ecosystems.
Research Area: Climate change; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Decomposing Sources of Variation in Marmot Flight Initiation Distance
Non-Technical Abstract: A variety of factors shape an animal?s antipredator behavior. Flight Initiation Distance (FID) is a common measurement for evaluating antipredator behavior and is used to assess an individual?s shyness or boldness. Numerous FID studies have shown that an animal?s FID is an economic decision that is sensitive to both the costs and benefits of flight. While there is some evidence that individual animals may have consistent FIDs, and there are several genes associated with FID, few studies have quantified the heritability of FID. Knowledge of heritability permits us to understand the potential of a trait to evolve within a population, and heritable variation is yet another mechanism that permits animals to respond to a dynamically changing world. I propose to study the heritability of FID in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer). I will use a statistical model (called the ?animal model?) to identify the degree to which genetic and non-genetic factors explain the variation of antipredator behavior. To my knowledge, there are only two previous studies that have calculated the heritability of FID in any species. Thus, while we generally expect that an animal?s fear response is shaped by both genetic and environmental factors, if we find strong heritability associated with FID, we can infer that an animal?s fear response is relatively ?fixed? and less likely to fluctuate given the situation. This might suggest that new human-induced threats in the environment may lead to an evolutionary response and select for either bolder or shyer animals. If bolder animals are favored, as has been suggested in theoretical models, marmots (and other species with heritable fear response) may become more vulnerable to predation. Additionally, predicting how animals will respond to new threats like urbanization or ecotourism could be a valuable tool for wildlife managers in the face of rising human-wildlife conflict.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The causes and consequences of pollen defenses
Non-Technical Abstract: The pollen of multiple plant taxa has been demonstrated to produce toxic compounds or to exhibit mechanical defense. At least some of these defenses have been found to be detrimental to pollinators. However, the causes for the presence of defended pollen and the ecological and evolutionary consequences of these defenses remain mostly unknown. The goal of my project at RMBL is to determine the causes and consequences of chemical and mechanical defenses in pollen. I am conducting experiments to test if 1) pollen defense compounds protect flowers against pollen consuming antagonists, 2) if those compounds affect visitation by pollinators, and 3) if pollen defense restricts the host-plant use of bees.
Research Area: Insect biology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Facilitation and Phylogenetic Structure of Montane Plant Communities
Non-Technical Abstract: One important question in community ecology is how species interact with one another, and whether these interactions are beneficial or detrimental. Co-flowering of different species within a plant community may increase competition for pollinator resources, but it may also be facilitative and increase pollinator visits and plant fitness. Climate change is also driving shifts in phenology that may change co-flowering patterns. This study aims to determine whether co-flowering in plant communities changes the fitness outcomes for the co-flowering species. These interspecies interactions may also be a factor in community phylogenetic makeup. I will investigate whether co-flowering and associated fitness benefits are related to the phylogenetic makeup of the community. With plots at three different elevations, I will also determine whether the relationship between co-flowering, fitness, and phylogenetic relationships changes between elevations.
Research Area: Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Conifer and Aspen effect on SOC, hydrological, and weathering dynamics
Non-Technical Abstract: Forests made of aspen and sub-alpine fir are common in mountainous regions. These regions are experiencing change in temperature, precipitation, and length of growing season, which may have a direct impact on the vegetation that thrives. As such, sub-alpine fir trees have been encroaching on aspen stands in several parts of the U.S. Since carbon pools behave differently beneath the two stand types, this may influence the processes that are happening in the soils. Most importantly, this may alter the rate of soil formation, chemical weathering fluxes, and more generally the carbon budget. Therefore, the aim of this research is to answer the question: How sensitive are carbon and weathering fluxes to a shift in vegetation (aspen vs. conifer) in montane systems? To address this question, we will collect soil and root data up to 110 cm deep and parameterize a reactive transport model to quantify the differences in solute and carbon fluxes from the critical zone.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Microbiomes; Modeling; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Consequences of phenological shifts and pollination for plant populations
Non-Technical Abstract: Non-technical Abstract (Project 1): Climate change is predicted to decrease biodiversity by increasing the extinction risk of many species, but there are very few examples of climate change actually leading to population declines, because this is a challenging topic to study. One prominent way that climate change is expected to affect populations is by changes in the timing of life-cycle events, such as flowering date or date of emergence from hibernation. Despite changes in the timing of such events being one of the most widespread biological responses to climate change, incredibly little is known about whether and how changes in timing affect popualtions, especially for plants. This project therefore aims to link climate change-induced shifts in the timing of life-cycle events, such as leaf-out and flowering, to plant population dynamics. We are conducting a field experiment where we experimentally advance the timing of leaf-out and flowering in several plant species by melting the snow early. These plants will be compared to control plants to learn how these earlier life-cycle events affect plant survival and reproduction. The data from the field study will be used to build population models that will allow us to understand whether earlier life-cycle events increase or decrease plant popualtions, and why (or have no effect). In doing so, this project will be one of the most comprehensive assessments to date of the risk that climate change-induced earlier life-cycle events pose to plant biodiversity. Non-technical Abstract (Project 2): Pollinator populations are declining, but we have a very poor understanding of the ecological consequences of these declines. There is widespread concern that many flowering plant species will decline in tandem with pollinators because approximately 87% of flowering plants rely on animal pollination for their reproduction. Increases in pollination typically increase the number of seeds a plant can make, and because of this, scientists who study pollination often assume that changes in the amount of pollination have direct consequences for the persistence of plant populations. However, the number of seeds a plant makes typically does not limit population growth, especially for perennial plants. This suggests that alterations to pollination may not actually have extensive consequences for plant populations. But no studies have connected pollinator-mediated declines in seed output to the actual ability of a plant population to persist. This project makes that connection using mathematical population models informed by data from a field experiment. In doing so, this project will advance basic scientific knowledge by bridging two ecological subfields that are surprisingly disconnected, and it will increase our understanding of the ecological consequences of pollinator declines.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions
