Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
Non-Technical Abstract: My proposed research focuses on how climate change is impacting Tiger Salamander populations through both observation and experimentation. Climate change is particularly strong at high elevations and potentially influential on the biology of amphibians. Building upon three decades of research, my collaborators and I are exploring how changes in temperature and precipitation have and continue to change the life history and population dynamics of this species. Specifically, we propose to continue our population monitoring, increase our environmental monitoring, continue implanting internal temperatures within the salamanders themselves, and conduct a series of experiments aimed at understanding how elevation, temperature, and density may interact to affect important developmental milestones. Additionally, my lab proposes to continue our work at understanding the disease issues affecting Boreal Toads and to explore methods that can aid the restoration of this state-endangered species.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Disease ecology; Food web biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Species Interactions; Theory; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Connection Between Parasitism and Reproduction in Parasitic Plants
Non-Technical Abstract: Parasitic plants attach to other plants and ?steal? water and nutrients. Accounting for approximately 1% of all flowering plants, parasitic plants cause billions of dollars worth of damage to agricultural fields annually. In natural systems, parasitic plants have been shown to play important ecological roles due to their close associations with host plants. Despite this, basic research that addresses how the process of parasitism may affect parasitic plant evolution is lacking. Characterizing the genetic mechanisms that underlie parasitic attachment to host plants will be integral to understanding the ecology and evolution of parasitic plants. Recent work on the gene expression during the attachment process suggests that parasitic attachment genes may also play an important role in the function of pollen as part of the normal reproductive process in plants. If the genes that control parasitic attachment also play a role in normal reproduction, that may impact the way in which parasitic plant reproductive systems evolve. To investigate this connection further, I will 1) compare the genes expressed during attachment and reproduction and 2) conduct a series of experiments to compare pollen function in parasitic vs. non-parasitic plants. My results will have implications for the broader process of diversification in parasitic plants.
Research Area: Genetics; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating sedimentation rates and carbon storage in beaver ponds
Non-Technical Abstract: Beavers are ecosystem engineers, modifying the physical complexity of rivers and floodplains. Beaver dams can attenuate and store water, sediment, carbon, and other constituents, but many questions remain. For example, the timescale and spatial variability of sediment accumulation behind beaver dams has been investigated over long timescales (e.g., centuries to millenia) and short timescales (e.g.,

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Plant-Herbivore Interactions Along Elevational Gradients
Non-Technical Abstract: Insects feeding affects plant growth and has driven plants to evolve and invest in costly defenses. The evolutionary ecology of plant-herbivore interactions has important implications for understanding both natural ecosystems and for the agricultural systems that humans depend on for both food and fiber. The elevational gradients surrounding RMBL provide a natural laboratory to study how plant-herbivore interactions vary in response to climatic variation. We are testing how plant damage varies from low to high elevations and, correspondingly, how plant investment in herbivore defenses varies. This work provides insight into the evolution of plant defense, and also how these interactions are likely respond to climate change.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Ecology and impacts of non-native mustards in the subalpine zone
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants in the Brassicaceae (mustard) family are of broad interest to biologists. Phytochemical compounds unique to the Brassicaceae (i.e., glucosinolates) include secondary compounds that deter generalists, attract specialist insect herbivores, and deter fungal pathogen attacks. The specific concentrations and combinations of these compounds vary across different mustard taxa and may also change in response to abiotic conditions and through time. In high altitude meadow ecosystems like those around RMBL, native mustard species such as Boechera stricta, Cardaminecordifolia, and others are important hosts to specialist butterfly larvae. However in recent years, several exotic mustards such as Thlaspi arvense, Lepidium latifolium, Capsella species and Barbarea vulgaris, have been rapidly increasing in abundance across sub-alpine meadow and grassland/sage habitats, posing potential novel ecological and evolutionary interactions with native butterflies. In other ecosystems, invasive mustards are also known to disrupt native plant-mycorrhizal interactions and we have recently found this to be the case in the subalpine zone as well. The current project is a renewal of ongoing research on the ecology and impacts of non-native mustards in sub-alpine ecosystems. Over the next few years, my general plan of study is to begin to comprehensively document spatial and temporal variation in the phytochemistry and distributions of native and non-native mustard plants in the sub-alpine ecosystem around RMBL and the surrounding landscape. My specific research objectives are to: document abundance and distribution of invasive mustard species across local environmental/elevation gradients; measure temporal and spatial variation in the phytotoxicty and fitness of focal Brassicaceae species; and develop new experiments to test phytochemical responses to specific abiotic variables. The work will involve training new PhD students and REU students at RMBL and the research will inform our understanding of novel species interactions across spatial gradients now and under future climate scenarios.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Phenology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How a range shifting taxa alters interactions of established pond community
Non-Technical Abstract: Organisms that feed on plants play important roles in moving energy and nutrients though ecosystems, which underlies many services that ecosystems provide societies such as fisheries, clean drinking water, and carbon storage. However, the identity and abundance of organisms in ecosystems is changing as warm-climate species move into previously cooler regions that are disproportionately impacted by climate change. Understanding how these species movements alter ecosystem processes is an important step in anticipating and managing the impacts of climate change on ecosystems and their services. This research will investigate how the establishment and subsequent population boom of a novel aquatic insect species into high elevation wetlands influences the timing and magnitude of processes central to all ecosystems: the consumption of plant material, the cycling of nutrients that support plant and animal growth, the availability of prey for predators, and the connections between freshwater habitats and the surrounding terrestrial environment. In addition to scientific advancement, this research will advance early childhood education via kids? science camps, provide opportunities for public outreach via science tours at a field station, and train the next generation of scientists by engaging undergraduate students from historically underrepresented groups in field-based ecological research.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Species Interactions; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Pollination Network Structure, Function, and Response to Perturbation
Non-Technical Abstract: This renewal research application covers three distinct but related projects, all focused on pollination networks, their responses to perturbation, and the relationship between their structure and function. The first project, ?Quantitative Network Structure and Function? has two primary objectives: A) accurately measuring of quantitative network structure (i.e. intensity of interactions) with a focus on testing predictions about quantitative structure from theoretical work we are leading; and B) comparing network structure and function (seed production across multiple plant species) in drought (2018, 2020, 2021, potential future years) vs. non-drought years (2016, 2017, 2019, potential future years). The second project, ?Snowmelt Acceleration and Pollination Network Structure and Function?, is focused on temporally shuffling interaction partners in pollination networks via medium-scale (10 x 14 m) snowmelt acceleration experiments that are controlled and spatially replicated. The temporal re-shuffling occurs via changes in plant flowering phenology in manipulated patches, whereas we expect the pollinator community to remain relatively unchanged given that the scale of movement of individual pollinators is typically much larger than the spatial scale of our plots. The third project, ?Understanding Pollinator Functional Responses and Benefit Accrual Under Perturbation? is focused on improving the integration between models and empirical data in pollination networks. In particular, this work will for the first time empirically estimate the functional forms of 1) multi-species pollinator functional responses, i.e. how pollinator visitation changes with plant density, as well as plant and pollinator species identity; and 2) the numerical response (reproductive benefit accrual) of plants with respect to pollinator visits, i.e. how fecundity changes with pollinator visit frequency change. The benefit accrual component will involve new experiments focused on plant seed set. These empirically validated functional forms will then be incorporated into models, which we will subsequently test by conducting short-term perturbation experiments, in a full modeling-empirical cycle.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating the Impact of Climate Change on Ecosystem Function
Non-Technical Abstract: I will be using the pre-existing WaRM network where warming and dominant species removal happens at a high and low elevation to determine how warming and removal impacts an ecosystem over the course of a growing season. Paying extra attention to the spring and fall, I will try to quantify how warming and removal impact ecosystem function (such as plant productivity).
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Understanding Watershed Processes in Complex Terrain
Non-Technical Abstract: Mountain headwaters provide much of the world?s water. In western North America, the Colorado River provides water for 30 million people and 4 million acres of irrigated agriculture. The western Colorado Rockies and the watersheds therein contribute a large portion of this water, making this region a key component of this hydrologic system to understand. The East River watershed and the Snodgrass Hillslope specifically, are representative mountain headwater systems with low human impact, making them ideal study locations. We plan install gages to measure streamflow at two locations on the Snodgrass Hillslope. We also plan to measure soil moisture at a multitude of locations across the hillslope. Having both sets of measurements, we can see how the two are related and begin to make broader inferences about the hydrologic processes of this hillslope and others like it. Additionally, our group and collaborating groups are recording atmospheric data, including things such as air temperature, wind speed, relative humidity, and others. This information can be used to approximate how much water is evaporating from the hillslope. Together, all of this information can start to tell us how much of the water that falls in an area is useable by humans and how much lost. It can also show us how various factors, take air temperature for example, might affect the amount of available water. Armed with this improved understanding, we can go on to hypothesize how changes in certain factors might change the availability of water in the future.
Research Area: Hydrology; Meteorology; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Mechanisms of alpine community assembly
dispersal choice of female golden-mantled ground squirrels
Non-Technical Abstract: Natal dispersal, the movement of individuals from birthplace to breeding site where they find mates, is crucial to understand because it plays a major role in population demography, genetic diversity, social structure, and distribution of individuals. To help made important decision like dispersal, animals must use cues from the environment to evaluate the decision between staying and leaving. Cues that juvenile animals may use to determine the dispersal decision include the density of adult animals in the natal area, density and interactions of siblings or closely related individuals, and their body condition at the time of dispersal. In this study, we will investigate whether body size at time of dispersal, density of kin, and kin interactions affect dispersal choice of the golden-mantled ground squirrels (Callospermorphilus lateralis), an asocial ground-dwelling squirrel in the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). In addition to newly collected data, we will also analyze archived data on female juvenile location and activity collected from the same population since 1990 at RMBL to test our hypotheses.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Area: Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The effects of advanced plant phenology on herbivory and plant demography
Non-Technical Abstract: The annual timing of life cycle events, known as phenology, can have strong effects on survival, growth, and reproduction, and can also affect species interactions. Phenology is often regulated by seasonal climatic cues, and therefore climate change is advancing phenology to earlier dates in many species across the world. However, plant phenology is advancing at a faster rate than the organisms that eat plants (herbivores), which invites the possibility of temporal misalignment between plants and herbivores that typically interact. Herbivory strongly impacts plant survival, growth, and reproduction, and therefore plant populations. Changes to plant populations can have ecosystem-wide consequences, so it is critical to investigate how altered timing of plant-herbivore interactions affects plants. However, almost no research considering this link focuses on consequences for plants, instead focusing on the herbivores. My research therefore investigates how advanced plant phenology changes herbivory and subsequently plant growth and reproduction. To do this, I will experimentally induce early plant phenology by causing the snow to melt early, since early snowmelt will be a major consequence of climate change. I will observe herbivory and plant growth and reproduction to decipher how plant performance is affected by altered plant-herbivore phenology.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Impacts of dandelions (Taraxacum officinale) on plant-pollinator networks
Non-Technical Abstract: The purpose of this project is to document how non-native dandelions (Taraxacum officinale) affect plant-pollinator communities near RMBL. Jones (2004) tested if dandelions compete for pollinators with Delphinium nuttallianum, by removing dandelion flower heads from experimental plots. Although dandelions did not depress D. nuttallianum seed-set, Jones? (2004) study provides a unique opportunity to resurvey these plots after 25 years to address several questions as to how dandelions might be competing with native plants for pollinators and altering species interactions. The purpose of this project is to address the following three questions: Has dandelion flower abundance increased over the past 25 years? Do dandelions rewire plant-pollinator visitation networks? Do dandelions alter pollen-transport networks?
Research Area: Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effect of Accelerated Snowmelt on Plant-Pollinator Interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: This project is an extension of the accelerated snowmelt manipulation and network interaction sampling experiments from Berry Brosi?s Research Application. In addition to the plant-pollinator interactions and plant fecundity components included in the Brosi lab Research plan, I will extend this work by 1) collecting pollen from captured pollinators for DNA metabarcoding; 2) collecting flower stigmas to examine patterns of stigmatic pollen deposition; and 3) collecting seeds to subsequently investigate genetic diversity. Plant-pollinator mutualisms are dependent on the timing (phenology) of both species, i.e. plants must produce flowers at the same time that insects are foraging. Many plants that grow in high altitude habitats use snowmelt as a trigger for flower production, while insect phenology is driven largely by temperature [1]. In these montane habitats, snow is melting earlier than in the past [2]. This accelerated snowmelt may cause a de-coupling of emergence cues in plant-pollinator interactions, leading to a temporal mismatch. This concern is underscored by previous studies showing that plants are more likely to advance their phenology in response to warmer temperatures than insects [1]. In addition, earlier flowering in certain species can cause a decrease in plant fitness [3], specifically in high-altitude plants that bloom early in the season and are dependent on snowmelt timing [4]. The Brosi lab project investigating this topic involves snowmelt acceleration manipulations that are covered in detail in the Brosi lab Research Application. The work proposed here will extend the research from the Brosi lab Research Description in three ways. First, I will remove pollen from the insects that are captured from field sampling, for later DNA metabarcoding back at the University of Washington (UW). The pollen DNA metabarcoding will provide information about which plant species the pollinator visited prior to being captured [5]. This will also allow for a direct comparison of the networks built through interaction sampling and those built through metabarcoding [6]. Second, for the target plants for which the Brosi lab collects fecundity data, I will collect stigmas and seeds for a subset of individuals. The stigma collection component will further illuminate how earlier snowmelt is affecting plant reproduction by allowing me to connect snowmelt manipulation to conspecific pollen transfer, which is a key metric of pollination success. I will collect seeds for subsequent population genetic analyses (using ddRADseq, given that we are working with non-model organisms) analysis back at my home institution. This will allow me to better understand if the snowmelt acceleration experiments impact pollinator visitation in ways that cascade to gene flow (e.g. more or fewer visits to flowers within the same plant individual, or close by individuals).
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Drivers and consequences of bumble bee body size variation
Non-Technical Abstract: Body size is arguably one the most important traits influencing the physiology and ecology of animals. For bumble bees, size variation between and within castes is an essential component of their social organization. However, the precise ecological drivers and consequences of size variation remains poorly understood for bumble bees, which are both ecologically and economically important insect pollinators. Despite their ubiquity and importance, bumble bees are experiencing declines across the globe and over a third of assessed species are currently at risk of extinction. Bumble bees are hypothesized to be particularly at risk of decline in part because of their relatively large body size. In addition, there is evidence bumble bees are experiencing declines in body size, consistent with broader trends of declines in animal body size in response to climate change. By combining field-based size distribution data, foraging ecology, and data from long-term population monitoring, my research will shed light on potential mechanisms that drive bumble bee size declines and the outcomes of these declines on bumble bee ecology.
Research Area: Community ecology; Insect biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Adaptive Plasticity of Coloration in Response to Environmental Change
Non-Technical Abstract: When rapid environmental changes occur, different selective forces can create phenotypic trade-offs in which a trait can provide fitness benefits or costs under different environmental conditions. Amphibians are particularly vulnerable to environmental change, and previous research has revealed that some species will plastically respond to variation in temperature and ultra-violet radiation (UVR) by altering their coloration. Divergent selection on coloration may change with elevation and climate induced shifts in temperature because high temperatures are likely to result in lighter color morphs but as elevation increases, UVR exposure increases leading to the prediction that darker color morphs will be more common. I will evaluate the adaptive plasticity of coloration in Ambystoma mavortium, the tiger salamander, by testing the following hypotheses: 1) increased UVR levels will more strongly affect color plasticity than temperature; 2) older individuals will converge on similar coloration because color plasticity is more important to larval fitness; and 3) coloration will influence the thermal preference of salamanders. I will compare variation in coloration metrics of wild A. mavortium present at different developmental stages (hatchlings, larvae, and adults) along an elevational gradient in western Colorado. Individuals will be photographed, and coloration metrics (saturation, brightness, and hue) will be quantified using Adobe Photoshop to compare differences in coloration. The information I gather in this study can be used to further understand both phenotypic shifts organisms face under environmental changes and the consequences of those shifts, allowing scientists to better manage amphibians and providing a guide for the conservation of other species.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Topography, forest structure, and drought response in subalpine forests
Non-Technical Abstract: Forests are key components of water and carbon budgets in the Rocky Mountains. These ecosystems are increasingly exposed to water and temperature stress as drought conditions intensify across the western U.S. Understanding forests? sensitivity to drought and the factors that influence forest drought responses is essential for developing management strategies that conserve forests? ecological, recreational, and cultural value. The primary objective of the proposed research is to clarify the role of environmental and physiological factors in conditioning forest responses to drought. I propose to pursue three objectives over the next two years: (1) Complete a network of instrumented forest monitoring plots to understand the variable effects of solar radiation, snow accumulation, and subsurface properties on forest structure, growth, and dynamics; (2) quantify how tree growth rates vary with space and time over the climate record of the area; (3) characterize the variability of transpiration in the watershed?s dominant conifer species.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Reproductive phenology in golden-mantled ground squirrels
Non-Technical Abstract: Mammals living in high-altitude environments must time their reproduction carefully so that offspring are born when food is available. For hibernating squirrels, food does not become available in the spring until melting snow stimulates growth of green vegetation, hence these squirrels often must emerge from hibernation and mate before the snow melts. However, we don?t know what cues females use to anticipate the time of snow melt, in order to determine the correct time to mate, and we don?t know what the consequences are for females that mate too late or too early. This study proposes to address both questions. The results will not only increase our understanding of how mammals adapt to the strong seasonality of high-altitude environments, but it also may enhance our understanding of the effects of climate change. Scientists fear that one consequence of warming temperatures is that the cues that animals use to anticipate seasonal events may no longer accurately predict those events.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Genetics; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Microbial processes in the wetlands of the Brush Creek confluence
Non-Technical Abstract: Wetlands are the largest natural source of methane emissions, responsible for approximately one third of anthropogenic and natural emissions. Microbes are largely responsible for the methane emission in wetlands. Here I am proposing a field campaign where I sample the microbial communities of fifty soil samples taken at five different wetland pools adjacent to the Brush Creek confluence of the East River. I will use metagenome resolved metagenomics to study what microbes live in these wetlands and what their metabolic capacity is (in other words, what chemicals are they able to produce and consume). I am also interested in how these microbial processes with vary with distance from the drainage site, how these processes vary with depth, and how these processes vary from upstream to downstream. I anticipate that this analysis will be beneficial to other RMBL scientists, who are interested in understanding biogeochemical processes across ecosystems.
Research Area: Microbiomes; Microbiology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Microclimate effect on FBPase and larval development
Non-Technical Abstract: I am interested in how the environment affects organism development through natural genetic variation of metabolic processes. I am proposing a study using Colias eriphyle to look at how microclimate differences influence the natural genetic variation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, a glycolytic enzyme, and larval development. Using a field set-up involving two locations, one in direct light and one in partial light, I will be able to determine if warming affects the survival and development of whichever genotypes are found to be present in the study population.
Research Area: Genetics; Insect biology; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Vertebrate antipredator and communication studies
Non-Technical Abstract: Since 2001, I have had an approved UCLA protocol to study antipredator behavior and communication in free-living birds by employing simple experiments. Many of these projects have been designed to study questions associated with wildlife conservation and management and/or to better understand human impacts on wildlife. In 2008 I extended this UCLA protocol to include other vertebrates (mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and fishes). UCLA supports this (admittedly) very flexible protocol that focuses on methods but not specific questions. Much of the proposed work will be conducted by undergraduate students at the RMBL (much of the UCLA work is conducted by students in my field and marine biology classes). Rather than citing specific references to justify a single question, I append relevant publications that illustrate the types of projects we have conducted below. At the RMBL I will design specific projects with the students? interests in mind. Projects will have to fit within procedures identified in this protocol. There are some that might not be focused on 'animals' per se and thus fall outside this protocol. For instance, there may be projects that broadcast sounds in the environment to study the 'habitat acoustics'. Such an experiment would not be targeted towards animals. I will provide close supervision of all work. The methods I describe below can be used to ask a variety of research questions and it is these methods that will likely be used by students conducting their projects. The experimental manipulations are relatively noninvasive. The animals are observed, but not handled, and are only minimally stressed or disturbed by a brief change in the environment. Similar sorts of experiments that I've done over the past two decades have caused limited disturbance.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The marmots of RMBL
Non-Technical Abstract: The study of yellow-bellied marmots at the RMBL is the third-longest study of free-living, individually-marked mammals in the world. Over the next five years we aim to continue to collect demographic, genetic/genomic, behavioral, and endocrinological data to help develop a comprehensive view of marmot population biology and evolutionary dynamics of a variety of behavioral, physiological and life history traits. We will continue our studies of aging and senescence and hope to expand our studies of the causes and consequences of microbial diversity in the intestinal and oral microbiomes.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Disease ecology; Genetics; Long-term research; Microbiomes; Modeling; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Ecohydrological Controls on the Soil CO2 Flux up an Elevation Gradient
Non-Technical Abstract: Mountainous ecosystems are currently experiencing a lot of change in their water inputs. With the dominant water source, snowpack, decreasing and melting earlier. This change in the primary water source not only influences the aboveground functioning of the ecosystem, but also the belowground part as well. The belowground ecosystem is comprised of microbes that breakdown organic matter and plant roots that are growing to access crucial nutrients and water. Both the microbes and roots respire CO2 when they are conducting these functions in the belowground ecosystem. Our research aims to understand how changes in moisture inputs, such as changes in snow depth and monsoon rains influences these belowground ecosystem up an elevation gradient in the East River Watershed, near Crested Butte Colorado. We will quantify the CO2 produced by both the microbes and the roots up the elevational gradient and see how each respond to environmental changes within and between years. To do this, we will combine continuous soil CO2 measurements with spatially distributed soil surface CO2 measurements and novel radiocarbon methods which will enable us to separate the plant and microbial sources of the CO2 and identify how they vary in space and time. These measurements will be paired with forest green up, snow melt, microbial activity, and environmental factors such as air and soil temperature, soil moisture, and groundwater flow. These sampling sites will be taken in the two dominant forest types, Spruce/Fir, and Aspen in the East River Watershed. Our work is motivated by our overarching hypothesis that separately quantifying how below-ground microbe and roots are influenced by the changing water inputs, is necessary for understanding the below-ground forested ecosystems resilience to a changing environment.
Research Area: Climate change; Long-term research; Microbiology; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Response of plant volatiles to a changing thermal environment
Non-Technical Abstract: Flowering plants emit hundreds of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) through their leaves and flowers that give them characteristic scents. Those compounds can be attractive to pollinators or deter herbivores, and contribute to processes of reproductive isolation and speciation. However, how the emission of these volatiles might vary in response to changing environmental conditions, and whether this plasticity is adaptive, remains poorly understood. The overall amount or composition of scent blends could change with temperature, potentially altering communication cues and consequently levels of pollination or herbivory. This project uses artificial warming chambers to manipulate the temperature of plants in the field, to examine how plant volatile organic compounds known to be important for pollinator visitation respond to increased temperature, using a well-established plant system that is already experiencing a changing growing season.
Research Area: Climate change; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Field collections of Dipterans (flies) for genetic and seasonal monitoring
Non-Technical Abstract: My lab studies how insects adapt to variable environments to tolerate environmental extremes and to synchronize their life cycles with seasonal variability. In this project we will be collecting several fly species that we will use to establish lab lines for environmental manipulation experiments, and one species that we will use as one of many geographic samples in a larger study of adaptation across the landscape.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Insect biology; Phenology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Paleoenvironmental reconstruction in the Gunnison Basin from sediments
Non-Technical Abstract: Lake and fen sediments are rich archives of information about past environments. Near RMBL, these sediments have the potential to reach back 18,000 years to the Last Glacial Maximum. Through the analysis of pollen grains, charcoal fragments, and sediment geochemistry, the goal of this project is to reconstruct past vegetation communities, fire dynamics, and climate in greater RMBL region. Increased understanding of the impacts of past climate changes on ecosystems provides valuable information that will help land managers better prepare for future conditions.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Response of plant and microbial respiration to changing cold season climate
Non-Technical Abstract: Winter is changing in the western US mountains. There is less snowfall, snow is melting earlier in the spring, and the warm summers are becoming longer. These changes in winter and water availability impact forests. Belowground in the forest soil, microorganisms break down organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide (CO2), an important greenhouse gas that is warming Earth. Plant roots produce CO2 also, via their metabolism. Our research seeks to understand how changes in winter snowpack influence the amount of CO2 produced in soils in the East River watershed, near Crested Butte, Colorado. We will quantify the production of CO2 by microorganisms and plant roots across different elevations and seasons. We will work in the two main forest types of the region, evergreen spruce/fir and deciduous aspen, applying unique experimental measurements. We will make use of existing long-term measurements to understand how past changes in snow amount and duration of cover have affected soil CO2. Information gathered from our experimental work and data analyses will be used to improve predictions of soil CO2 produced in the future using models. Our proposed work is motivated by the hypothesis that changing winter snow amounts will impact how microorganisms and roots function separately, and thus understanding these influences is necessary to predict how the ecosystems will respond to future climate.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Phenology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Beaver Ponds: Methylmercury Production and Export in the Western U.S
Non-Technical Abstract: The western United States (U.S.) is experiencing severe drought conditions exacerbated by climate change. As annual precipitation and runoff generation decline, American beaver (Castor canadensis) populations are increasing, in part due to reintroduction efforts aimed at restoring water resources. With time beaver institute a pattern of dam building and abandonment that drastically influence the river corridor through alterations to the geomorphology and the biogeochemistry. Beaver dams have variable impacts on the production of methylmercury (MeHg), a neurotoxin that can bioaccumulate and biomagnify with successive trophic levels. Methylation is driven by myriad biogeochemical processes that are mediated by geomorphic processes and the physical template. Previous work has demonstrated that beaver ponds create conditions for methylation, the rate of which fluctuates throughout the year (Roy et al., 2009a; Roy et al., 2009b). In Summer 2024, I will collect samples to quantify total mercury (THg), MeHg, sulfate (SO42-) reduction rates (SRR), methylation and demethylation rates, among other biogeochemical measurements in sediment, surface, and porewater. Together, the data will reveal the dominant mechanisms within differently aged beaver ponds throughout the year that drive the production and export of MeHg, providing information to stakeholders about the implications beaver have for water quality. Effectively communicating science to the community that uses the resource under investigation is crucial. Final steps will include making CZ case studies that can be used by the geoscience community for undergraduate teaching and to present to the community that the research was conducted in.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Plant community dynamics in a changing environment
Non-Technical Abstract: Predicting the responses of species to environmental change is a key goal for community ecology, especially in applied management and restoration contexts. My research focuses on this general challenge in two complementary contexts: alpine plant community assembly, and quaking aspen forest responses to drought and other stressors.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Vegetation Recovery after Termination of Heating
Non-Technical Abstract: Much research at RMBL and elsewhere has focused on the effects of climate warming on plant communities. Less studied is how these communities will recover upon termination of heating. Although society is unlikely to actually reduce atmospheric greenhouse gas levels in the coming decades, it is nevertheless of interest to understand how reversible are the ecological effects of warming. Do ecosystems undergo tipping-point-like transitions under warming that lock in change even when warming is reversed, or can we expect recovery of our altered ecosystems should society ever be able to undo the current phase of warming? If so, on what time scale? RMBL provides an opportunity to address these questions by taking advantage of the termination in 2019 of the long-term meadow-warming experiment. In that experiment, measurements revealed significant shifts in plant dominance and flowering success in heated versus control plots. This study will measure these same vegetation variables at least up to 7 years post-termination, to determine the degree to which vegetation in the former heated plots is recovering to levels observed in the former control plots.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Climate change; Community ecology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Insects on Ligusticum
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants are consumed by a variety of insect herbivores. These herbivores vary in abundance from place to place and over time. The purpose of this project is to monitor the abundance and phenology of insects and other arthropods on the focal plant Ligusticum porteri. The primary herbivore of interests are aphids, which colonize host plant flowering stalks. Since 2017, we have conducted weekly censuses at twenty sites along an elevation gradient. These different sites provide varying combinations of temperature and snow melt timing, which we also monitor. We use these data to assess associations between herbivore abundance and the biotic and abiotic factors that vary among sites and study years. These associations provide insights into the impacts of climate change on plant-herbivore interactions.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Phenology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils
Non-Technical Abstract: Regional Assessment of Drought Impacts on Soils: Development of an integrated soil functional mapping framework. Soils serve critical roles in most terrestrial ecosystems. In particular, the accumulation of soil organic matter is an important function supporting ecosystem productivity and serving as a feedback to climate change. With the more frequent occurrence of extensive and persistent drought conditions in the Western US, there is an urgent need to improve our ability to map soil organic matter and forecast how it may respond. To address this need, we are developing and testing an integrated framework for measurement, mapping, and modeling of soil functions at a regional scale in the East River and surrounding watersheds. This work will result in development of detailed maps of soil properties, a community accessible archive of soil samples, and an integrated framework for modeling changes in soil functions (not limited to soil organic matter storage) across the region.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Wildflower Reproduction Phenology and Seed Traits under Early Snowmelt
Non-Technical Abstract: As snow melts earlier in the spring due to climate change, it has the potential to cause shifts in flowering time, especially for spring wildflowers. However, research on this topic often focuses solely on flowering time, with little regard for subsequent seed production and maturation timing. Cohesive research on the entire reproductive stage (flowering and seed production), and how timing of this stage impacts seed traits, is crucial for truly understanding the effects of early snowmelt on wildflower reproduction. Therefore, for three seasons, I will monitor the flowering and seed maturation of six subalpine spring wildflower species at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory from both early snowmelt and control plots. I will then collect a subset of these seeds and analyze their viability, germination, and traits in the Chicago Botanic Garden laboratory and greenhouses.The results of this study will provide novel insight into early snowmelt impacts on spring wildflowers, as well as provide a framework for restorationists who struggle to determine the appropriate seed collection timing and quantity under climate change.
Research Area: Phenology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Expanding Natural History and Community Science Resources at RMBL
Non-Technical Abstract: Natural history collections and community science are increasingly recognized as important data sources for the study of global change biology. Natural history collections, such as herbaria, document changing diversity, distribution, phenology, morphology and genetics over decades and centuries. They also provide many opportunities for education and outreach in taxonomy, ecology and conservation. Community science initiatives, such as iNaturalist, likewise expand the range, in time and space, of data generated on species distributions and phenology and provide an engaging platform for education and outreach in natural history. The natural history collections and curated iNaturalist observations at RMBL serve an increasingly wide array of users and the herbarium is an important resource for plant identification and data archiving for scientists, students and the public. Over the next 5 years I plan to expand and improve the collections, facilitate access to collection data, and utilize natural history collections and community science for research, education and outreach.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Bumble bee thermal tolerance, climate variation, and population trends
Non-Technical Abstract: All living things are bounded by temperature. Too hot, and biological functions start to breakdown, like a car overheating. Too cold, and life hits pause, like a computer freezing. Different species have different temperature limits, depending on where they live and what season they are active in, and individual organisms can have different limits depending on their life stage and body size. Understanding these limits and how they vary can help us better understand how species cope with their natural environment and environmental change. Some animals, like humans, can make their own heat and maintain a constant internal temperature regardless of their surroundings, while some, like reptiles, rely on environmental sources of heat, like the sun. A few groups of animals do both, including bumble bees. Like other insects, bumble bees are sensitive to environmental temperatures, but are also able to vibrate their wing muscles to warm their bodies. This is part of what allows bumble bees to live in cold environments, like the Colorado Rocky Mountains. However, bumble bees can vary a lot in ways that may affect their ability to tolerate temperature extremes. Different species are active at different times of the year, as are the social castes queens and workers, which may influence their hot and cold tolerance. Different individual bees may also vary in their thermal tolerance based on their body size, as smaller sized organisms tend to lose heat faster and get colder more quickly. These difference in thermal tolerance are important for the basic biology of bumble bees and can help us predict how bumble bees may be affected by changing temperatures under climate change.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Modeling Drivers of Summer Streamflow Changes at the Micro-catchment Scale
Non-Technical Abstract: Mountainous watersheds, such as the Colorado River Basin, are key sources for a diversity of human needs and are under threat from climate change. The Colorado has seen a precipitous drop in river flows, endangering the water supply of 1 in 10 Americans. This study posits increased summertime evapotranspiration (ET) from rising temperatures is a primary driver of this water loss. Furthermore, subsurface flow will continue to subsidize high ET-areas causing future streamflow declines as temperatures in the Colorado River Basin continues to accelerate. To investigate these theories, an intensive monitoring and data collection campaign will occur on the representative micro-catchment of Snodgrass Mountain outside Crested Butte, CO to quantify and bound ET dynamics. Data collected on Snodgrass will be then used to help inform a high-resolution hydrologic model of the watershed to simulate future ET trends, with important implications for water supply and management.
Research Area: Climate change; Hydrology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Clay formation and organic matter stabilization across an alpine watershed
Non-Technical Abstract: Soil organic carbon (OC) constitutes the largest terrestrial pool of carbon, and changes in its size have the potential to modulate atmospheric CO2 levels. As such, the underlying controls on OC stabilization and their sensitivities to climatic change have been increasingly scrutinized. The existing paradigm for OC stabilization suggests that due to their high specific surface areas and negatively charged surfaces, secondary clay minerals that form in soil protect OC from oxidation. Thus, a direct relationship between clay mineral abundance and OC may hold across soil types and climates. Despite this understanding, reactive transport models (RTMs) cannot reconcile soil geochemistry and OC profiles, pointing to knowledge gaps regarding organo-mineral interactions and their constitutive controls. Consequently, these challenges result in great uncertainty in the treatment of soil OC dynamics in Earth systems models and their concomitant effects on future climate projections. To further understand clay mineral formation and its relationship with OC dynamics over a hydrologic year, Here we propose to advance our understanding of clay mineral formation, OC stabilization, and their controls across a recently deglaciated, headwater catchment (East River watershed) using high-frequency geochemical analyses that track clay mineral formation. Preliminary analyses, including a numerical inversion of a solute time series show that the amount of cation uptake by clay varies on short (event) timescales. These same events also feature changes in dissolved carbon species, which may be plausibly linked to the dynamics of clay mineral cycling. Following these results, we designed preliminary RTMs that include Li isotopes: a novel proxy for clay formation. The models predict a covariation in Li isotope ratios (in sediment and soil water) with solid-phase and dissolved OC. Together, these results support clay mineral formation as a dynamic and seasonally modulated process that is closely linked to OC dynamics. Planned measurements of Li isotope ratios of soil, river water, and bedrock in the East River, along with new RTMs with variable organo-mineral couplings, will help validate these preliminary findings.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Evaluating mechanisms underlying disturbance-related demographic change
Non-Technical Abstract: Human development is expanding rapidly into wildlands to keep up with exponential population growth, forcing wildlife to either emigrate or adapt to increased disturbance. Species that adapt often exhibit behavioral changes that can have subsequent survival consequences. Despite a strong focus on urbanization?s impact on species behavior, there is increasing evidence of behavioral shifts occurring at a low-density, rural scale. In particular, changes in antipredator behavior and sociality may be altered by small-scale anthropogenic development. Antipredator vigilance and flight initiation distance can directly affect survival-related behaviors such as foraging or reproduction. Social structure and individual social relationships have been found to have complex impacts on species survival. While both vigilance and sociality have been studied extensively, little is known about how built structures may alter these behaviors by impeding an animal?s visibility of a landscape. The yellow-bellied marmot (Marmota flaviventer), a social, behaviorally adaptable rodent, is an ideal model species to analyze the relationship between rural human disturbance and behavior. Previous studies have determined that marmot behaviors, such as vigilance and mating, influence their survival, which may impact their demography. Marmots can acclimate to humans, which may also have long-term survival consequences. My study goals are to: 1) determine whether there are significant differences in antipredator behaviors in disturbed versus undisturbed areas; 2) determine whether there are significant differences in social behaviors in disturbed versus undisturbed areas; and 3) use statistical models to pinpoint any underlying mechanisms that may influence species demography in response to human disturbance. I aim to fill a crucial knowledge gap in how wildlife are influenced by rural anthropogenic development through changes in landscape visibility. My results can be useful for future studies on how disturbance influences wildlife behavior and may create novel insights for the conservation management of social species in human-modified environments.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Beaver dam influence on floodplain hydro-biogeochemistry
Non-Technical Abstract: This research investigates the ecological impact of beaver dam analogs (BDAs) on gravel bed river floodplains, focusing on Trail Creek in Gunnison County, Colorado. Historically, there were significant reductions in North American beaver populations, altering floodplain dynamics including, but not limited to, reduced hydrologic connectivity, depleted summer baseflow, and lessened capacity to store carbon and metals. Recently, the importance of beaver dams for riparian water and nutrient retention, as well as other ecosystem benefits, have been recognized. This study aims to understand how BDAs can enhance summer and late season baseflow volumes and hydrologic connectivity while also assessing their role in trapping colloidal carbon and metals. The project will leverage already installed and planned BDAs, as well as natural beaver dams, to establish before-and-after datasets. The findings are expected to contribute valuable insights into low-tech process-based restoration techniques and improve our understanding of complex ecosystem interactions and adaptations to climate-induced changes in glaciated mountain landscapes.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effects of herbivory on life-history and long-term demography.
Non-Technical Abstract: The effects of herbivore damage on plant reproductive success are most often assessed by counting fruit and seed production over a few years. Long-term, demographic data sets can be extraordinarily useful in elucidating patterns that cannot be revealed within the timeframe of a typical, 2-4 year project. I have monitored the demography of several populations of two long-lived, perennial plants, Sticky Polemonium (Polemonium foliosissimum) and Scarlet Gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata) in and around the RMBL, off and on, for over 12 years for each species. Both are subject to frequent predispersal seed predation and herbivory by deer which sometimes reduces their annual reproductive success to zero. The two species are uniquely different in that one, Scarlet Gilia, is a long-lived but monocarpic perennial and the other, Sticky Polemonium, also a long-lived perennial, exhibits a rare breeding system (gynodioecy) in which some individuals are typical, hermaphrodites while others function only as females. These differences in reproductive strategies, along with other life-history traits, provide exciting opportunities to ask questions about the effects of herbivory on demographic processes, sex-ratios, and life-history traits. Over the next five years, I aim to accomplish two overarching goals: 1) analyze my long-term data sets for each species to reveal the ways in which herbivore damage affects life history traits and population growth rates; and 2) continue to monitor populations of Sticky Polemonium to examine the stability of sex ratios within and among populations over time and assess if herbivory levels are correlated with changes in sex ratios.
Research Area: Long-term research; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Impacts of Climate Change on Bee Behavior across Socio-Ecological Contexts
Non-Technical Abstract: In order to understand how climate change will impact bee populations, it is important to learn how increased temperature will alter bee behavior. This project will explore the impacts of heat stress on the behavioral mechanisms of two different bee populations to understand how the socio-ecological environment influences bee response to climate change. This research will also test a molecular mechanism for regulating heat stress and behavior across socio-ecological environments.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Genetics; Insect biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Impacts of Early Snowmelt on Subalpine Plant Reproduction and Survival
Non-Technical Abstract: Snowmelt is a vital spring water source and also cues the phenology (life cycle event timing) of subalpine plants. Climate change is causing snowmelt to happen earlier in the spring and precipitation to become more variable, which can affect plant-pollinator interactions, plant reproduction, and plant survival; over time, these impacts could threaten plant species persistence in mountain areas. In my research, I experimentally changed both snowmelt timing and precipitation amount to understand the consequences of climate change for subalpine plants. Specifically, I used shade cloth set out in early spring to cause earlier snowmelt and rain out shelters to reduce precipitation and then measured the flowering timing, plant and flower size, flower rewards (nectar and pollen), pollinator visitation frequency, drought stress, survival, and number of seeds of four subalpine plant species. My preliminary results from conducting these experiments from 2021-2023 suggest that while earlier snowmelt causes a consistent shift to earlier flowering timing in all species studied, it has both negative and positive effects on pollinator visitation, plant size and fruit number depending on the seasonality of the year and the species. For example, some species had reduced plant size and fruit number in the earlier snowmelt treatment but other species did not, and these trends were not consistent across both years. Understanding the impacts of early snowmelt and reduced precipitation and which species may be more vulnerable to climate alterations will allow us to better predict climate changes impacts on mountain ecosystems.
Research Area: Climate change; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stream Tracker: Documenting flow duration on non-perennial streams
Non-Technical Abstract: This project will expand an existing program, Stream Tracker, into the Upper Gunnison River Basin. Stream Tracker aims to expand monitoring on non-perennial streams through both sensors and crowd-sourcing. We will establish stream sensors in non-perennial streams across a climate gradient, set up Stream Tracker visual monitoring points along roads and trails, and conduct training for any volunteers interested in contributing to the project.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Species Traits Influence Response of Ant-Aphid Mutualism to Thermal Changes
Non-Technical Abstract: Studying changes in species interactions allows us to better predict and plan for future global change. In this study system, aphids feed on the host plant, Ligusticum poteri. Ants harvest the honeydew excreted by the aphids, and in return, protect the aphids from predators. This research will utilize long-term observational data as well as artificial warming experiments in 2024 to determine how traits among varying ant species impact their behaviors and how these changes alter interactions within the plant-herbivore-predator network. Observations will count insect abundance and track plant phenology, and the experiment will warm host plants and control ant access to the plant colonies. Models will be created to illustrate how aphid distribution and abundance is tied to temperature and the traits of ants tending their colonies.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Modeling; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Underwood-Inouye long-term phenology
Non-Technical Abstract: The long-term phenology project tracks the flowering phenology (timing within season) for ~130 plant species in 35 permanent plots in the RMBL area. This dataset shows evidence of climate change advancing the flowering times of most species.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Phenology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Joint fates of genetic variation and demography under changing climates
Non-Technical Abstract: In a changing climate, a central research goal is to understand whether and how wild populations will persist despite rapid shifts in environmental drivers like precipitation and temperature. As such, many researchers aim to monitor population dynamics across space and time to discern how variation in environmental drivers shape population growth, and use this information to project performance and viability under future climate scenarios. Much less is known, however, about the consequences of environmental change for genetic variation within populations. The extent and persistence of genetic variation in wild populations determines their ability to adapt evolutionarily to changing conditions, and also may directly influence population dynamics and persistence. In this project, I will establish long-term study sites to jointly monitor population dynamics, environmental variation, and genetic variation across a range of populations of the ecological model organism Boechera stricta, a perennial wildflower in the mustard family. These complementary datasets will allow me to directly track how population performance and genetic polymorphism change over time in response to variation in climate variables like precipitation and temperature, and to test for effects between population-level genetic variation and population viability.
Research Area: Genetics; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effect of drought on floral scent and plant-pollinator interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: Plant-pollinator interactions are important for biodiversity and supporting healthy ecosystems. With climate change posing a threat to floral traits that attract pollinators, our focus extends to the often-overlooked olfactory signals and stimuli. Floral scent, composed of diverse volatile organic compounds (VOCs), plays an important role in communication between plants and pollinators. While pollinators use scent to identify and locate rewards, the integration of olfactory stimuli into plant-pollinator networks is still in its early stages. Climate change-induced factors, such as drought and temperature shifts, can disrupt these interactions at both individual and community levels. Our study aims to bridge this knowledge gap, investigating the impact of climate change on floral scent and its role in shaping plant-pollinator networks. By experimentally manipulating precipitation to simulate drought conditions and assessing visual and chemical floral traits across a community, we will employ network analysis to investigate the changes in visitation patterns in plant-pollinator networks under environmental stress. This research aims to advance our understanding of how climate-induced changes in floral scent influence plant-pollinator dynamics at the community level.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The functional response of Bombus sp. in multi-resource environments.
Non-Technical Abstract: Phenology shifts among plants and their pollinators are producing novel species assemblages at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). To address the resulting impact on pollination services, it is necessary to know how pollinator visitation rates vary across flower assemblages and densities; this is known as a functional response. More generally, functional responses characterize key biological rates underlying community function. Functional responses were originally developed for predator-prey interactions; however, the generalization of consumer-resource models has bridged this theory to mutualistic interactions. In this study, I will develop a functional response for Bombus sp. which are highly efficient, and therefore important, pollinators in the RMBL ecosystem. I will first define a set of possible functional response forms describing the following foraging behaviors characteristic of Bombus sp.: generalist niches, adaptive foragers, and individual behavioral variation. I will then empirically measure visitation rates of Bombus sp. across a range of flower assemblages and densities observed during three consecutive summers at RMBL. With the empirical data, I will evaluate which model is the best fit and therefore which behaviors most strongly determine visitation rate. This functional response will be the first one developed for mutualistic interactions using empirical data. In future research, it can be incorporated into models to forecast how pollination services will change in response to floral resource perturbations.
Research Area: Community ecology; Modeling; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Continuing Archival Research of the Environmental History of RMBL
Non-Technical Abstract: This project will continue conducting historical research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL), a high-altitude biological field station located on the Western Slope of the Colorado Rockies. The Lab was built on the site of an old silver mining town, Gothic, which flourished briefly in the early 1880s. In their anthology The Ecology of Place, editors Ian Billick and Mary Price argue that the power of place often motivates ecologists in the field, and that citizens and scientists could work more collaboratively to solve environmental problems if built upon ?a sense of place that sees humans as part of the ecological system, not separate from it.? This project explicitly investigates this more place-based scientific inquiry developing over time, in a place where perennially returning scientists themselves are becoming nearly ?indigenous,? spending entire careers conducting summer field work to understand the dynamics of specific ecosystems or species.
Research Area: Long-term research; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term research on the ecology of ponds in a changing climate
Non-Technical Abstract: High elevation wetlands harbor unique biodiversity, are important components of Rocky Mountain water systems, and are subject to accelerating rates of environmental change. This application summarizes the next 5 years of long-term research by co-PIs Hamish Greig and Amanda Klemmer on the invertebrates that are critical to the diversity and function of high-elevation wetland ecosystems. In 2023, we collected the 34th year of data on wetland caddisflies at a sentinel RMBL field site, the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve, continuing monitoring initiated by Scott Wissinger in 1989. These long-term data document changes in insect abundances and distributions in response to rapid climate change, including several caddisfly species that have moved upslope from wetlands on the valley floors to ponds at treeline. We plan to explore the consequences of fluctuations in the abundance and distributions of these range-expanding species for salamanders that prey on caddisflies, invertebrate communities, and the ecosystem processes such as carbon and nutrient dynamics that influence water quality. We are also working with collaborators to understand how climate alters feedbacks between predator and prey species in pond food webs, and how this influences the response of invertebrates and salamanders to climate stress. In addition to testing new hypotheses, our research will train undergraduate and graduate students, be used as the basis for multiple community outreach events, and the co-PIS will contribute to the administration and strategic direction of RMBL through committee and Board of Trustees service.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Species Interactions

Research Area: Climate science; Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Soil moisture and growth responses to climate extremes in subalpine forests
Non-Technical Abstract: The large objective of this project is to clarify the how environmental and community factors condition subalpine forest responses to climate extremes. Subalpine forests are outsize contributors to the hydrological budget of the Rocky Mountains, but they are exposed to increasing water and temperature stresses associated with climate change. Prior research in these systems has not adequately described the seasonally varying relationships between plant-available water, atmospheric demand, and tree growth. To address these knowledge gaps, I aim to (1) maintain an existing sensor network monitoring soil volumetric water content (?), temperature, conductivity, and atmospheric fluxes to evaluate spatial and temporal variability in soil water dynamics; and (2) to conclude an ongoing dendrochronology campaign seeking to quantify how tree growth rates vary over space and time, across species, and with the instrumented climate record of the watershed. My proposed research is motivated by three core expectations: (1) where water availability is the limiting factor in tree productivity, moisture deficit will be associated with low growth, but there may be other limiting factors present (radiation, pests, or pathogens) that override water limitation; (2) to sustain productivity, trees alternate uptake between shallow and deep water sources where possible and may also redistribute water to replenish dry pools; (3) water availability and plant water use vary across sites as a function of precipitation input, soil properties, and species traits. This effort will shed needed light on the coupling vegetation dynamics and hydrology in headwater forests.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Community ecology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Plant biology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How interactions with mutualists & predators shape plant coexistence
Non-Technical Abstract: Plant community structure is controlled by interactions between individuals that are mediated by shared resources, mutualists, and enemies. It is difficult to study each of these three classes of interactions in parallel due to their great complexity. We propose to isolate the relative effects of each class of interactions by a study of perennial plant coexistence. Perennial plants have life cycles in which competition via resources, pollinators, and seed predators are separated temporally. We will therefore manipulate floral communities of four perennial plant species to parameterize a model which identifies how different forms of interaction impact the viability of plant coexistence and pathways of community assembly.
Research Area: Community ecology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Tracking Bumble Bee Movement Patterns in Subalpine Meadows
Non-Technical Abstract: It is helpful to know how pollinators move around the landscape, because it can allow us to learn things about their natural history, foraging behavior, and navigation strategies. For example, it can help us address questions such as: Where do bees nest? How far do they travel for food, and how does that depend on the amount, quality, and isolation of food resources? Do movement patterns differ between open meadows and urban landscapes? While movement information can help answer these types of questions, it has been hard to collect for insects. They are too small to carry GPS trackers like those used on larger animals, such as deer, so we have relied on visual observations and tracking devices with very small ranges. However, there is a new radio tag device that is small and light enough to put on bumble bees! In this exploratory study, I plan to use this device to track the movement patterns of bumble bee workers in the meadows near RMBL. I hope to combine the information about these bee?s movement patterns with data from other researchers at RMBL to learn about their natural history and foraging behavior, and to compare it with similar data I collect at urban sites to learn about how bees might be navigating these landscapes differently.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Chronic Ndeposition and Didymosphenia geminata blooms
Non-Technical Abstract: Nuisance blooms of the algae Didymosphenia geminata have become increasingly common and widespread over vast portions of its native range over the last several decades. However, unlike most algal blooms, blooms of this species of stalk-producing diatom appear to occur exclusively in streams with very low nutrient concentrations. Moreover, formation of blooms appears to be a recent phenomenon, as few reports of bloom formation by this algal species were reported prior to ~1990 from anywhere across its native range. That this now happens across a large geographic area suggests a driver that operates over large (i.e. continental) scales. This project proposes a preliminary investigation into the potential role of one such driver, chronic atmospheric nitrogen deposition, in facilitating the increased occurrence of D. geminata blooms.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Anoxic microsites control methanogenesis at terrestrial-aquatic interfaces
Non-Technical Abstract: Anaerobic microsites, a defining feature of soil redox heterogeneity, are zones of oxygen depletion in otherwise oxic environments. Subsequently, anaerobic microsites can serve as hot spots for biogeochemical (BGC) processes, generating and exporting reduced products to oxic environments. Anoxic microsites have been predicted to contribute 21% to the global production of methane (CH4), an important greenhouse gas affecting climate change. They are often generated at terrestrial?aquatic interfaces (TAIs), such as riverine floodplains, which are dynamic transition zones between land and water, where seasonal changes in river and groundwater flow conditions lead to redox fluctuations. As a result, TAIs play a significant role for elemental cycling and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, while only occupying small areas of the Earth?s surface (0.07%?0.22%). Despite the presumed importance of anaerobic microsites in TAIs, significant knowledge gaps still exist regarding their abundance over time and space under varying environmental conditions, as well as their specific contributions to BGC processes, especially with regard to CH4 production. Using the novel LOAMS (Laboratory for Observing Anaerobic Microsites in Soils) approach, we will specifically detect and examine the role of anaerobic microsites in methanogenesis and metal redox processes across spatial and temporal scales at current DOE-ESS natural floodplain research sites. The main objectives of this work are to: (i) quantify the abundance and the impact of anaerobic microsites on methanogenesis and elemental speciation; (ii) compare microscale anaerobic microsite characteristics to macroscale field observations of methanogenesis and metal redox chemistry; and (iii) quantify reaction kinetics of relevant BGC processes within anaerobic microsites based on data from controlled laboratory experiments paired with modeling. Furthermore, our experimental data and parametric modeling results will support the future development of refined conceptual and quantitative models, and improve predictions of metal cycling and production of GHG emissions in TAI environments. For this study, we have selected three rivers/creeks (East River, Slate River, Cold Creek) as field sites at the Greater East River Watershed Observatory (GERWO), given that previous field measurements have indicated a potential relevance of anaerobic microsites for methane production at these sites. In addition, these sites allow us to study redox fluctuations due to seasonal changes in hydrological conditions, and provide the possibility to support our research with additional data from the ongoing DOE-BER supported Watershed Function SFA.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Geology; Hydrology; Microbiology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Geographic variation in floral shape and scent in Polemonium brandegeei
Non-Technical Abstract: We are studying honey Jacob?s ladder (Polemonium brandegeei), a subalpine perennial plant with strongly scented, creamy flowers and skunky leaves. This species is visited by many pollinator groups, including hummingbirds, hawkmoths, and solitary bees. Variation among populations in floral visitors may affect natural selection on floral scent, colour and shape. However, changes in environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, moisture levels) may also cause populations to differ in floral traits. We are comparing flower shape, colour and scent in natural populations ranging from New Mexico to Wyoming to plants from these populations grown in a common greenhouse environment. This study will help our understanding of the relative effects of genetics and environment on floral traits, and potential responses to changes in pollinator abundance.
Research Area: Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Aquatic invertebrates and trout in beaver ponds of different ages
Non-Technical Abstract: Beavers are ecological engineers, creating a variety of habitats within aquatic ecosystems by constructing dams and ponds. As beaver ponds age, they accumulate sediment and become more wetland-like. This leads to ponds of different ages having different characteristics. These differences will influence what types of aquatic invertebrates will inhabit these ponds, and potentially what kind of prey trout are foraging for. We plan to survey three newer beaver ponds and four older beaver ponds on tributaries to the East River in the Gothic Corridor to assess the aquatic invertebrate community composition and taxa richness. We will follow aquatic invertebrate sampling with catch-and-release angling to obtain fish diet samples to determine if trout are foraging in beaver ponds of different ages. Learning more about the biodiversity associated with successional stages of beaver ponds can inform evaluation criteria for restoration using beaver or beaver dam analogues and improve our understanding of beavers? role in the ecosystem for land management planning.
Research Area: Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Pollen limitation in an insect-pollinated, masting perennial
