Non-Technical Abstract: Masting is a dramatic example of plant reproduction, creating incredible boom and bust patterns of fruits, seeds, or flowers across years and over large spatial areas, including and up to entire continents. In some years, individuals reproduce in great amounts, all at once. In other years, individuals will reproduce very little, or not at all. Examples of masting species can be wind-pollinated, like oak or pine trees. However, animal-pollinated masting species are less often studied. Ecologists are interested in both how and why masting plants reproduce at the same time, even though plants cannot move or communicate with each other. Masting is thought to be beneficial because it can maximize the number of seeds produced in years with many flowers. In other words, when there are many flowers, animal pollinators such as bees are more likely to fertilize flowers than in years where there are few flowers. I would like to test whether this is true in a population of Monument Plant (Frasera speciosa), a species of Gentian that reproduces synchronously in the East River Valley, CO. Frasera speciosa has tall flowering stalks that attract many and diverse pollinators. I plan to experimentally add pollen to some flowers, but not to others, and compare how that affects the number of seeds produced. This work will build upon long-term research on this species in the East River Valley to help address important evolutionary hypotheses in herbaceous, animal-pollinated masting species.
Research Area: Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Warming and Species Removal in Mountains (WaRM)
Research Area: Climate change; Long-term research; Microbiomes; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Investigating the Ecological Significance of Secondary Metabolites in Fruit
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants produce thousands of secondary metabolites ? chemical compounds that mediate ecological interactions ? but the roles of most of these compounds remain unknown, especially outside of leaves. Fruits are particularly rich in secondary metabolites, which shape interactions with seed dispersers, seed predators, and pathogens. However, the ecological effects of fruit secondary metabolites are complex and context-dependent ? the same compound can influence multiple frugivores with opposing effects (e.g., toxins can repel both harmful seed predators and beneficial seed dispersers), and compounds can have synergistic effects. To understand the ecological and evolutionary significance of fruit secondary metabolites, it is therefore essential to determine the combined effects of multiple compounds on a range of frugivores. I propose to investigate how the concentrations and diversity of nutrients and defensive secondary metabolites mediate interactions surrounding fruit. Using observational field and lab studies, experimental manipulations of fruit chemistry, and analytical chemistry techniques, I will assess patterns of secondary metabolite allocation to fruits, as well as how chemical composition and diversity shape seed dispersal and fruit defense. This research will improve understanding of processes critical to plant reproduction and evolution, with potential applications to conservation and agriculture. The data generated will provide the foundation for the PI to establish a longer-term research program at RMBL.
Research Area: Community ecology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Pollination and life history of Erythronium grandiflorum
Non-Technical Abstract: (1) On my property at Irwin, I conduct annual experiments to measure the pollination success of an early-flowering lily. (2) In a transplant garden, I annually record flower production and fruiting success in about 230 plants. Two progress reports have been published. When these plants have entered dormancy, I exhume the corms to be weighed and photographed. The data are archived.
Research Area: Climate change; Pollination; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Isolating chytrid fungi from high alpine soils and aquatic habitats
Non-Technical Abstract: I aim to study and identify chytrid fungi from high-altitude soils and water near melting snow in Colorado during the early summer. These fungi, commonly found in wet environments like soil and water, are known to thrive in extreme conditions, including high-elevation regions such as the Colorado mountains. To carry out this research, I will collect samples near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) and work with them on-site in the lab at RMBL. Using specific techniques, I will isolate and grow the fungi in pure cultures before identifying them through DNA sequencing. The most promising samples will be sent back to my home lab at North Carolina State University for cryopreservation and further analysis. During this multi-year project, I aim to uncover the diversity and abundance of chytrids, including new species, to better understand their evolutionary history and ecological roles in high-alpine ecosystems.
Research Area: Genetics; Microbiology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term studies of evolutionary rescue in plants
Non-Technical Abstract: Climate change is threatening many populations around the world. A population can avoid extinction by dispersal to more favorable locations, but that is not possible for many plants with limited seed dispersal. An alternative is evolutionary change in which changes in traits increase fitness and result in rescue of an otherwise endangered population. Some populations of a subalpine herb, Scarlet gilia, are threatened by increasingly early spring snowmelt due to climate change, which dries the soil and reduces survival. Long-term field data on this species presents a unique opportunity to examine if evolutionary rescue is likely in a plant population. We are measuring the strength of natural selection on several vegetative traits and floral traits (including flower scent), and our many decades data set allows us to examine how selection depends on the date of spring snowmelt that year. Combined with previous estimates of the heritability of traits (which affects speed of evolution), and the direct responses of traits to date of snowmelt (plasticity), we can test whether evolutionary rescue is likely in this species. Our work capitalizes on the longest data set in the world on natural selection on plant morphology to provide one of the first applications of evolutionary rescue models to natural populations.
Research Area: Climate change; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Motus station at RMBL
Non-Technical Abstract: I propose to establish a transect, or potentially a small grid, of sensors for detecting radio tags on Broadtailed Hummingbirds or other migratory birds (tagged elsewhere) passing nearby. I would like to confirm an observation from several years ago that male hummingbirds fly about a thousand feet up the side of the valley to roost at night. I will collaborate with graduate student Katja Kochvar on her behavioral study of territorial male Broadtailed Hummingbirds. The sensors would be accessible to any other RMBL researchers who want to put radio tags on animals.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Landscape biology; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Phenological mismatch between birds and insects in montane meadows
Non-Technical Abstract: An important frontier in climate change ecology is understanding how community interactions may change because of mismatched phenological shifts. Phenological mismatch between insect prey and American migratory bird species may be emerging and is anticipated to have detrimental consequences on bird reproductive success. Moreover, the abundance and biomass of insect prey in the Rocky Mountains have declined over the past 35 years. Climate effects such as snowmelt timing are drivers of change for many taxa, and consequences may vary by elevation. I ask 1) does the demand for insect prey by birds change over time during the summer breeding season in montane wet meadow habitats? 2) Does the peak of insect prey demand by birds align with the current peak of insect abundance and biomass? And 3) Do these dynamics change with elevation? I have established a partnership with the Colorado Parks and Wildlife lead avian biologist (Dr. James Gammonley) with whom I will prepare outcomes of this research for use in guiding management of non-game bird species in the state.
Research Area: Climate change; Food web biology; Species Interactions; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Aquatic invertebrates in beaver ponds of different successional stages
Non-Technical Abstract: As beavers continue to expand their ranges and ecologically engineer streams and wetlands within Colorado, beaver ponds of different ages can be found throughout the landscape. Ponds of different ages have varying levels of sediment accumulation and habitat structure, which could impact which aquatic invertebrates inhabit them. This proposed research aims to determine if older beaver ponds house different aquatic invertebrate communities than newer beaver ponds. Ponds of varying ages and successional stages will be sampled in the Trail Creek drainage and the upper East River valley. Using a 1-m D-net sweep, invertebrates will be caught, identified pondside in the field, enumerated, and released back into the pond. Results will provide insight into the relationship between aquatic invertebrates and beaver engineering.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Community ecology; Insect biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Abiotic and biotic controls on chemical weathering rates
Non-Technical Abstract: Precipitation falling on mountainous watersheds is exposed to surface and subsurface processing, such as chemical weathering, before eventually leaving as streamflow. In turn, this processing is governed by a variety of abiotic and biotic interactions involving, e.g., the type of rock that governs geomorphology and mineralization and the type of vegetation that can generate acidity. The proposed work will focus on the role of vegetation as a means to influence water chemistry and quality. By employing a multi-scale approach, the project will address the following questions: 1) Does landscape-scale heterogeneity in vegetation, climate, and geology impart unique, spatially-variable signatures on soil production and chemical weathering rates? 2) What roles do the legacies of Pleistocene glaciation and Holocene geomorphic processes play in determining modern-day solute concentrations in surface waters? 3) Are physical erosion and chemical weathering rates linked at the watershed scale, and can these rates be predicted from watershed characteristics? These questions will be addressed in the physical and ecological setting of the East River watershed near Crested Butte, Colorado. The proposed technical approach will assess controls on weathering and solute generation at the soil profile, landform, and watershed scales. At the soil profile scale, soil production and chemical weathering rates will be quantified with cosmogenic nuclides and geochemical mass balance at sites that span biotic, climatic, and geologic gradients in order to isolate the key drivers of chemical weathering. At the landform scale, solute concentrations in surface waters will be used to assess whether surficial deposits generated by different geomorphic processes impart unique weathering signatures. At the watershed-scale, cosmogenic nuclides will be used to measure erosion rates. A series of reactive transport models will be constructed to place the field-based findings into a framework for making predictions regarding the roles that vegetation, climate, and geomorphology play in solute generation. The proposed research complements ongoing BER investments at the LBNL Watershed Science SFA Science Focus Area.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Geology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Beaver wetlands as ecosystem control points for river water quality
Non-Technical Abstract: Beaver dams and the wetlands they create are ubiquitous, landmark features to glaciated river corridors in the West. By building dams and diverting river water into floodplains, beavers fundamentally alter how water flows through a watershed and the biogeochemical processes that occur within the critical zone. Amplified soil weathering conditions, abundant transitional redox boundaries, and heightened aqueous concentrations of iron and dissolved organic matter set the stage for beaver wetlands to be influential bioreactors that can alter downstream water quality. Highly associated with floodplains but marginally understood are colloids; reactive and mobile nanoparticles formed at subsurface redox interfaces, typically rich in iron, organic carbon, and trace metals, and, thus, with the potential to enhance passage of metals and carbon to streams. Unlike hydrologically disconnected floodplains, beaver wetlands are highly engineered systems with substantial advective pathways that allow chemically altered waters, and potentially iron-rich nano-colloids, to be mobilized and transported directly into adjacent streams. My research seeks to understand 1) whether iron-rich colloids are generated in beaver wetlands, 2) whether iron-rich colloids are present in river water downstream of beaver wetlands, 3) how seasonal hydrologic variability influences the abundance and structure of iron within beaver wetlands, and 4) the overall mass loading of iron to rivers from beaver wetlands through surface and subsurface flow paths. Iron particles are widely recognized for their ability to adsorb toxic, redox-sensitive metals from arsenic to uranium, so by focusing on iron this work tracks the water quality implications for harmful trace metals that can be repartitioned within beaver wetlands. In completing this work, I will identify the role beaver wetlands play as an ecosystem control point for river water quality with respect to iron and other affiliated elements and substances.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Response of bumblebee foraging rate to variation in flower density
Non-Technical Abstract: Asynchronous phenology shifts among species have the potential to disrupt not only the timing of key ecological processes but also their rates. Colorado?s subalpine communities have documented phenology shifts for plant and pollinator species driven by climate change. As a result, pollinators are becoming exposed to novel flower assemblages with unknown consequences to their foraging rates and ultimately population growth. In this study, I will investigate the response of bumblebee foraging rates to variation in flower density by (1) evaluating the relevant spatial scale of flower density for bumblebees foraging rates and (2) fitting a multi-species functional response to bumblebee foraging rates with respect to flower density at that spatial scale. This study will identify which flower species, if increased in density, will most increase foraging rates of vulnerable bumblebee species as well as the appropriate spatial extent for seeding them in restoration. Further, future studies can incorporate this functional response into population dynamic models to project plant-pollinator community resilience over long timescales.
Research Area: Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Experimental Warming of Ligusticum and Aphids
Non-Technical Abstract: Insects play important roles such as herbivores, pollinators, disease vectors, and decomposers. However, changing patterns of temperature and precipitation are upending the abundances for many insect populations. These population changes may arise from direct effects, as warmer temperatures may accelerate insect population growth. Insects do not exist in isolation, and this project explores the impacts of warming temperatures on the host plants that insects depend on. These plants, in turn, rely on close association with soil microbes, which themselves may be impacted by changing temperatures. Our project will determine the impacts of warming for insect populations arising from this web of above- and belowground interactions.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Forecasting integrated plant-aphid dynamics in a rapidly warming community
Non-Technical Abstract: Changing weather patterns are expected to disrupt the lifecycles and population growth of many organisms, especially ones that are sensitive to changes in temperature like insects. But when insects rely on other organisms like plants, microbes or other insects for food, protection or habitat, it becomes harder to predict how they will respond, because these organisms may also be affected by these changes. Because mountain ecosystems are harsher environments, not as many different species live there, making it easier to observe these interactions. This project will use many years of observations of aphids, ants, plants and microbes to build a computer model that will integrate these interactions and make predictions about how different patterns of environmental change will affect the abundance and long-term survival of these species.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Local adaptation in plant-aphid dynamics across a temperature gradient
Non-Technical Abstract: Insect herbivores such as aphids play an outsized role in both natural and agricultural ecosystems. Consequently, understanding factors that control aphid abundance is critical for ecosystem management. Temperature can directly impact aphid development, growth, and survival and shift how these insect herbivores interact with plants. Genetic differences among aphid and plant populations can also influence how these organisms respond to rising temperatures. This project will assess local adaptation in plant-aphid interactions across a temperature gradient in a well-studied Rocky Mountain ecosystem. Findings from this work will be used to create models that predict plant-aphid dynamics under different climate conditions, develop educational materials for K-12 students about plant and insect ecology, and train rising students to become future scientists.
Research Area: Climate change; Insect biology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Wing loading and wing color tradeoffs in Speyeria mormonia
Non-Technical Abstract: I propose to study the tradeoff between wing coloration and wing loading in adult butterflies. Specifically, I am conducting research on the Mormon fritillary butterfly to deduce allocation relationships across butterfly size and the flight season. Wing pigments are expensive to make and are a part of mate signaling, which makes them an interesting allocation pathway to study. Similarly, wing loading is important for males to search for mates and females to search for oviposition sites. These two measurements are indicative of indirect reproductive allocation, which influence the likelihood of acquiring a mate and overall fitness.
Research Area: Insect biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Exploring the Drivers of Variation in Broad-tailed Hummingbird Displays
Non-Technical Abstract: This project will explore the factors that drive variation in Broad-tailed Hummingbird male courtship display behavior on territories. Detailed characterization of male territories and behavioral observation across the breeding season will allow us to assess the environmental features that drive variation in display effort. Experimental playbacks studies will elucidate the features of female cues that are most salient in eliciting male displays. Together, these studies will give us a better picture of when and why males perform these conspicuous displays.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Phenology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How does the abiotic & biotic environment shape interaction specialization?
Non-Technical Abstract: Theory predicts the conditions under which species? diets become more or less specialized. These predictions, such as limited food resources leading to an expanded diet breadth, have experimental support in various systems under controlled conditions. But we know much less about how these predictions play out under realistic and variable field conditions, nor do we understand the direct and indirect biotic and abiotic drivers of diet breadth. Therefore, I propose to investigate the environmental drivers of interaction specialization and generalization using a long-term (10-yr, ongoing) well-studied plant-pollinator interaction system. Focusing on the floral diets of bumble bees (Bombus spp.), I will analyze how pollinator interaction specialization (i.e. diet breadth) is shaped directly and/or indirectly by biotic factors (e.g., floral abundance), abiotic factors (e.g., climate conditions), and their combinations. This work will leverage 10+ years of data on natural environmental variation and bumble bee floral resource use. My results will aid in our fundamental understanding of how ecological interactions are shaped by the environment. Simultaneously, it will help us understand how plant-pollinator interactions may play out under projected environmental change for an ecologically important group of organisms?wild bumble bees.
Research Area: Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Using Remote Sensing to Assess Floral Distribution on a Landscape-Scale
Non-Technical Abstract: The pattern in which flowering plants occur across landscapes is challenging to map. However, it is important to create such maps because animals that depend on these flowering plants?for example, pollinators such as bees?are affected by the distributions of the plants. To help increase our understanding of these plant and pollinator species, I plan to combine long-term field data collected by RMBL researchers with high-resolution imagery taken from airplanes as part of the NSF NEON program to create a model predicting the locations of flowering plant species throughout the upper East River valley. Then, using other existing data and new measurements, I will calculate the quantity of food resources (nectar and pollen) that those flowering plants could provide to pollinators. I will assess the accuracy of these maps by comparing them to observations I make of the actual plant species and food resources in test locations. Finally, I will test whether this information about food resources allows us to predict the reproductive rate and abundance of bees. Together, this work will create a set of maps that can be used by other RMBL researchers, and will serve as a test of this flower distribution modeling method, which could also be used in other places.
Research Area: Community ecology; Insect biology; Landscape biology; Modeling; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term monitoring of solitary bee population ecology
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the consequences of climate change for insect pollinators, plants, and their interactions is critical to sustaining ecosystems and the human food supply. While mounting evidence indicates that climate change is affecting bee abundance, studies are still scarce that document the mechanisms underlying these patterns. In particular, few studies have examined the consequences of climate change for bee reproductive output and survival during different life cycle stages. To fill this knowledge gap, this long-term study aims to understand the population dynamics of solitary bee species in the family Megachilidae. These species provide an ideal study system to identify the sensitivity of solitary bee demographic metrics to climate variation.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Crown temperature differences between species using drone thermal imaging
Non-Technical Abstract: This work focuses on understanding the relationship between tree crown temperatures, net radiation, and transpiration from drone thermal imaging and sap flow measurements. The main canopy tree species in the study area are Engelmann spruce, subalpine fir, lodgepole pine, and quaking aspen. Using high-resolution drone imagery of the watershed and sap velocity measurements from approximately 30 trees, this research aims to explore variations in land surface temperatures (LST) across the landscape, how much of that variation is driven by net radiation, topographic position, and transpiration. In this study we also plan to investigate the role of transpiration in driving changes in crown temperature throughout the growing season, and variations in those seasonal changes by species. The findings will help clarify how species-specific hydraulic strategies influence temperature patterns, and how well land surface temperature can indicate transpiration changes.
Research Area: Climate change; Landscape biology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Chronic N deposition and the recent proliferation D. geminata blooms
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Landscape biology; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Bee phenology and abundance, disease, and invasive plants
Non-Technical Abstract: My five-year research plan is split across four projects. (Projects 1 and 2) Assessing how climate variability affects bee phenology and abundance and the mechanisms involved. We will add to a 15-year dataset that is addressing how climate and flowering patterns directly and indirectly affect the phenology and abundance of bees, and how bee life history traits may buffer them (or make them more susceptible) to changes in climate. This dataset is publicly available online and is well-resolved to the species level, making it an exemplary resource for not only my lab and the RMBL community but also the scientific community at large. (Project 3) Effects of sunflower pollen on bee disease. We are building off a tritrophic effects framework to assess how pollen diets have indirect effects on bees by mediating host-parasite interactions. (Project 4) Ecology and management of invasive plants. We will finish a long-term management project on Linaria vulgaris assessing how various management strategies affect L. vulgaris abundance and spread.
Research Area: Community ecology; Disease ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-Term Ground Temperature Data to Study Colias meadii Larval Diapause
Non-Technical Abstract: Ground temperatures, used as a proxy for larval body temperature during diapause, are measured with a dense sensor network in the habitats of Colias meadii butterflies. These data, collected every five minutes and 25-100 feet apart for over six years, create a unique record of microclimates in alpine and montane environments. Research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) has shown that Colias meadii populations above and below treeline exhibit distinct thermal adaptations that affect fitness, and stabilizing selection for these adaptations despite the ability to migrate. However, the effects of the environment on larvae during their long overwintering diapause remain less studied. Other insect studies suggest that extreme cold events, such as exposure to 0°F prior to lower temperatures, can influence larval survival and adult fitness. By collecting microclimate data at biologically relevant time and space scales in C. meadii habitats, we are building a unique record of potential thermal shocks that could impact these larvae. The dense dataset also allows us to refine coarse measurements like snowmelt dates, which affect phenology, and develop models to assess variability in rapidly changing habitats, influenced by factors like wind and cloud cover. This research adds to RMBL?s long-term data sets, expands the region's microclimate understanding, and contributes to the thermal ecology of Colias butterflies, a genus studied at RMBL for over 50 years.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Insect biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Phenology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Biodiversity of aquatic insects in the Upper Gunnison Basin of Colorado.
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the taxonomy and distribution of aquatic insects and other taxa helps us understand the ecology and status of our local freshwater streams and ponds. https://www.gunnisoninsects.org/
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Carbon storage in created freshwater marshes: A 40 year study
Non-Technical Abstract: Wetland soils contain some of the highest stores of soil carbon in the global biosphere. However, there is little understanding of the quantity and distribution of carbon stored in our remaining wetlands which is important to the societal goal of limiting release of carbon to the atmosphere to hinder climate change. Under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, draining of wetlands hydrologically connected by surface waters to a navigable waterway may require wetland mitigation whereby a developer constructs a wetland to offset the loss of the original drained wetland. Previous research by Gutrich, Taylor and Fennessy (2009) has assessed the floristic community development over time of constructed inland freshwater marshes compared to natural reference wetland sites. In this study, we propose to assess the carbon storage and accretion in soils of constructed wetlands in Colorado that now display over 40 years of ecological succession since construction. This scientific research is critical to the management of inland freshwater wetlands in the United States as carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic carbon release to the troposphere.
Research Area: Climate science; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Community Assembly of Nectar Microbes: interactions, dispersal, filtering
Non-Technical Abstract: Floral nectar supports a diverse and dynamic microbiome of yeast and bacteria that shape plant-pollinator interactions. These nectar microbes also provide a tractable system to test fundamental questions in community assembly and metacommunity ecology. Individual flowers can serve as replicated habitat islands connected via pollinator-mediated dispersal, forming natural metacommunity microcosms. Within local communities, nectar yeast and bacteria have strong interspecific interactions that lead to alternative community states. At larger scales, pollinators maintain structured and species-specific dispersal between flowers. Nectar also serves as a strong environmental filter, excluding many microbial species. In this project, I will characterize the interacting roles interspecific interactions, dispersal, and environmental filtering on the outcomes of community assembly in this nectar microbe metacommunity. The project will also add to the current dearth of information of the floral nectar microbiome across spatial and temporal scales and contribute to our understanding how shifting phenology may affect the assembly of nectar microbiomes, with potentially important consequences for the persistence plant-pollinator interactions.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Color vision, courtship and foraging in Broad-tailed Hummingbirds
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Mercury Source and Sink Behavior in a Beaver-Dominated Stream Reach
Non-Technical Abstract: In Summer 2025, I will quantify a mercury (Hg) budget in a beaver-dominated and an unimpounded (control) reach that includes stream inputs and losses, groundwater contributions, volatilization, and estimates of atmospheric deposition (Fig. 1). The objectives of constructing a Hg budget of a beaver-dominated reach are twofold; (1) merge fluvial geomorphology and biogeochemistry principles to advance our characterization of element cycling in river corridors (RCs) under unique drivers and (2) provide land managers with relevant water quality data to better inform them of how beaver activity influences surface water quality. Within the beaver-dominated reach, the Hg budget integrates the four ecogeomorphic units (EGUs) included in my work from the last two years. The EGUs are created through the unique modifications of the RC by beavers. My comparison of the beaver-dominated reach to the unimpounded reach will allow us to evaluate how changing fluvial geomorphology driven by beaver impacts storage and transport of Hg. Further, the reach scale budget data will demonstrate how multiple consecutive beaver ponds in a reach ? the manner in which beaver ponds most commonly occur ? are increasing transport of Hg downstream compared to an unimpounded reach.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Community response to climate change using a transplant experiment
Non-Technical Abstract: The RMBL turf transplant experiment, established in 2017, simulates climate change by moving large, intact blocks of plants and soil along a temperature and elevation gradient. By transplanting to the warmer and drier conditions predicted to occur with future climate change, we can observe the responses of the soil microbes and plants to novel environments. Annual monitoring has already documented rapid community responses through changes in community composition and functioning. Extending annual monitoring will further enhance our understanding of the resilience and vulnerability of mountain communities and ecosystems. Additional data will also be beneficial towards collaborations with the TransPlant Network, an international group of researchers conducting similar turf transplant experiments around the world, including the newly established Niwot Ridge turf transplant experiment.
Research Area: Climate change; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Gene-level species recognition in heterospecific pollen-pistil interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: When plants live in diverse communities, they have the potential to exchange pollen with one another. Interspecific pollen transfer is generally known to reduce the number of seeds produced in the recipient flower, thus, it may benefit a plant to be able to recognize and respond differently to different pollen-types. Using RNA sequencing, we will investigate the genes that are involved in pollination responses to same-species pollen as well as pollen from close and distant relatives. After pollen lands on a flower, it germinates a structure called a pollen tube, which has the primary function of delivering sperm to the ovules that are at the base of the flower. Successful reproduction in flowering plants is highly dependent on the successful growth of the pollen tube, which may be aided or impeded by species-specific pollination responses. Therefore, we will also measure pollen tube growth rates during the crosses that we have sampled RNA from. We expect that the number of genes turned on and off in response to pollination will decrease as the parent species are more distantly-related. Additionally, we hypothesize that these species-specific responses will lead to differences in pollen tube growth rates that vary according to relatedness between parent species.
Research Area: Community ecology; Genetics; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Watershed Function Science Focus Area
Non-Technical Abstract: Watersheds provide key resources for human populations, with pressing demands for clean water, food, and energy. In parallel, changing hydroclimate, diminished snowpack, and interacting temperature-driven disturbances, are significantly reshaping interactions within watersheds. The Watershed Function Scientific Focus Area (SFA) is addressing the grand challenges of understanding how mountainous watershed functions respond and adapt to increasing disturbances. Our focus is on understanding the interactions of warming and drought with hydro-biogeochemical functioning in mountainous watersheds of the Upper Colorado River Basin and their retention or release of water, carbon, nitrogen, and other biologically critical elements. Our multi-lab SFA will identify watershed functional traits, which are observable characteristics that mechanistically link to ecosystem performance. These traits will be assessed within a new trait-based hydro-biogeochemical modeling capability (ATS-EcoSIM) that considers watershed compartments? hydrological, ecological, and biogeochemical interactions and adaptation in response to disturbances and feedbacks. High-resolution process-based models will be used to achieve mechanistic understanding across scales. Combining remote sensing, field-based observations, laboratory experiments, and machine learning (ML), we will decipher patterns of watershed functional trait covariance and develop ML-based surrogate models to transfer and scale mechanisms. Our research is organized into three Research Focus Areas (RFAs) and a ModEx integration core, addressing hypotheses related to disturbance impacts and resilience, pathways of adaptation, and trait covariance, aggregation, and transfer. Our goal is to gain a predictive understanding of mountainous watershed function and provide valuable insights for sustainable water resource management, land use planning, and climate change adaptation in mountainous regions worldwide.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Geology; Hydrology; Long-term research; Microbiomes; Microbiology; Modeling; Soil/microbial ecology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Plant adaptation to fine-scale topographic variation in the alpine
Non-Technical Abstract: This project will investigate how an alpine plant from the Rocky Mountains will respond and adapt to climate change. In the alpine, climate change causes earlier snowmelt that makes the alpine growing season longer, drier, and more stressful for alpine plants, but these shifts are mediated by microsite conditions, such as aspect of the slope and amount of direct sun exposure. This project uses a native alpine plant, Androsace septentrionalis, to study how the plant is adapted to microclimate variation from north and south-facing slopes across latitudes. Using collections, greenhouse experiments, genomic analyses, and spatial models, the project will predict how the species might move its range or adapt to climate change in the future. This research improves understanding of plant adaptation in the alpine and how the alpine can be managed and protected in the future.
Research Area: Climate change; Landscape biology; Phenology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Genomics of adaptation underlying a transition to herbivory
Non-Technical Abstract: Herbivorous insects are among the most successful?and destructive?organisms on Earth. One third of all animal species are herbivorous insects, and they collectively remove over 20% of plant biomass in both natural and agricultural systems. Yet we know surprisingly little about how herbivory originates: how insects transition from ancestral diets like detritus, microbes, or other insects to feeding on living plants. To illuminate this process, we are comparing the genomes and traits of herbivorous insect species with closely-related non-herbivorous relatives, in order to infer the changes that occur when insects evolve to be herbivorous. In particular, we are focusing on fly species closely related to Drosophila melanogaster, a microbe-feeding fly that is the leading model organism for genetics studies. One of these focal herbivorous species, Scaptomyza nigrita, has been studied for decades at RMBL where it feeds exclusively on wild mustard plants along alpine streams and seeps. I plan to collect S. nigrita flies at RMBL, sequence their genome, and use this genome in a broader analysis with other herbivorous and non-herbivorous fly genomes to help illuminate the genetic changes that allow insects to feed on living plants. While our primary goal is to understand how herbivory evolves, this work also has practical implications. By identifying genes and traits essential for herbivory, we aim to uncover new targets for protecting crops from insect pests. More broadly, by studying how organisms adapt to novel diets, we also hope to shed light on genes that mediate the link between diet and health?which may inform our understanding of the relationship between diet and disease in humans.
Research Area: Genetics; Insect biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Patterns of Diversity in Rocky Mountain Alpine Flora
Non-Technical Abstract: I hope to investigate drivers in the patterns of diversity in alpine plant communities of the Rocky Mountains by assessing latitudinal gradients in taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic diversity of alpine plant communities on either side of the Continental Divide from New Mexico to northern Idaho and Montana, and to investigate climatic underpinnings of observed spatial patterns.
Research Area: Community ecology; Plant biology; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term ecophysiological responses in a montane plant hybrid zone
Non-Technical Abstract: Climate change is causing significant alterations to temperature and precipitation patterns, including more intense and frequent climatic events that can negatively impact species persistence. My overarching goal is to understand whether rapid evolution in response to accelerating climate change can rescue natural populations from extinction, leveraging the unique long-term data set amassed for Ipomopsis wildflowers in the Colorado Rocky Mountains. Over 20 years ago, I determined that the genetic structure of this hybrid zone depends on a mixture of pollinator and habitat-mediated selection; in summer 2026 I will revisit Poverty Gulch, CO to measure the ecophysiological and floral traits that I?ve shown to influence fitness in this system, and determine if these populations have been able to track documented environmental change.
Research Area: Long-term research; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term studies of wildflowers and pollinators
Non-Technical Abstract: I propose to continue studies initiated in 1973 on flowering phenology and plant demography, and hummingbird demography. Also similar studies initiated more recently but mostly decades ago. Phenology will be monitored 3X/week in permanent plots, and individually tagged plants of three species will be monitored annually. Other annual counts include the number of flowering Frasera speciosa in the East River valley. A long-term Malaise trap study in the Research Meadow will be continued, with two different types of traps collecting samples 2-3 days/week. I will continue efforts to reduce deer herbivory in my study plots and to estimate the resident deer population. I will continue establishment of a Motus station for tracking radio-tagged animals, continue collaboration with Cassie Stoddard?s lab members, and initiate a collaboration on songbirds with Savannah Troy.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Predicting range dynamics from climate-demography relationships
Research Area: Landscape biology; Long-term research; Modeling; Plant biology; Other

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Effects of stress on colony-level personality in Western Thatch Ants
Non-Technical Abstract: Cooperation is a complex behavior in which individuals act in ways that increase the reproductive success and survival of others, often at a cost to themselves. Cooperation is observed across a variety of species, from ants, to birds, to humans. Animals can have cooperative personality, meaning that individuals display consistency in their cooperative behavior across time and are consistently different from others. Individual personality can be driven by many physiological systems that are affected by early development and environmental stress. In eusocial species, individuals that make up a colony are so tightly connected they are often referred to as a ?superorganism? that display collective cognition and collective behavior. Therefore, in eusocial species, environmental stressors may affect the physiology of the entire colony, leading to distinct personalities at the level of the colony, not the individual. Colony-level personality in eusocial species is not well studied. In this study, we will examine whether environmental stress (bear attacks and nitrogen changes) leads to variation in cooperative colony personality in the Western thatch ant (Formica obscuripes), a eusocial, invertebrate that engages in a mutualistic relationship with honeydew producers. Specifically, thatch ants engage in a defensive mutualistic relationship with honeydew-producing aphids and will aggressively and cooperatively defend aphids from predation in exchange for their sugary excrement. Previous studies have shown that thatch ants that experience stressors are less aggressive when under threat at the nest and when defending their aphids. Previous work has also shown that nitrogen enrichment, can positively affect ants? interactions with aphids, suggesting nitrogen may mediate some of the negative predator effects. This study investigates how nitrogen enrichment affects the defensive mutualistic behaviors of thatch ants and whether predation and nitrogen?s effect on behavior is drives differences in colony-level personality.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Microbiomes; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Marmot moods: Quantifying affective state in a wild mammal
Non-Technical Abstract: Emotion plays a critical role in shaping animal decision-making and behaviors. However, little is known about the way wild animals experience and express emotion, or affective state, especially over extended periods. In order to predict how species will respond to disturbance, and ultimately adapt in a rapidly changing world, we must understand how to assess their emotional state. The goal of this research is to develop an index that evaluates affective state in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer). Once developed, I will use the index to (1) determine the relationship between affective state and environmental conditions, (2) experimentally validate the index and (3) examine whether emotions influence two fitness metrics. I will use this research to provide a framework that includes taxon-specific measures and can be implemented by other wildlife managers to better understand emotion across wild animal populations. This research will produce a novel study on the mechanisms that underlie wildlife behavior, their long-term consequences for survival and reproduction, and whether human-induced ecological changes may be driving changes in affective state.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How does subsurface connectivity regulate water and carbon processes?
Non-Technical Abstract: This research focuses on the layers of soil and bedrock known as the subsurface, and how its physical structure controls the movement of water and carbon into our rivers. While most of our river water travels through the subsurface before reaching the surface, this area remains difficult to study because it is largely "invisible" to traditional observation. Understanding these underground flow paths is critical because dissolved carbon affects the health of aquatic ecosystems, the cost of drinking water treatment, and the global climate. To bridge this gap, our team will use advanced technologies, including airborne sensors, that map the earth's internal structure from above, as well as high-resolution chemical analysis to fingerprint carbon molecules at the molecular level. By studying the Coal Creek watershed in Colorado, we will integrate these new data into powerful computer models to predict how water and carbon transport will change as temperatures rise and weather patterns become more extreme. Ultimately, the project seeks to reveal how the underground "plumbing" of the earth acts as a gatekeeper for the water quality and environmental health of our planet.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Geology; Hydrology; Modeling

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Behavior and Ecology of Burying Beetles
Non-Technical Abstract: The primary project explores many questions related to the behavior and ecology of the burying beetle (Nicrophorus). Burying beetles are well known for their biparental care, which takes place on a small vertebrate carcass (usually a mouse) that they bury underground. The parents prepare the carcass as well as defend it against intruders, ensuring a food supply for their larvae. Behavioral studies provide insight into the factors that influence reproductive and parental decisions and success, such as individual size and age, carcasses quality, soil temperature, and competition from other carrion-feeding species. Long-term (> 25 years) ecological studies provide insight into the factors that influence the distribution and population dynamics of interacting carrion beetle species, including studies linking rodent populations (determined using live capture-mark-release-recapture techniques) to beetle populations (also marked and released), habitat associations based on microclimate, historical range shifts, and the influence of soil temperature and snowmelt on overwinter survival and emergence patterns. Burying beetles and rodent carcasses are also important components of the decomposer food web- and thus we also study their influence on soil nutrients and plant growth. Secondary projects include 1) deployment of motion-activated cameras to detect wildlife behaviors and activity on human trails and at key resources such as mineral licks and sapsucker wells and 2) collection of insects for genetic, identification, and taxonomic purposes.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Bio-logging to reveal the hidden lives of Yellow-bellied marmots
Non-Technical Abstract: The goal of this project is to complement the outstanding long-term data collection on Yellow-bellied marmots at RMBL with bio-logging technologies which will allow for remote and continuous behavioral and physiological tracking. We will densely sample marmots? association patterns and movements throughout the day and year-round. These data will give us novel insight into marmots? subterrain behavior and movement ecology - data that is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to collect via human observations. With these new data in hand, we aim to (1) better understand how an increasingly unpredictable subalpine climate drives marmot social relationships and plasticity, (2) illuminate marmot?s below-ground social lives for the first time and how above- and below-ground behaviors covary, and (3) map wild marmot?s behavior during hibernation and how summer social behavior may drive hibernation survival and success.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Climate change; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Phenological mismatch between birds and insects in montane meadows
Non-Technical Abstract: An important frontier in climate change ecology is understanding how community interactions may change because of mismatched phenological shifts. Phenological mismatch between insect prey and American migratory bird species may be emerging and is anticipated to have detrimental consequences on bird reproductive success. Moreover, the abundance and biomass of insect prey in the Rocky Mountains have declined over the past 35 years. Climate effects such as snowmelt timing are drivers of change for many taxa, and consequences may vary by elevation. I ask: Do nest provisioning rates by breeding birds change over time with invertebrate phenology during the summer breeding season in montane wet meadow habitats? Does the peak of insect prey demand by birds align with the current peak of insect abundance and biomass? Does bird reproductive success correlate with invertebrate phenology? And do these dynamics change with elevation? I have established a partnership with the Colorado Parks and Wildlife lead avian biologist (Dr. James Gammonley) with whom I will prepare outcomes of this research for use in guiding management of non-game bird species in the state. I am also studying driver behavior in response to different road signage intended to reduce small animal road mortality. I will experimentally test which style of messaging most reduces observed animal road kill events during peak summer tourism season in the back country.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Integrating river science, education, mentoring and community connections
Non-Technical Abstract: RMBL shares the Upper East River basin with other special interests, such as recreation, development of open space associated with the Mt. Crested Butte ski area, abstraction of water for snowmaking and irrigation, hard rock mining and cattle grazing. Such multiple uses of the basin potentially threaten the quality of the receiving streams critical not only to the integrity of the ecosystem, but also to sustaining research, education and community connection functions of RMBL. In 1976 the RMBL obtained a non-consumptive water rights (NCWR) decree that protects minimum flows in streams of the basin. Since that time stream ecologists at RMBL have used invertebrates as biological indicators of stream quality, with the objective of protecting the health and biodiversity of those streams. We have observed some concerning changes over the 50 year time course of this study. For example, changing climate conditions are causing increases in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events, including severe floods, protracted periods of drought and increasing water temperatures, all of which have the potential to degrade the streams of our region. Periodic drought conditions, increasing water temperatures, lower snow pack and earlier spring snowmelt not only affect the distribution and abundance of sensitive species of macroinvertebrates, but also have contributed to proliferation of a nuisance diatom, Didymosphenia geminata (Didymo), which has altered its growth form and has the potential to threaten the health and biodiversity of otherwise pristine tributaries of the Colorado River. The primary goal of this project is to continue ongoing quantitative invertebrate sampling of eight streams in the Upper East River basin two times per summer, estimate biovolume of Didymo, and monitor abiotic parameters, such as water temperatures, light levels, hydrology, and conductivity. This long-term record of biotic and abiotic variables enables early detection of environmental problems and potential effects of climate change. We are positioned to influence public policy to prevent or mitigate human-mediated changes that fall outside the range of acceptable conditions needed to sustain healthy stream biota. We strive to provide a model system for assessing threats to high elevation streams such as human accelerated environmental change, extraction of mineral resources, proliferation of invasive species, population growth and streamflow diversions. This dataset obtained from relatively pristine streams within a backdrop of environmental change can thereby be used as a reference for comparison to streams in other parts of the Colorado River basin that are vulnerable to ongoing and future threats.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Climate change; Community ecology; Food web biology; Hydrology; Insect biology; Long-term research

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Proposed GW/SW interactions course, near on Slate River, July 2026
Non-Technical Abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is holding a training course focusing on field methods for identifying and quantifying stream and groundwater connectivity. For the field components of this class, we intend to focus our stream corridor teaching efforts along the Slate River, along the reach from the Oh Be Joyful campground down to the SLAC research area/Gunsight bridge. Proposed field activities would occur between July 27th and July 31st, 2026. Proposed field components would mainly take place on 7/28 and 7/29 (the rest of the course is offered in a classroom setting), and no equipment would be left installed after the end of the training week. Proposed activities include: The brief installation of seepage meters/piezometers/permeameters, and fiber optic cable (placed at the streambed interface) for collecting distributed temperature measurements; a small drone-based data collection demonstration; non-invasive thermal methods including thermal infrared mapping with cameras and water and bed temperature collection via probes; non-invasive geophysical data collection on the streambanks; and the injection of inert tracers to identify spatially distributed groundwater inflows along the reach via dilution. We plan to make the various field data collected during the course publicly available for possible future research use, and so they could be leveraged to augment the ongoing 'baseflow' related data being collected along the Slate River by the USGS and others. The course teaching will highlight the wide range of RMBL, University, National Laboratory, and Federal data collected throughout the East River watershed related to groundwater-surface water exchange processes.
Research Area: Hydrology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Species and functional shifts in plant communities under climate change
Non-Technical Abstract: Scientific understanding of biodiversity responses to climate change have come from ecological modeling; however, the data that go into these models are limited and violate many ecological and statistical assumptions, resulting in unreliable predictions. Therefore, long-term monitoring is the best option for investigating biodiversity shifts due to climate change, especially in areas with reduced human activities that can confound climate effects. This proposed research will revisit and survey plant communities that were surveyed by Dr. Langenheim in 1948-1952 and Dr. Zorio between 2013-2014 to investigate temporal beta diversity and community shifts due to climate change. These sites were selected along elevational gradient giving us a chance to assess plant community resilience and vulnerability under different local conditions.

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Pollination ecology in Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii
Non-Technical Abstract: This research description proposes two projects for the summer 2026 field season. The first project aim to investigate hummingbird pollination of Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii, with a focus on quantifying the interaction outcomes for both the birds and the plants in these interaction. Specifically, this project will measure the per-visit seed set affected by Broad-tailed and Rufous hummingbirds, as well as the per-visit energy gain hummingbirds receive from consuming floral nectar. Additionally, this project will investigate whether these per-visit measures of interaction benefit are correlated with floral shape, specifically length and width. The second project aims to investigate passive acoustic monitoring as a tool for monitoring pollination visits from different pollinator guilds. Also focused on Ipomopsis aggregata and Delphinium nelsonii, this second project will deploy acoustic monitors into the field to collect recordings of pollinator visits. We will then use machine learning to determine the accuracy with which acoustic recordings can be indicative of pollinator guild (e.g., hummingbird, bee, fly).
Research Area: Pollination; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Effects of Abiotic and Biotic Factors on Bumblebee Phenology
Non-Technical Abstract: Bumblebee abundance at various life stages is affected by a variety of environmental factors like climate and flowers. However, how these environmental factors affect bumblebee phenology is less well understood. Life stages, called ?castes,? are specific events within the life-cycle of a bumblebee colony. They include queens, which emerge in the early season, female workers, which emerge after queens, and males, which emerge later in the summer. I propose to study the emergence timing of bumblebee castes that are found near RMBL, as they relate to floral abundance and snowmelt timing. I will study caste emergence by contributing to an 11-year long bumblebee monitoring project that includes weekly bumblebee monitoring at six distinct fieldsites, as well as weekly floral censuses of flowers pollinated by bumblebees at each of these sites. Additionally, I will assist in the collection of bumblebee legs for a 5-year genetic study on bumblebee colonies in these same sites to better understand how colony size and abundance may impact bumblebee phenology. I will leverage my past three years of fieldwork experience on these specific projects at RMBL to contribute to these long-term datasets. My results will contribute to our understanding of pollinator phenology, as well as the relationship among sequential life events in bumblebees.
Research Area: Community ecology; Genetics; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long-term monitoring of solitary bee populations under climate change
Non-Technical Abstract: Understanding the consequences of climate change for insect pollinators, plants, and their interactions is critical to sustaining ecosystems and the human food supply. While mounting evidence indicates that climate change is affecting bee abundance, studies are still scarce that document the mechanisms underlying these patterns. In particular, few studies have examined the consequences of climate change for bee reproductive output and survival during different life cycle stages. To fill this knowledge gap, this long-term study aims to understand the population dynamics of solitary bee species in the family Megachilidae. These species provide an ideal study system to identify the sensitivity of solitary bee demographic metrics to climate variation.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Ecological Restoration Following Impacts of Invasive Mustards
Non-Technical Abstract: Anthropogenic pressures such as global trade, increased human population, and climate change have led to the introduction of non-native species. As these threats intensify, there is an increasing need for understanding their impacts to native ecosystems and creating new tools restoration post-disturbance. Invasive species in high elevation ecosystems such as subalpine meadows of Colorado are becoming more common. Members of the Brassicaceae (mustards) have recently been introduced into these otherwise pristine areas and are a threat to local diversity and community dynamics. This proposal aims to understand an introduced mustard, Thlaspi arvense, its impacts to the native plant and soil-microbial communities, and to test a new restoration method using microbial inoculation in invaded areas. Over the span of 3 summer field seasons, I will conduct field surveys at Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory to assess T. arvense damage on the diversity and functioning levels of native meadow vegetation and soil communities. A greenhouse experiment will be conducted to test if native microbial inoculation can be used to actively restore diversity and functioning levels post-disturbance. This work has the potential to increase understanding in an area of ecology that is not well understood and provide stakeholders with new, accessible restoration methods.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Plant biology; Soil/microbial ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Long term repeat resurveys of the Gothic earthflow plant community
Non-Technical Abstract: Repeat resurveys of a landslide area outside of the Gothic townsite have shown an unusual plant community that has recolonized the site in the past 100 years. This area gives us the opportunity to study plant successional communities in highly disturbed areas, in order to understand their dynamics, productivity, and species diversity. Various biodiversity patterns from macroecological theory can be tested against the data that are collected on this site, to understand how disturbance may affect the plant community structure.
Research Area: Community ecology; Landscape biology; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Intra-annual variation in pollen and nectar nutrition
Non-Technical Abstract: I present a project to (1) assess intra-seasonal variation in the quantity and nutritional content of pollen and nectar and (2) link nutritional variation to foraging patterns in a community of wild insect pollinators. It is reasonable to expect that nutritional traits may exhibit substantive intra-seasonal variation, likely in response to phenological and environmental drivers, but we currently lack any framework for assessing the extent of such variation and how it could impact survival, foraging, and pollen transfer by insect pollinators. My goal with this project is to characterize weekly variation in nectar and pollen nutrients and assess how that variation impacts pollinator foraging and pollen collection. I hypothesize that the nutritional traits of pollen and nectar will vary in response to phenological and environmental drivers and that this intra-seasonal nutritional variation has a substantive impact on pollinator foraging.
Research Area: Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Plant biology; Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Sinks or sources: beaver pond fluxes of carbon, nutrients, and insects
Non-Technical Abstract: Beaver dams and their complexes of ponds and riparian wetlands are prominent features of small mountain streams and are widely recognized for their ability to alter hydrology, sedimentation, carbon and nutrient cycling, and aquatic insect communities. Yet, our understanding of whether an individual beaver dam?pond complex functions as a source or sink of carbon, nutrients, and aquatic insects remains highly uncertain. In this study, we examine how the position of beaver dams along a stream channel and the vertical height (head height) of dams influence ponds as a sink or source of downstream fluxes of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and insects. Using paired upstream?downstream measurements of stream discharge, chemistry, insect communities, and greenhouse gas exchanges, together with high-resolution drone imagery that characterizes pond and floodplain elevation, geometry, and vegetation type, we will link landscape position and pond geomorphology to carbon, nutrient, and insect dynamics. This work aims to clarify when and where beaver dam?pond complexes enhance retention versus export of materials in mountain streams. The work will be performed over multiple seasons and years to assess how the dams-ponds operate during wet and dry periods. The research is part of a field course focused on aquatic ecosystems ecology and watershed processes and provides hands-on research training for undergraduate and graduate students in aquatic biogeochemistry, hydrology, and ecosystem ecology. Efforts are focused on the East River, Slate River, Oh-be-joyful Ck, and Ohio Ck drainages of the upper Gunnison River, CO watershed where beaver dams occur.
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Food web biology; Hydrology; Insect biology; Landscape biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How do the abiotic and biotic environment shape species interactions?
Non-Technical Abstract: Theory predicts the conditions under which species? diets expand or contract. These predictions, such as limited food resources leading to an expanded diet breadth, have experimental support in various systems under controlled conditions. However, we know much less about how these predictions play out under realistic and variable field conditions, nor do we understand their direct and indirect biotic and abiotic drivers. Therefore, I propose to investigate the environmental drivers of interaction specialization and generalization using a long-term (11-yr, ongoing) well-studied plant-pollinator interaction system. Focusing on the floral diets of bumble bees (Bombus spp.), I will analyze how pollinator interaction specialization (i.e. diet breadth) is shaped directly and/or indirectly by biotic factors (e.g., floral abundance), abiotic factors (e.g., climate conditions), and their combinations. This work will leverage 11+ years of data on natural environmental variation and bumble bee floral resource use. While conducting this fieldwork, I will concurrently use my unique training in bumble bee nest searching to locate and document bumble bee nesting traits?the most understudied facet of their life history, and the basis of their population ecology. My results will aid in our fundamental understanding of how ecological interactions are shaped by the environment, and illuminate how plant-pollinator interactions may play out under projected environmental change. I, too, will advance our knowledge of the least understood stage of the bumble bee life cycle through collecting information on bumble bee nesting ecology. Preliminary results from this work have found diet breadth diversity amongst the bumble bee community in our system, with two major groups emerging: relative diet generalists (B. bifarius, B. flavifrons, B. mixtus, B. occidentalis, B. rufocinctus) and diet specialists (B. appositus, B. californicus, B. nevadensis). This information will be used in a structural equation model to untangle how the biotic and abiotic environment has shaped diet diversity in this bumble bee community across the last decade.
Research Area: Pollination; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Adaptation of bumblebee traplines to natural variation in flower density
Non-Technical Abstract: Bumblebee workers adaptively allocate foraging preferences both across co-occurring flower species in a flower patch and across flower patches in a landscape. These adaptive foraging behaviors improve the resilience of their foraging rates to spatial and temporal variation in resource availability. In my first dissertation chapter I characterized the functional response form of within-patch foraging rates with respect to flower density. In this project, I will characterize the functional response form of across patch foraging rates with respect to flower density. To do so I will measure how the traplines of bumblebee workers evolve during their lifetime, both in terms of patch acceptance rate and patch residence time, in response to natural variation in Delphinium barbeyi density at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL). The results of this study will be used to develop a nested functional response model accounting for adaptive foraging behavior of bumblebees both within and across patches. With this model, I will explore the resilience of bumblebee and plant populations to resource perturbations.
Research Area: Landscape biology; Modeling; Pollination; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: How does longterm N deposition impact pollination interactions in Almont?
Non-Technical Abstract: Nitrogen is being deposited from the atmosphere at significant levels at near-global scales, and this deposition has the potential to transform formerly nitrogen limited communities into entirely new spaces, with altered growth, traits, and interactions with other species. In spite of this significance, it is poorly understood how long term nitrogen deposition impacts plant-pollinator interactions, which are of special concern to humanity due to the billions of dollars per year that pollination represents as an ecosystem service. Through collaboration with Josh Grinath (Idaho State University), I plan to utilize his 17 year nitrogen addition experiment at the Almont Triangle (Gunnison County) to assess how plant-pollinator interactions are affected by nitrogen deposition. I will survey interactions between plants and pollinators for one hour per experimental plot per week, and then I will construct interaction networks to compare the network structure throughout the growing season between nitrogen addition plots and control plots using the r package bipartite. Ultimately, this work stands to demonstrate how nitrogen deposition (exacerbated by anthropogenic emissions) impacts plant-pollinator community structure and interactions.
Research Area: Climate change; Climate science; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Long-term research; Phenology; Plant biology; Pollination

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Reconstructing Holocene hydroclimate from sedimentary biomarkers in lakes
Non-Technical Abstract: Alpine regions of the Western US are key sources of freshwater for 10s of millions of people. Modern warming and drying trends in this region threaten the security of this resource, especially in the form of a diminishing snowpack. To better understand the trajectory of water availability in the Rocky Mountains, this project aims to reconstruct (coupled) changes in temperature and hydroclimate over the past ~10,000 years by analyzing lake sediment archives. Using a combination of geophysical and sedimentological analyses, we will reconstruct fluctuations in lake water levels as they respond to prolonged (multi-millennial scale) droughts. We will additionally analyze molecular "fossils" - the organic remains of bacteria and vegetation on the landscape - which can provide information on temperature and precipitation regimes. These data will ultimately be used to better understand the hydrologic history of the region and improve forecasting of its future.
Research Area: Biogeochemistry; Climate change; Climate science; Geology; Hydrology; Snow Science

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stream Tracker: Documenting flow duration on non-perennial streams
Epidemiology and evolution across environments in a plant?pathogen system
Non-Technical Abstract: Infectious diseases vary in severity across time and space. This variation makes it difficult to forecast epidemics, so there is a need to describe the underlying factors that contribute to diverse disease outcomes across populations. A growing body of work attests to the role of environmental context in shaping epidemics. At the most basic level, environment can alter host and pathogen physiology and landscape distribution. These changes could cascade to affect host and pathogen evolution by altering selection, leading to different coevolutionary trajectories across environments. However, there are few model systems where ecological measures of disease prevalence and severity across environments can be integrated with genetic data to test hypotheses about how ecological context shapes host evolution. Established in 2018, the Flax Rust Project leverages the powerful system of Lewis flax (Linum lewisii), a supalpine wildflower abundant on the slopes near RMBL, and flax rust (Melampsora lini), its conspicuous fungal pathogen. Populations occur across a steep elevational gradient, allowing the measurement of a wide variety of weather conditions that contribute to the spread of disease. Through long-term observation of disease transmission in study populations, we investigate how hosts balance adaptation to both their abiotic environment and their pathogens. Lewis flax is also a burgeoning model system in genomics, so we can further integrate field measurements of disease with genetic information about our study populations to investigate the role of disease in molecular evolution of this host. Understanding the impacts of environment on epidemics and host evolution will shed light on how disease might be expected to shift as the climate warms and whether we expect hosts to adapt to changing pressures.
Research Area: Climate change; Disease ecology; Genetics; Landscape biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The role of ants in plant indirect defense
Non-Technical Abstract: Plants interact with both harmful insects that eat them and helpful insects that protect them. Ants often defend plants from herbivores, but they do so while farming sap-feeding aphids that produce honeydew. This means plants, aphids, and ants form a three-way relationship?one that plants may be able to influence through their own defensive chemistry. This project investigates how activating plant defense hormones affects aphid growth, which ant species arrive, and how much protection those ants ultimately provide. Because ant species differ greatly in how aggressively they defend plants, even small changes in which ants show up can alter plant outcomes. This project tests these ideas in the well-studied aspen?aphid?ant system. This project also asks whether plants can ?anticipate help? from ants. Using young aspen sunflower, the project will examine whether simple exposure to ants?before plants offer rewards?leads them to invest less in costly chemical defenses because they expect protection. Together, these studies will reveal how plants shape ant behavior and how indirect defense fits into broader plant strategies in natural communities.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology; Food web biology; Insect biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions; Theory

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Praxis of Climate Change Researchers
Non-Technical Abstract: Although there are landmark works that study the life worlds of scientists such as "Laboratory Life" by Bruno Latour, little attention has been paid to the ethical foundations that motivate scientists in the field. Using work such as "Because This Land Is Who We Are: Indigenous Practices of Environmental Repossession" as a model, this project intends to interview scientists working at RMBL in an attempt at a philosophical exploration of the virtues, experiences, and ideologies that shape the work happening on the front-line of climate change. Research at RMBL will be paired with similar ethnographies, such as of those involved in the Novel Ecosystem conference, and researchers at the University of Georgia Marine Institute at Sapelo Island.
