Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Regional patterns and drivers of tiger salamander life history variation
Research Area: Aquatic Biology; Long-term research; Vertebrate biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Unveiling environmental determinants of nectar phenotypes in a selfer
Non-Technical Abstract: The evolutionary transition from outcrossing to self-pollination is known to have consequences for the genetic and morphological traits of flowering plants. However, little is known about how selection has shaped pollinator-reward phenotypes in selfers. By characterizing (1) the genetic and environmental drivers of nectar variation and (2) the ecological and evolutionary consequences of variable nectar traits in Boechera stricta, my research will explore why nectar reward phenotypes persist in this selfing species. During this project, I will phenotype nectar traits in wild populations of B. stricta at RMBL and employ a genome-wide association study under manipulated environmental conditions at the University of Chicago to determine the relative effects of genetic and environmental variation in shaping nectar traits. Furthermore, I will quantify how variation in nectar traits influence insect visitation, and how this may have shaped long-term patterns of genetic variation across the species range. Finally, I will use a common garden experiment to test whether variation in nectar traits influence fitness in natural conditions. Overall, the results will help reveal why selfing species maintain investment in nectar phenotypes, with implications for understanding genetic and environmental controls of gene flow.
Research Area: Genetics; Insect biology; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Stomatal trait responses to climate change in the Rocky Mountains
Non-Technical Abstract: The RMBL turf transplant experiment, established in 2017, simulates climate change by moving large, intact blocks of plants and soil along a temperature and elevation gradient. By transplanting to the warmer and drier conditions predicted to occur with future climate change, we can observe how the plant?s stomata respond to novel environments. Although annual monitoring has already documented rapid community responses through shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning, little is known about how stomata respond at the morphological and functional levels. The impact of stomatal traits on plant physiology and productivity points to an unresolved mechanism underlying drought stress responses. Because any change in stomatal behavior is crucial for accurately modeling carbon and water cycling under future climatic conditions, understanding stomatal morphology and its plasticity becomes essential. Additional data will also be beneficial towards collaborations with the TransPlant Network, an international group of researchers conducting similar turf transplant experiments around the world.
Research Area: Climate change; Community ecology; Long-term research; Plant biology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Larval mayfly fear responses to predator kairomones at RMBL
Non-Technical Abstract: In aquatic ecosystems, predator-prey interactions are largely mediated by chemical cues. Numerous studies in the East River and its tributaries near Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have investigated antipredator behavior involving multiple predators (McIntosh and Peckarsky 1999), but the cues that may mediate these behaviors themselves have not been identified. Through experiments using mayfly larvae as prey, we hope to further confirm these behaviors but also identify the chemical cues the prey are exposed to. These investigations will be part of a larger study looking to determine if a universal fear cue exists across multiple aquatic ecosystems, including coastal ecosystems up into mountain river systems.
Research Area: Animal Behavior; Community ecology

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: General Observations of Plant-Lichen \& Plant-Herbivore Interactions
Non-Technical Abstract: We will continue to conduct a series of surveys/observations in the US Forest Service's Gunnison District and at RMBL to examine plant-lichen associations in alpine meadows and the long-term dynamics of grasshopper populations. The research focused on plant-lichen associations will examine the variety of ways in which the plant influences lichen establishment and growth and the ways in which the lichen influences plant establishment and growth. Preliminary results indicate that the lichen's presence in xeric alpine meadows may be due to an association with the plant. However, the plant's growth appears to be independent of the lichen's presence. In the near term, we will examine the potential influence of the lichen on various aspects of the plant's life history particularly establishment. The current plan is focused on observational studies and no manipulative experiments are being planned at this time. In the near future, we are considering potential experiments that may include manipulations in the plant-lichen system.
Research Area: Insect biology; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: Ipomopsis aggregata seed for pilot genetic and genomic screening
Non-Technical Abstract: A small sample of seed will be harvested and grown in the greenhouse at my institution. These seedlings will be used to obtain genomic DNA samples that will allow testing of various sequencing technologies for potential genome assembly and characterization.
Research Area: Climate change; Genetics; Plant biology; Species Interactions

Research Plan: Research Plan Name: The Spatial Ecology of Environmental Change in the Upper Gunnison Basin
Non-Technical Abstract: This project investigates how rapid climate change is reshaping the mountain landscapes of the Upper Gunnison Basin. By combining advanced technology with traditional fieldwork, the research aims to track these environmental shifts in great detail. Using drones and sensors placed in forest gaps, the team will create 3D maps of temperature and humidity to better understand how trees manage water loss. Additionally, the project will build a sustainable network of weather stations to ensure a reliable, long-term record of local climate and snow conditions, preserving crucial historical data. The team will also continue vital ongoing monitoring efforts. This includes generating "Flower Forecasts" to predict wildflower blooms—verified by community "Flower Blitz" events —and using aerial imagery paired with tree-ring analysis to monitor forest health. All collected data feeds into the RMBL Spatial Data Platform, a digital atlas that provides detailed environmental maps to scientists and the public, helping us understand the resilience of these fragile high-altitude ecosystems.
Research Area: Atmospheric Science;Biogeochemistry;Climate change;Climate science;Community ecology;Landscape biology;Long-term research;Meteorology;Modeling;Plant biology;Snow Science
